citations.quote:
Assume the Axiom of Choice. Let $n\ge2$, let $\Omega\subseteq\mathbb R^n$ be a
bounded open set with no boundary regularity assumed, let $1\le p<n$ and
$p^{*}=\frac{np}{n-p}$. For every $1\le q<p^{*}$ the space
$W^{1,p}_0(\Omega)$ is compactly embedded in $L^q(\Omega)$: every sequence
bounded in $W^{1,p}_0(\Omega)$ has a subsequence converging in $L^q(\Omega)$.

Assume the Axiom of Choice ([[def-axiom-of-choice]]). Let $\Omega\subseteq\mathbb R^n$ be open, $n\ge2$, $1\le p<n$ and $p^{*}=\frac{np}{n-p}$. There is $C(n,p)$ with
$$\|u\|_{L^{p^{*}}(\Omega)}\le C(n,p)\|Du\|_{L^p(\Omega)}$$
for every $u\in W^{1,p}_0(\Omega;\mathbb K)$.

Let $(X,\mathcal A,\mu)$ be a measure space, let $p,q\in[1,\infty]$ be
conjugate exponents, and let $f,g$ be measurable real-valued functions.

1. If $1\le p<\infty$ and $q<\infty$ with $f\in\mathcal L^p(\mu)$ and
   $g\in\mathcal L^q(\mu)$, then
   $$\int |fg|\,d\mu\le\|f\|_p\|g\|_q.$$
2. If $p=1$ and $q=\infty$ with $f\in\mathcal L^1(\mu)$ and
   $g\in L^\infty(\mu)$, then
   $$\int |fg|\,d\mu\le\|f\|_1\|g\|_\infty.$$
3. If $p=\infty$ and $q=1$ with $f\in L^\infty(\mu)$ and
   $g\in\mathcal L^1(\mu)$, then
   $$\int |fg|\,d\mu\le\|f\|_\infty\|g\|_1.$$

In every case the right-hand side is finite, so $fg$ is integrable.

Assume Countable Choice. For any open $\Omega\subseteq\mathbb R^n$,
$n\ge1$, any $1\le p\le\infty$ and any
$\mathbb K\in\{\mathbb R,\mathbb C\}$, extension by zero
$$E_0u(x)=u(x)\ \ (x\in\Omega),\qquad E_0u(x)=0\ \ (x\notin\Omega),$$
acted on representatives, sends $W_0^{1,p}(\Omega;\mathbb K)$ linearly into
$W^{1,p}(\mathbb R^n;\mathbb K)$. For every $u\in W_0^{1,p}(\Omega;\mathbb K)$
and every coordinate direction $i$, the class $D_i(E_0u)$ is the zero
extension of the class $D_iu$, and every $L^p$ component norm is preserved:
$$\|E_0u\|_{L^p(\mathbb R^n)}=\|u\|_{L^p(\Omega)},\qquad \|D_i(E_0u)\|_{L^p(\mathbb R^n)}=\|D_iu\|_{L^p(\Omega)},$$
so that $\|E_0u\|_{W^{1,p}(\mathbb R^n)}=\|u\|_{W^{1,p}(\Omega)}$.

Assume Countable Choice. Let $\Omega\subseteq\mathbb R^n$ be open with $n\ge1$ and $\mathbb K\in\{\mathbb R,\mathbb C\}$. Then $C_c^\infty(\Omega;\mathbb K)$ is dense in $L^2(\Omega;\mathbb K)$: for every $f\in L^2(\Omega;\mathbb K)$ and every $\delta>0$ there is $\varphi\in C_c^\infty(\Omega;\mathbb K)$ with $\|\varphi-f\|_{L^2(\Omega)}<\delta$. Consequently $H^1_0(\Omega)$ is dense in $L^2(\Omega)$, and if a class $h\in L^2(\Omega)$ satisfies $(h,v)_{L^2}=0$ for all $v\in H^1_0(\Omega)$, then $h=0$.

Let $n \ge 1$ and **assume the Axiom of Countable Choice**
([[def-countable-choice]]). Then:

1. $\lambda_n$ is sigma-finite ([[def-finite-sigma-finite-and-semifinite-measures]]):
   the cubes $(-k,k]^n$ are Lebesgue measurable with
   $\lambda_n\big((-k,k]^n\big) = (2k)^n < +\infty$, they increase with $k$, and
   their union over $k \in \mathbb{N}$ is $\mathbb{R}^n$.
2. Every bounded subset $E \subseteq \mathbb{R}^n$
   ([[def-metric-bounded-diameter]]) has $\lambda_n^*(E) < +\infty$; a bounded
   Lebesgue measurable set therefore has finite measure, and every compact
   subset of $\mathbb{R}^n$ is Lebesgue measurable of finite measure.

Let $m \in \mathbb{N}$ with $m \ge 1$ and let $a, b \in \mathbb{R}$ with $a < b$.

1. **Fundamental theorem, second part, in $\mathbb{R}^{m}$.** Let
   $f : [a,b] \to \mathbb{R}^{m}$ be differentiable at every point of $[a,b]$ as
   a function on $[a,b]$ ([[def-vector-valued-derivative-and-integral]]), and
   suppose $f' : [a,b] \to \mathbb{R}^{m}$ is integrable. Then
   $$\int_a^b f' \;=\; f(b) - f(a).$$
2. **A bounded derivative gives a Lipschitz function.** Let
   $f : [a,b] \to \mathbb{R}^{m}$ be continuous on $[a,b]$ and differentiable at
   every point of $(a,b)$, and let $M \ge 0$ satisfy
   $\lVert f'(t)\rVert_2 \le M$ for every $t \in (a,b)$. Then
   $$\lVert f(t) - f(s)\rVert_2 \;\le\; M\,|t-s| \qquad \text{for all } s,t \in [a,b],$$
   that is, $f$ is Lipschitz with constant $M$ as a map
   $([a,b], d_{\mathbb{R}}) \to (\mathbb{R}^{m}, d_2)$
   ([[def-lipschitz-holder-contraction]], [[lem-real-line-is-a-metric-space]],
   [[lem-metrics-on-rn]]).

Let $(X,\mathcal A,\mu)$ be a measure space, let $p,q\in[1,\infty]$ be
conjugate exponents, and let $f,g$ be measurable real-valued functions.

1. If $1\le p<\infty$ and $q<\infty$ with $f\in\mathcal L^p(\mu)$ and
   $g\in\mathcal L^q(\mu)$, then
   $$\int |fg|\,d\mu\le\|f\|_p\|g\|_q.$$
2. If $p=1$ and $q=\infty$ with $f\in\mathcal L^1(\mu)$ and
   $g\in L^\infty(\mu)$, then
   $$\int |fg|\,d\mu\le\|f\|_1\|g\|_\infty.$$
3. If $p=\infty$ and $q=1$ with $f\in L^\infty(\mu)$ and
   $g\in\mathcal L^1(\mu)$, then
   $$\int |fg|\,d\mu\le\|f\|_\infty\|g\|_1.$$

In every case the right-hand side is finite, so $fg$ is integrable.

**Assume the Axiom of Countable Choice ([[def-countable-choice]]) and the Axiom of Dependent Choice ([[def-dependent-choice]]).** Let $K$ be a nonempty compact metric space and $\mathcal F\subseteq C(K,\mathbb R)$. Its closure in the supremum metric is compact if and only if $\mathcal F$ is equicontinuous and pointwise bounded.

Assume Countable Choice. Let $\Omega\subseteq\mathbb R^n$ be open with
$n\ge1$, let $k\in\mathbb N_0$, let $1\le p\le\infty$, and let
$\mathbb K\in\{\mathbb R,\mathbb C\}$.

Every $\varphi\in C_c^\infty(\Omega;\mathbb K)$ belongs to
$W^{k,p}(\Omega;\mathbb K)$. Indeed $\varphi$ is bounded with compact support,
hence lies in $L^p(\Omega;\mathbb K)$ for every exponent in range, and each of
its classical partial derivatives is again smooth and compactly supported,
hence lies in $L^p(\Omega;\mathbb K)$ and is the corresponding weak derivative
by [[lem-classical-derivatives-are-weak-derivatives]].

Define the **zero-boundary Sobolev space**
$$W_0^{k,p}(\Omega;\mathbb K):=\overline{C_c^\infty(\Omega;\mathbb K)},$$
the closure taken in the normed space
$(W^{k,p}(\Omega;\mathbb K),\|\cdot\|_{W^{k,p}(\Omega)})$ of
[[def-sobolev-space-wkp-and-its-norm]]. The norm is a genuine norm on classes
by [[lem-sobolev-norm-is-well-defined-and-definite]], so this is the usual
metric closure of a subset of a normed space: $u\in W_0^{k,p}(\Omega;\mathbb K)$
if and only if for every $\delta>0$ there is
$\varphi\in C_c^\infty(\Omega;\mathbb K)$ with
$\|u-\varphi\|_{W^{k,p}(\Omega)}<\delta$. Write
$H_0^k(\Omega):=W_0^{k,2}(\Omega;\mathbb K)$ when the scalar field is fixed by
context.

Three warnings are part of the definition. First, this is a closure of
almost-everywhere classes, and all its equalities are equalities of Sobolev
classes. Second, no pointwise boundary values and no trace characterization
are asserted: a description of $W_0^{k,p}$ by vanishing boundary data belongs
to the later trace theory and is not used here. Third, the closure is defined
for every $1\le p\le\infty$, but for $p=\infty$ it is not claimed that every
compactly supported $W^{k,\infty}(\Omega)$ function lies in $W_0^{k,\infty}(\Omega)$;
the definition merely names the closure of the test functions.

Assume Countable Choice. Let $\Omega\subseteq\mathbb R^n$ be open with
$n\ge1$, $k\in\mathbb N_0$, $1\le p\le\infty$, and
$\mathbb K\in\{\mathbb R,\mathbb C\}$. Write
$$\mathcal A_k=\{\alpha\in\mathbb N_0^n:|\alpha|\le k\}.$$
This is a finite nonempty set: every coordinate of such an $\alpha$ lies in
$\{0,\ldots,k\}$, and it contains the zero multi-index.

The real and complex $L^p$ classes use the conventions in
[[def-l-p-space-as-a-quotient-by-null-functions]] and
[[def-complex-lp-and-euclidean-test-function-conventions]]. Their quotient
norm values are supplied by
[[thm-the-l-p-norm-descends-to-the-quotient-and-makes-l-p-a-normed-space]]
for real scalars and
[[thm-complex-holder-minkowski-and-the-quotient-norm]] for complex scalars.

Define $W^{k,p}(\Omega;\mathbb K)$ to be the set of classes
$u\in L^p(\Omega;\mathbb K)$ such that, for every $\alpha\in\mathcal A_k$,
there is an $L^p(\Omega;\mathbb K)$ class with a locally integrable
representative $v_\alpha$ satisfying
$$\int_\Omega u\,D^\alpha\varphi\,dx =(-1)^{|\alpha|}\int_\Omega v_\alpha\varphi\,dx \qquad\text{for every }\varphi\in C_c^\infty(\Omega).$$
Here the weak derivative is the one in
[[def-weak-derivative-of-a-locally-integrable-function]]. Under
[[def-countable-choice]], local integrability of $L^p$ representatives and
invariance under null-set changes follow from
[[lem-weak-derivative-is-independent-of-lp-representatives]], while
[[lem-weak-derivatives-are-unique-almost-everywhere]] gives uniqueness of each
locally integrable derivative class. Thus this condition is a condition on the
$L^p$ class $u$, and each resulting derivative determines one $L^p$ class,
denoted $D^\alpha u$. The test pairing is bilinear, without conjugation.

For the zero multi-index, set $D^0u=u$. Since $\mathcal A_0=\{0\}$,
$$W^{0,p}(\Omega;\mathbb K)=L^p(\Omega;\mathbb K).$$
The Sobolev norm expression is
$$\|u\|_{W^{k,p}(\Omega)}= \begin{cases} \left(\displaystyle\sum_{\alpha\in\mathcal A_k} \|D^\alpha u\|_{L^p(\Omega)}^p\right)^{1/p},&1\le p<\infty,\\[1ex] \displaystyle\max_{\alpha\in\mathcal A_k} \|D^\alpha u\|_{L^\infty(\Omega)},&p=\infty. \end{cases}$$
The formula is finite because each derivative class belongs to $L^p$ and
$\mathcal A_k$ is finite; at $k=0$ it reduces to the $L^p$ norm expression.
The finite maximum is defined because $\mathcal A_k$ is nonempty. The norm
axioms for this expression are a separate assertion from this definition.

For open $U\subseteq\Omega$ with $\overline U$ compact and contained in
$\Omega$, the notation $W^{k,p}_{\mathrm{loc}}(\Omega;\mathbb K)$ means that
the restriction of the class belongs to $W^{k,p}(U;\mathbb K)$ for every such
$U$.

If $\Omega=\varnothing$, the $L^p$ space and every $W^{k,p}$ space contain
only the zero class, and the displayed norm expression is zero.

The **Axiom of Choice** (AC) is the following statement.

> Every family of nonempty sets has a choice function
> ([[def-choice-function]]).

Written out: for every set $\mathcal{F}$ all of whose members are nonempty,
there exists a function $g$ with domain $\mathcal{F}$ satisfying $g(S) \in S$ for
all $S \in \mathcal{F}$.

An equivalent formulation is that a product of nonempty sets is nonempty: if
$X_i \ne \emptyset$ for every $i \in I$, then $\prod_{i \in I} X_i \ne \emptyset$.
Here $\prod_{i \in I} X_i$ is the set of functions $f$ with domain $I$ such that
$f(i) \in X_i$ for every $i \in I$; when a family of nonempty sets is indexed by
itself, such an $f$ is precisely a choice function for it.

In ZF, assume the Axiom of Choice. Then the Axiom of Countable Choice holds.
Moreover, if $R\subseteq X\times X$ is a serial relation on a nonempty set
$X$ and $a\in X$, there is a sequence $(x_n)_{n\in\mathbb N}$ such that
$x_0=a$ and $x_nRx_{n+1}$ for every $n$. Thus AC supplies the
prescribed-initial-point form of Dependent Choice.

The **Axiom of Countable Choice**, written $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$, is the following
statement.

> For every family $(X_n)_{n \in \mathbb{N}}$ of nonempty sets indexed by
> $\mathbb{N}$ there is a function $f$ with domain $\mathbb{N}$ such that
> $f(n) \in X_n$ for every $n \in \mathbb{N}$.

Equivalently, in the vocabulary of [[def-choice-function]]: every at most
countable family of nonempty sets ([[def-countable]]) has a choice function.

Let $X$ be a set and let $R \subseteq X \times X$ be a binary relation on $X$.
Call $R$ **entire on $X$** when

$$\text{for every } x \in X \text{ there is } y \in X \text{ with } x \mathbin{R} y .$$

The **Axiom of Dependent Choice**, written $\mathrm{DC}$, is the following
statement.

> For every nonempty set $X$, every relation $R$ entire on $X$, and every
> $a \in X$, there is a function $x : \mathbb{N} \to X$ ([[def-function]],
> [[def-natural-numbers]]) with
> $$x_0 = a \qquad \text{and} \qquad x_n \mathbin{R} x_{n+1} \ \text{ for every } n \in \mathbb{N}.$$

Here a sequence in $X$ means a function from $\mathbb{N}$ to $X$, not necessarily
a real-valued sequence. As everywhere in this library $\mathbb{N}$ contains $0$, and the sequence is
indexed from $0$; the term $x_0$ is the prescribed starting point $a$ and every
later term is related to its predecessor.

**What DC adds to what came before.** [[def-choice-function]] and
[[def-axiom-of-choice]] select one element from each member of a family that is
fixed in advance, and [[def-countable-choice]] does the same for a family indexed
by $\mathbb{N}$. In both, the family is given before any selection is made. DC is
the principle needed when the $n$-th set to select from is not known until the
first $n$ selections have been made: here the admissible values of $x_{n+1}$ are
exactly the $R$-successors of $x_n$, so the family being chosen from is built
along the choosing. Thus the displayed recursion is directly an instance of
DC; it is not itself an application of the fixed-family formulation of
countable choice. This observation concerns the input to the two axioms and
makes no claim about a nonimplication between them.

**The starting point may be dropped.** The formally weaker statement obtained by
deleting the clause $x_0 = a$ — for every nonempty $X$ and every entire $R$ there
is a sequence with $x_n \mathbin{R} x_{n+1}$ for all $n$ — is an immediate
consequence of the form above, since $X$ is nonempty and any of its elements may
be taken as $a$. Conversely, assume the start-free form, and fix $X$, $R$ and $a$ as above. Let $P$ be the set of all functions $p:k\to X$ with nonzero $k\in\mathbb N$, $p(0)=a$, and $p(i)\mathbin R p(i+1)$ whenever $i+1<k$. It is a set by Separation inside $\mathcal P(\mathbb N\times X)$ ([[def-power-set]], [[def-cartesian-product]], [[def-axiom-schema-of-separation]]); a natural is the set of its predecessors ([[lem-nat-order-is-membership]]). The singleton path $\{(0,a)\}$ lies in $P$.

On $P$ let $p\mathbin S q$ mean that $q$ extends $p$ by exactly one new last entry. This relation is entire: for one particular $p:k\to X$, write $k=j+1$ ([[lem-nat-nonzero-is-successor]]); an $R$-successor $y$ of $p(j)$ exists, and $q=p\cup\{(k,y)\}$ is the required extension. This is existential instantiation for that path, not a simultaneous choice of successors. Start-free DC now supplies a sequence $(p_n)$ with $p_n\mathbin S p_{n+1}$; its first path need not be the singleton path, but every path in $P$ already starts at $a$.

Their graphs are nested. By induction ([[thm-induction-principle]]), $p_n$ has at least $n+1$ entries: the initial path is nonempty, and every step adds one entry. Hence $x=\bigcup_{n\in\mathbb N}p_n$ is a function with domain $\mathbb N$ and values in $X$. Indeed, nestedness makes all common values agree, every natural index eventually lies in a path, and no path has indices outside $\mathbb N$. Each path starts at $a$, so $x(0)=a$; for any $i$, a sufficiently long path contains both $i$ and $i+1$, giving $x(i)\mathbin R x(i+1)$. Replacement and Union form this union of the sequence of graphs. Thus the start-free and prescribed-start forms are equivalent in ZF. Every use below retains the prescribed-start convention.

**$R$ need not be an order and the terms need not be distinct.** What DC delivers
is a sequence, that is a function $\mathbb{N} \to X$, not a chain in the
order-theoretic sense ([[def-chain]]). The relation may be symmetric, and the
sequence may repeat a value or be constant; all that is asserted is
$x_n \mathbin{R} x_{n+1}$ at every index.

Let $X$ and $Y$ be normed spaces over the same field
$\mathbb K\in\{\mathbb R,\mathbb C\}$, read in the real case from
[[def-norm-and-normed-space]] and in the complex case from
[[def-complex-norm-and-complex-normed-space]], and suppose $X\subseteq Y$
with **continuous inclusion** $J:X\to Y$: there is a real $C\ge0$ with
$\|x\|_Y\le C\|x\|_X$ for every $x\in X$.

One says that $X$ is **compactly embedded** in $Y$, written $X\Subset Y$, when
the inclusion operator $J$ is a compact operator in the sense of
[[def-compact-linear-operator]]: the image under $J$ of every bounded
subset of $X$ ([[def-metric-bounded-diameter]]) has compact closure in $Y$
([[def-metric-compactness]]).

**The sequential form.** Assume the Axiom of Countable Choice
([[def-countable-choice]]) and the Axiom of Dependent Choice
([[def-dependent-choice]]). Then $X\Subset Y$ if and only if every bounded
sequence $(x_j)$ in $X$ has a subsequence $(x_{j_k})$ converging in $Y$:
Indeed, compact closure gives the sequence conclusion by
[[thm-metric-compactness-equivalences]]. Conversely, fix bounded $B\subseteq X$
and let $K=\overline{J(B)}$. For any sequence $(y_j)$ in $K$, Countable
Choice selects $b_j\in B$ with $\|y_j-b_j\|_Y<1/j$ (start at $j=1$);
a convergent subsequence of $(b_j)$ gives one of $(y_j)$ with the same limit,
which belongs to the closed set $K$. Thus $K$ is sequentially compact and
[[thm-metric-compactness-equivalences]] makes it compact. The empty case is
immediate. Both readings
of $X\Subset Y$ are used on this page; the second is the form in which the
compactness theorems below are stated.

Continuity of the inclusion is a separate hypothesis and is never inferred
from compactness: a compact operator is bounded by
[[def-compact-linear-operator]] and [[def-bounded-linear-operator]], but the
definition above fixes the continuity of $J$ in advance. On this page the
continuity of every Sobolev inclusion is verified separately, through the
corresponding Sobolev embedding theorem.

derivations.claim: If $\Omega=\varnothing$, then $W_0^{1,p}(\Omega)=L^2(\Omega)=\{0\}$ and the conclusion holds. Assume $\Omega\ne\varnothing$. First consider $d=1$. Choose a bounded open interval $I=(a,b)$ with $\overline\Omega\subset I$ and let $L=b-a$. By [F4] and the closure definition [F8], each $v\in W_0^{1,p}(\Omega)$ has zero extension $E_0v|_I\in W_0^{1,p}(I)$: choose $\varphi_m\in C_c^\infty(\Omega)$ converging to $v$ in $W^{1,p}$ and extend each by zero into $C_c^\infty(I)$. Countable Choice selects this approximating sequence. For every such smooth extension $\varphi_m$, [F6] gives $|\varphi_m(x)-\varphi_m(y)|\le |x-y|^{1-1/p}\|\varphi_m'\|_{L^p(I)}$ and $\|\varphi_m\|_{L^\infty([a,b])}\le L^{1-1/p}\|\varphi_m'\|_{L^p(I)}$, because it vanishes near both endpoints. Applying the second inequality to differences shows that $(\varphi_m)$ is uniformly Cauchy; its continuous uniform limit $w$ represents $E_0v|_I$ since $\varphi_m\to E_0v$ in $L^p(I)$. For every $\zeta\in C_c^\infty(I)$, uniform convergence and $\varphi_m'\to E_0(v')$ in $L^p(I)$ give $\int_Iw\zeta'=-\int_IE_0(v')\zeta$. Thus $w'=E_0(v')$ weakly and [F4] gives $\|w'\|_{L^p(I)}=\|v'\|_{L^p(\Omega)}$. Passing to the limit in the two displayed inequalities gives the same Hölder and supremum bounds for $w$.

Now let $d\ge2$. Put $s_0=\max(1,2d/(d+2))$ and $s_1=\min(p,d)$. The strict hypothesis gives $s_0<s_1$; set $r=(s_0+s_1)/2$. Then $1<r<p$, $r<d$, and $2<r^*=dr/(d-r)$. By finite-measure Hölder [F3], $W_0^{1,p}(\Omega)\hookrightarrow W_0^{1,r}(\Omega)$ continuously: the function and gradient $L^r$ norms are bounded by their $L^p$ norms, and a $C_c^\infty$ approximating sequence in $W^{1,p}$ also converges in $W^{1,r}$. Therefore [F1] gives compactness of $W_0^{1,p}(\Omega)\to L^2(\Omega)$.

For a bounded sequence $(v_j)$ in $W_0^{1,p}(\Omega)$, the representatives $w_j$ from step 1.1 are uniformly bounded by $L^{1-1/p}\sup_j\|
abla v_j\|_p$ and share the modulus $|w_j(x)-w_j(y)|\le |x-y|^{1-1/p}\sup_j\|
abla v_j\|_p$. Arzelà–Ascoli [F7] gives a uniformly convergent subsequence on the fixed compact interval $[a,b]$. Its restrictions converge in $L^2(\Omega)$ by [F5], proving compactness. For each $v\in W_0^{1,p}(\Omega)$ the same supremum estimate gives $\|v\|_2\le |\Omega|^{1/2}L^{1-1/p}\|
abla v\|_p\le L^{3/2-1/p}\|
abla v\|_p$, proving continuity.

For $v\in W_0^{1,p}(\Omega)$, [F2] and [F3] yield the continuous estimate $\|v\|_2\le |\Omega|^{1/2-1/r^*}\|v\|_{r^*}\le C|\Omega|^{1/r-1/p}\|\nabla v\|_p$, using the Sobolev inequality [F2] with exponent $r$. Thus the inclusion is continuous on the $W_0^{1,p}$ norm. Finally [F5] and the closure definition [F8] give $C_c^\infty(\Omega)\subset W_0^{1,p}(\Omega)$ dense in $L^2(\Omega)$. The preceding arguments prove the complete $d=1$ and $d\ge2$ branches; [F9] then gives the claimed compact embedding in its continuous/sequential sense.

citations.quote:
Let $(\Omega,\mathcal A,\mu)$ be a measure space and $X$ a real or complex
Banach space. A function $f:\Omega\to X$ is **strongly measurable** (or
**Bochner measurable**) if there are measurable $X$-valued simple functions
$s_n$ and a measurable null set $N$ such that

$$\lim_{n\to\infty}\|s_n(\omega)-f(\omega)\|=0$$

for every $\omega\in\Omega\setminus N$.

This is a norm-convergence condition. It is not, by definition, merely Borel
measurability of $f$ or measurability of every scalar function $x^*\circ f$.
Changing $f$ on a null set preserves strong measurability: enlarge $N$ by that
null set and retain the same approximants.

Let $(\Omega,\mathcal A,\mu)$ be a measure space and $X$ a real or complex
Banach space. A strongly measurable function $f:\Omega\to X$ is
**Bochner integrable** if there is a sequence of integrable $X$-valued simple
functions $(s_n)$ such that

$$\lim_{n\to\infty}\int_\Omega\|f-s_n\|\,d\mu=0.$$

For such a sequence define

$$\int_\Omega f\,d\mu:=\lim_{n\to\infty}\int_\Omega s_n\,d\mu.$$

The displayed norm limit exists: the simple integral inequality gives

$$\left\|\int s_n-\int s_m\right\|\leq\int\|s_n-s_m\|\leq\int\|s_n-f\|+\int\|f-s_m\|,$$

so the simple integrals form a Cauchy sequence, and $X$ is complete. The next
theorem proves that the value is independent of the approximating sequence and
characterizes existence by integrability of $\|f\|$.

For $E\in\mathcal A$, write
$\int_Ef\,d\mu:=\int_\Omega\mathbf1_Ef\,d\mu$ whenever this function is
Bochner integrable.

Assume the Axiom of Countable Choice.

Let $1 \le p < \infty$ and $f \in L^p(\mathbb{R}^n)$. Then

$$\|\tau_h f-f\|_p \longrightarrow 0 \qquad(h \to 0).$$

The **Axiom of Countable Choice**, written $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$, is the following
statement.

> For every family $(X_n)_{n \in \mathbb{N}}$ of nonempty sets indexed by
> $\mathbb{N}$ there is a function $f$ with domain $\mathbb{N}$ such that
> $f(n) \in X_n$ for every $n \in \mathbb{N}$.

Equivalently, in the vocabulary of [[def-choice-function]]: every at most
countable family of nonempty sets ([[def-countable]]) has a choice function.

Let $F : \mathbb{R} \to \mathbb{R}$ be nondecreasing and right-continuous, and let
$\mu_F$ be the associated Lebesgue-Stieltjes measure. Then for every Borel set
$E \subseteq \mathbb{R}$,

$$\mu_F(E) = \inf\{\, \mu_F(U) : E \subseteq U,\ U \text{ open} \,\} = \sup\{\, \mu_F(K) : K \subseteq E,\ K \text{ compact} \,\}.$$

If $\mu_F(E) < +\infty$, then equivalently: for every $\varepsilon > 0$ there
are an open set $U$ and a compact set $K$ with

$$K \subseteq E \subseteq U,\qquad \mu_F(U \setminus E) < \varepsilon,\qquad \mu_F(E \setminus K) < \varepsilon.$$

Let $(X,\mathcal A,\mu)$ be a measure space, let $p,q\in[1,\infty]$ be
conjugate exponents, and let $f,g$ be measurable real-valued functions.

1. If $1\le p<\infty$ and $q<\infty$ with $f\in\mathcal L^p(\mu)$ and
   $g\in\mathcal L^q(\mu)$, then
   $$\int |fg|\,d\mu\le\|f\|_p\|g\|_q.$$
2. If $p=1$ and $q=\infty$ with $f\in\mathcal L^1(\mu)$ and
   $g\in L^\infty(\mu)$, then
   $$\int |fg|\,d\mu\le\|f\|_1\|g\|_\infty.$$
3. If $p=\infty$ and $q=1$ with $f\in L^\infty(\mu)$ and
   $g\in\mathcal L^1(\mu)$, then
   $$\int |fg|\,d\mu\le\|f\|_\infty\|g\|_1.$$

In every case the right-hand side is finite, so $fg$ is integrable.

Let $(X,\mathcal A,\mu)$ be a measure space.

1. If $1\le p<\infty$ and $f,g\in\mathcal L^p(\mu)$, then
   $$\|f+g\|_p\le\|f\|_p+\|g\|_p.$$
2. If $f,g\in L^\infty(\mu)$, then
   $$\|f+g\|_\infty\le\|f\|_\infty+\|g\|_\infty.$$

statement.

countable family of nonempty sets ([[def-countable]]) has a choice function.

derivations.claim: Let $s(t)=\sum_{j=1}^m x_j\mathbf1_{E_j}(t)$ be a simple function with disjoint measurable $E_j$. Extend it by zero to $\mathbb R$. By [F2], $\|\mathbf1_{E_j}(\cdot-h)-\mathbf1_{E_j}\|_{L^p(\mathbb R)}\to0$ for each $j$; the triangle inequality and the finite sum show $\|s(\cdot-h)-s\|_{L^p(\mathbb R;X)}\to0$.

For an interval partition $\mathcal P$, let $P_\mathcal P f$ be the average of $f$ on each cell. Jensen's inequality makes $P_\mathcal P$ a contraction on $L^p$. By [F1] and [F3], continuous $X$-valued functions are dense in $L^p(0,T;X)$: approximate a simple function, approximate each of its measurable level sets in measure by a finite union of intervals, and round the finitely many jumps by continuous linear ramps. For continuous $g$, uniform continuity gives $\|P_\mathcal P g-g\|_{L^p}\le T^{1/p}\sup_{|s-t|\le\max|I|}\|g(s)-g(t)\|_X\to0$. For general $f$, contraction yields $\|P_\mathcal P f-f\|_{L^p}\le2\|f-g\|_{L^p}+\|P_\mathcal P g-g\|_{L^p}$; first choose $g$ close, then refine the partition.

Given $\varepsilon>0$, choose a simple $s$ with $\|f-s\|_{L^p(0,T;X)}<\varepsilon/3$ by [F1]. Extend both functions by zero outside $(0,T)$. Translation is an isometry of the whole-line Bochner norm because it preserves Lebesgue measure; step 1.1 therefore gives, for all sufficiently small $h$, $\|f(\cdot-h)-f\|_{L^p(\mathbb R;X)}\le2\|f-s\|_{L^p}+\|s(\cdot-h)-s\|_{L^p}<\varepsilon$. Restriction to compact subintervals proves the translation assertion.

Let $\rho_\delta$ be a nonnegative smooth scalar function supported in $[-\delta,\delta]$ with integral one. Minkowski [F4] gives on any compact subinterval $K\subset(0,T)$ $$\|\rho_\delta*f-f\|_{L^p(K;X)} \le\int\rho_\delta(s)\|f(\cdot-s)-f\|_{L^p(K;X)}\,ds.$$ The translation modulus from step 2.1 tends to zero uniformly for $|s|\le\delta$; hence the right-hand side tends to zero as $\delta\downarrow0$. This proves the mollification claim.
Steps 1.2, 2.1, and 3.1 prove convergence of interval averages, translation continuity, and convergence of time mollifiers, respectively.

citations.quote: Assume the ultrafilter lemma, DC and HB ([[def-ultrafilter-extension-principle]], [[def-dependent-choice]], [[def-hahn-banach-extension-principle-relative]]). Let $\Omega\subseteq\mathbb R^n$ be open, $n\ge1$, and let $1<p<\infty$. Then the real Banach space $W^{1,p}(\Omega)$ of [[def-sobolev-space-wkp-and-its-norm]] is reflexive ([[def-reflexive-banach-space]]).

Assume Countable Choice. Let $\Omega\subseteq\mathbb R^n$ be open with
$n\ge1$, let $k\in\mathbb N_0$, let $1\le p\le\infty$, and let
$\mathbb K\in\{\mathbb R,\mathbb C\}$.

Every $\varphi\in C_c^\infty(\Omega;\mathbb K)$ belongs to
$W^{k,p}(\Omega;\mathbb K)$. Indeed $\varphi$ is bounded with compact support,
hence lies in $L^p(\Omega;\mathbb K)$ for every exponent in range, and each of
its classical partial derivatives is again smooth and compactly supported,
hence lies in $L^p(\Omega;\mathbb K)$ and is the corresponding weak derivative
by [[lem-classical-derivatives-are-weak-derivatives]].

Define the **zero-boundary Sobolev space**
$$W_0^{k,p}(\Omega;\mathbb K):=\overline{C_c^\infty(\Omega;\mathbb K)},$$
the closure taken in the normed space
$(W^{k,p}(\Omega;\mathbb K),\|\cdot\|_{W^{k,p}(\Omega)})$ of
[[def-sobolev-space-wkp-and-its-norm]]. The norm is a genuine norm on classes
by [[lem-sobolev-norm-is-well-defined-and-definite]], so this is the usual
metric closure of a subset of a normed space: $u\in W_0^{k,p}(\Omega;\mathbb K)$
if and only if for every $\delta>0$ there is
$\varphi\in C_c^\infty(\Omega;\mathbb K)$ with
$\|u-\varphi\|_{W^{k,p}(\Omega)}<\delta$. Write
$H_0^k(\Omega):=W_0^{k,2}(\Omega;\mathbb K)$ when the scalar field is fixed by
context.

Three warnings are part of the definition. First, this is a closure of
almost-everywhere classes, and all its equalities are equalities of Sobolev
classes. Second, no pointwise boundary values and no trace characterization
are asserted: a description of $W_0^{k,p}$ by vanishing boundary data belongs
to the later trace theory and is not used here. Third, the closure is defined
for every $1\le p\le\infty$, but for $p=\infty$ it is not claimed that every
compactly supported $W^{k,\infty}(\Omega)$ function lies in $W_0^{k,\infty}(\Omega)$;
the definition merely names the closure of the test functions.

Assume Countable Choice. Let $\Omega\subseteq\mathbb R^n$ be open with
$n\ge1$, $k\in\mathbb N_0$, $1\le p\le\infty$, and
$\mathbb K\in\{\mathbb R,\mathbb C\}$. Write
$$\mathcal A_k=\{\alpha\in\mathbb N_0^n:|\alpha|\le k\}.$$
This is a finite nonempty set: every coordinate of such an $\alpha$ lies in
$\{0,\ldots,k\}$, and it contains the zero multi-index.

The real and complex $L^p$ classes use the conventions in
[[def-l-p-space-as-a-quotient-by-null-functions]] and
[[def-complex-lp-and-euclidean-test-function-conventions]]. Their quotient
norm values are supplied by
[[thm-the-l-p-norm-descends-to-the-quotient-and-makes-l-p-a-normed-space]]
for real scalars and
[[thm-complex-holder-minkowski-and-the-quotient-norm]] for complex scalars.

Define $W^{k,p}(\Omega;\mathbb K)$ to be the set of classes
$u\in L^p(\Omega;\mathbb K)$ such that, for every $\alpha\in\mathcal A_k$,
there is an $L^p(\Omega;\mathbb K)$ class with a locally integrable
representative $v_\alpha$ satisfying
$$\int_\Omega u\,D^\alpha\varphi\,dx =(-1)^{|\alpha|}\int_\Omega v_\alpha\varphi\,dx \qquad\text{for every }\varphi\in C_c^\infty(\Omega).$$
Here the weak derivative is the one in
[[def-weak-derivative-of-a-locally-integrable-function]]. Under
[[def-countable-choice]], local integrability of $L^p$ representatives and
invariance under null-set changes follow from
[[lem-weak-derivative-is-independent-of-lp-representatives]], while
[[lem-weak-derivatives-are-unique-almost-everywhere]] gives uniqueness of each
locally integrable derivative class. Thus this condition is a condition on the
$L^p$ class $u$, and each resulting derivative determines one $L^p$ class,
denoted $D^\alpha u$. The test pairing is bilinear, without conjugation.

For the zero multi-index, set $D^0u=u$. Since $\mathcal A_0=\{0\}$,
$$W^{0,p}(\Omega;\mathbb K)=L^p(\Omega;\mathbb K).$$
The Sobolev norm expression is
$$\|u\|_{W^{k,p}(\Omega)}= \begin{cases} \left(\displaystyle\sum_{\alpha\in\mathcal A_k} \|D^\alpha u\|_{L^p(\Omega)}^p\right)^{1/p},&1\le p<\infty,\\[1ex] \displaystyle\max_{\alpha\in\mathcal A_k} \|D^\alpha u\|_{L^\infty(\Omega)},&p=\infty. \end{cases}$$
The formula is finite because each derivative class belongs to $L^p$ and
$\mathcal A_k$ is finite; at $k=0$ it reduces to the $L^p$ norm expression.
The finite maximum is defined because $\mathcal A_k$ is nonempty. The norm
axioms for this expression are a separate assertion from this definition.

For open $U\subseteq\Omega$ with $\overline U$ compact and contained in
$\Omega$, the notation $W^{k,p}_{\mathrm{loc}}(\Omega;\mathbb K)$ means that
the restriction of the class belongs to $W^{k,p}(U;\mathbb K)$ for every such
$U$.

If $\Omega=\varnothing$, the $L^p$ space and every $W^{k,p}$ space contain
only the zero class, and the displayed norm expression is zero.

**Assume HB.**  If $X$ is a real or complex reflexive Banach space and
$Y\subseteq X$ is a closed linear subspace with the restricted norm, then $Y$
is reflexive.

Assume the Axiom of Countable Choice.

Let $1 \le p < \infty$. The finite linear combinations of indicator functions of
half-open boxes with rational endpoints and rational coefficients form a
countable dense subset of $L^p(\mathbb{R}^n)$.

Assume Countable Choice. Let $\Omega\subseteq\mathbb R^n$ be open with
$n\ge1$, $k\in\mathbb N_0$, $1\le p\le\infty$, and

This is a finite nonempty set: every coordinate of such an $\alpha$ lies in

For open $U\subseteq\Omega$ with $\overline U$ compact and contained in

If $\Omega=\varnothing$, the $L^p$ space and every $W^{k,p}$ space contain

A topological space $X$ is **separable** if some at most countable subset $D\subseteq X$ is dense in $X$ ([[def-dense-top]], [[def-countable]]). Equivalently, every nonempty open subset of $X$ meets $D$.

The **Axiom of Choice** (AC) is the following statement.

> Every family of nonempty sets has a choice function
> ([[def-choice-function]]).

Written out: for every set $\mathcal{F}$ all of whose members are nonempty,
there exists a function $g$ with domain $\mathcal{F}$ satisfying $g(S) \in S$ for
all $S \in \mathcal{F}$.

An equivalent formulation is that a product of nonempty sets is nonempty: if
$X_i \ne \emptyset$ for every $i \in I$, then $\prod_{i \in I} X_i \ne \emptyset$.
Here $\prod_{i \in I} X_i$ is the set of functions $f$ with domain $I$ such that
$f(i) \in X_i$ for every $i \in I$; when a family of nonempty sets is indexed by
itself, such an $f$ is precisely a choice function for it.

In ZF, assume the Axiom of Choice. Then the Axiom of Countable Choice holds.
Moreover, if $R\subseteq X\times X$ is a serial relation on a nonempty set
$X$ and $a\in X$, there is a sequence $(x_n)_{n\in\mathbb N}$ such that
$x_0=a$ and $x_nRx_{n+1}$ for every $n$. Thus AC supplies the
prescribed-initial-point form of Dependent Choice.

The **ultrafilter extension principle** says that every filter on a set is contained in an ultrafilter on that set ([[def-ultrafilter]]).

It is also called the **ultrafilter lemma** and is equivalent over ZF to the Boolean prime ideal theorem, abbreviated BPI. Items below write **assume UL/BPI** precisely when they use this extension principle; they do not thereby assume the full axiom of choice.

Let $X$ be a set and let $R \subseteq X \times X$ be a binary relation on $X$.
Call $R$ **entire on $X$** when

$$\text{for every } x \in X \text{ there is } y \in X \text{ with } x \mathbin{R} y .$$

The **Axiom of Dependent Choice**, written $\mathrm{DC}$, is the following
statement.

> For every nonempty set $X$, every relation $R$ entire on $X$, and every
> $a \in X$, there is a function $x : \mathbb{N} \to X$ ([[def-function]],
> [[def-natural-numbers]]) with
> $$x_0 = a \qquad \text{and} \qquad x_n \mathbin{R} x_{n+1} \ \text{ for every } n \in \mathbb{N}.$$

Here a sequence in $X$ means a function from $\mathbb{N}$ to $X$, not necessarily
a real-valued sequence. As everywhere in this library $\mathbb{N}$ contains $0$, and the sequence is
indexed from $0$; the term $x_0$ is the prescribed starting point $a$ and every
later term is related to its predecessor.

**What DC adds to what came before.** [[def-choice-function]] and
[[def-axiom-of-choice]] select one element from each member of a family that is
fixed in advance, and [[def-countable-choice]] does the same for a family indexed
by $\mathbb{N}$. In both, the family is given before any selection is made. DC is
the principle needed when the $n$-th set to select from is not known until the
first $n$ selections have been made: here the admissible values of $x_{n+1}$ are
exactly the $R$-successors of $x_n$, so the family being chosen from is built
along the choosing. Thus the displayed recursion is directly an instance of
DC; it is not itself an application of the fixed-family formulation of
countable choice. This observation concerns the input to the two axioms and
makes no claim about a nonimplication between them.

**The starting point may be dropped.** The formally weaker statement obtained by
deleting the clause $x_0 = a$ — for every nonempty $X$ and every entire $R$ there
is a sequence with $x_n \mathbin{R} x_{n+1}$ for all $n$ — is an immediate
consequence of the form above, since $X$ is nonempty and any of its elements may
be taken as $a$. Conversely, assume the start-free form, and fix $X$, $R$ and $a$ as above. Let $P$ be the set of all functions $p:k\to X$ with nonzero $k\in\mathbb N$, $p(0)=a$, and $p(i)\mathbin R p(i+1)$ whenever $i+1<k$. It is a set by Separation inside $\mathcal P(\mathbb N\times X)$ ([[def-power-set]], [[def-cartesian-product]], [[def-axiom-schema-of-separation]]); a natural is the set of its predecessors ([[lem-nat-order-is-membership]]). The singleton path $\{(0,a)\}$ lies in $P$.

On $P$ let $p\mathbin S q$ mean that $q$ extends $p$ by exactly one new last entry. This relation is entire: for one particular $p:k\to X$, write $k=j+1$ ([[lem-nat-nonzero-is-successor]]); an $R$-successor $y$ of $p(j)$ exists, and $q=p\cup\{(k,y)\}$ is the required extension. This is existential instantiation for that path, not a simultaneous choice of successors. Start-free DC now supplies a sequence $(p_n)$ with $p_n\mathbin S p_{n+1}$; its first path need not be the singleton path, but every path in $P$ already starts at $a$.

Their graphs are nested. By induction ([[thm-induction-principle]]), $p_n$ has at least $n+1$ entries: the initial path is nonempty, and every step adds one entry. Hence $x=\bigcup_{n\in\mathbb N}p_n$ is a function with domain $\mathbb N$ and values in $X$. Indeed, nestedness makes all common values agree, every natural index eventually lies in a path, and no path has indices outside $\mathbb N$. Each path starts at $a$, so $x(0)=a$; for any $i$, a sufficiently long path contains both $i$ and $i+1$, giving $x(i)\mathbin R x(i+1)$. Replacement and Union form this union of the sequence of graphs. Thus the start-free and prescribed-start forms are equivalent in ZF. Every use below retains the prescribed-start convention.

**$R$ need not be an order and the terms need not be distinct.** What DC delivers
is a sequence, that is a function $\mathbb{N} \to X$, not a chain in the
order-theoretic sense ([[def-chain]]). The relation may be symmetric, and the
sequence may repeat a value or be constant; all that is asserted is
$x_n \mathbin{R} x_{n+1}$ at every index.

Work over ZF. The **real dominated-extension principle**, denoted **HB**, is the following assertion:

For every real vector space $X$, every sublinear functional $p:X\to\mathbb R$ in the sense of [[def-sublinear-functional]], every real linear subspace $M\le X$ in the sense of [[def-linear-subspace]], and every real linear functional $g:M\to\mathbb R$ in the sense of [[def-algebraic-dual-and-linear-functional]],
$$\bigl(\forall m\in M,\ g(m)\le p(m)\bigr)\ \Longrightarrow\ \exists F:X\to\mathbb R\ \bigl(F\text{ is real linear},\ F|_M=g,\ \forall x\in X,\ F(x)\le p(x)\bigr).$$

This names an additional principle; it does not assert a proof of HB in ZF. Subsequent results explicitly state when they assume HB. Neither topology nor completeness is part of this assertion. The subspace may be $\{0\}$ or all of $X$. Sublinearity at scalar zero gives $p(0)=0$, and a linear functional has value zero at zero.

every at most countable family of nonempty sets has a choice function

derivations.claim: If $\Omega=\varnothing$, then $W_0^{1,p}(\Omega)=\{0\}$, which is a separable reflexive real Banach space, and the claim holds. Assume $\Omega\ne\varnothing$. By [F2], $W_0^{1,p}(\Omega)$ is a closed linear subspace of $W^{1,p}(\Omega)$. The latter is reflexive by [F1], and [F3] therefore makes $W_0^{1,p}(\Omega)$ reflexive.

Extend each $g\in L^p(\Omega)$ by zero to $\mathbb R^d$. This is an isometry into $L^p(\mathbb R^d)$ because $\Omega$ is measurable, and restriction of the rational box-step dense family in [F4] shows that $L^p(\Omega)$ is separable. Finite products of this countable dense family are countable and dense in $Y:=L^p(\Omega)^{d+1}$. The map $u\mapsto(u,\partial_1u,\ldots,\partial_du)$ embeds $W^{1,p}(\Omega)$ isometrically into $Y$ by [F5]. Thus $W_0^{1,p}(\Omega)$, viewed as a subspace of $Y$, has a countable base obtained by intersecting it with the countable rational-ball base of $Y$.

Choose one point from each nonempty member of that countable relative base, using Countable Choice [A1]. The chosen countable set meets every nonempty relatively open set, so it is dense in $W_0^{1,p}(\Omega)$. Together with step 1.1 this proves both assertions.

Let $V$ be a normed space over $\mathbb K\in\{\mathbb R,\mathbb C\}$, in the sense of [[def-norm-and-normed-space]] for $\mathbb R$ and [[def-complex-norm-and-complex-normed-space]] for $\mathbb C$, with
induced metric $d(x,y)=\|x-y\|$ (in the complex case supplied by [[lem-complex-norm-realification-is-a-real-norm]]). Then $V$ is a **Banach space** when this
metric space is complete in the sense of [[def-complete-metric-space]].

Equivalently: every Cauchy sequence in $V$ for the norm metric converges to a
point of $V$.

Let $(\Omega,\mathcal A,\mu)$ be a measure space and $X$ a real or complex
Banach space. A function $f:\Omega\to X$ is **strongly measurable** (or
**Bochner measurable**) if there are measurable $X$-valued simple functions
$s_n$ and a measurable null set $N$ such that

$$\lim_{n\to\infty}\|s_n(\omega)-f(\omega)\|=0$$

for every $\omega\in\Omega\setminus N$.

This is a norm-convergence condition. It is not, by definition, merely Borel
measurability of $f$ or measurability of every scalar function $x^*\circ f$.
Changing $f$ on a null set preserves strong measurability: enlarge $N$ by that
null set and retain the same approximants.

Let $(\Omega,\mathcal A,\mu)$ be a measure space and $X$ a real or complex
Banach space. A strongly measurable function $f:\Omega\to X$ is
**Bochner integrable** if there is a sequence of integrable $X$-valued simple
functions $(s_n)$ such that

$$\lim_{n\to\infty}\int_\Omega\|f-s_n\|\,d\mu=0.$$

For such a sequence define

$$\int_\Omega f\,d\mu:=\lim_{n\to\infty}\int_\Omega s_n\,d\mu.$$

The displayed norm limit exists: the simple integral inequality gives

$$\left\|\int s_n-\int s_m\right\|\leq\int\|s_n-s_m\|\leq\int\|s_n-f\|+\int\|f-s_m\|,$$

so the simple integrals form a Cauchy sequence, and $X$ is complete. The next
theorem proves that the value is independent of the approximating sequence and
characterizes existence by integrability of $\|f\|$.

For $E\in\mathcal A$, write
$\int_Ef\,d\mu:=\int_\Omega\mathbf1_Ef\,d\mu$ whenever this function is
Bochner integrable.

Let $(X,\mathcal A,\mu)$ be a measure space, let $p,q\in[1,\infty]$ be
conjugate exponents, and let $f,g$ be measurable real-valued functions.

1. If $1\le p<\infty$ and $q<\infty$ with $f\in\mathcal L^p(\mu)$ and
   $g\in\mathcal L^q(\mu)$, then
   $$\int |fg|\,d\mu\le\|f\|_p\|g\|_q.$$
2. If $p=1$ and $q=\infty$ with $f\in\mathcal L^1(\mu)$ and
   $g\in L^\infty(\mu)$, then
   $$\int |fg|\,d\mu\le\|f\|_1\|g\|_\infty.$$
3. If $p=\infty$ and $q=1$ with $f\in L^\infty(\mu)$ and
   $g\in\mathcal L^1(\mu)$, then
   $$\int |fg|\,d\mu\le\|f\|_\infty\|g\|_1.$$

In every case the right-hand side is finite, so $fg$ is integrable.

Let $(X,\mathcal A,\mu)$ be a measure space.

1. If $1\le p<\infty$ and $f,g\in\mathcal L^p(\mu)$, then
   $$\|f+g\|_p\le\|f\|_p+\|g\|_p.$$
2. If $f,g\in L^\infty(\mu)$, then
   $$\|f+g\|_\infty\le\|f\|_\infty+\|g\|_\infty.$$

Let $(X,\mathcal A,\mu)$ be an arbitrary measure space. Let $f_n:X\to[0,+\infty]$ be measurable for every $n\ge1$, with $0\le f_1\le f_2\le\cdots$, and suppose $f_n(x)\uparrow f(x)$ for every $x\in X$. Then
$$\int f_n\,d\mu\uparrow\int f\,d\mu.$$

Let $(X,\mathcal A,\mu)$ be an arbitrary measure space. All functions below have domain $X$. Let $f$ and $(f_n)$ be measurable complex-valued functions such that
$f_n\to f$ almost everywhere and $|f_n|\le g$ almost everywhere for a single
nonnegative measurable function $g$ with $\int g\,d\mu<+\infty$. Then
$f\in L^1(\mu)$,
$$\int|f_n-f|\,d\mu\longrightarrow0,$$
and hence
$$\int f_n\,d\mu\longrightarrow\int f\,d\mu.$$

Let $\mu$ be a measure and let $(E_k)_{k\in\mathbb N}$ be measurable. Then

$$\mu\left(\bigcup_{k\in\mathbb N}E_k\right)\le\sum_{k=0}^{\infty}\mu(E_k).$$

For every $m\in\mathbb N$ one also has

$$\mu\left(\bigcup_{k<m}E_k\right)\le\sum_{k<m}\mu(E_k),$$

including $m=0$, where both sides are $0$.

The **Axiom of Countable Choice**, written $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$, is the following
statement.

> For every family $(X_n)_{n \in \mathbb{N}}$ of nonempty sets indexed by
> $\mathbb{N}$ there is a function $f$ with domain $\mathbb{N}$ such that
> $f(n) \in X_n$ for every $n \in \mathbb{N}$.

Equivalently, in the vocabulary of [[def-choice-function]]: every at most
countable family of nonempty sets ([[def-countable]]) has a choice function.

derivations.claim: By [A1], choose a subsequence $(f_k)$ of the Cauchy sequence such that $\|f_{k+1}-f_k\|_{L^p(X)}\le2^{-k}$ for each $k\ge1$. Put $g_N(t)=\sum_{k=1}^N\|f_{k+1}(t)-f_k(t)\|_X$. Minkowski [F3] gives $\|g_N\|_{L^p}\le\sum_{k=1}^N2^{-k}\le1$. Monotone convergence [F4] therefore gives $g(t)=\sum_{k\ge1}\|f_{k+1}(t)-f_k(t)\|_X\in L^p(0,T)$; in particular $g(t)<\infty$ for almost every $t$.

At every such $t$, the series of successive differences is absolutely convergent in $X$, so [F1] gives a pointwise limit $f(t)\in X$. Define $f=0$ on the exceptional null set. For each $k$, take simple functions $s_{k,m}$ converging almost everywhere to the strongly measurable $f_k$. Dominated convergence [F5] applied to the indicators of $\{t:\|s_{k,m}(t)-f_k(t)\|_X>2^{-k}\}$ lets us choose $m_k$ so this set has measure at most $2^{-k}$. Countable subadditivity [F5] shows that almost every $t$ lies in only finitely many of these bad sets. Therefore the simple functions $s_{k,m_k}$ converge almost everywhere to $f$, proving that $f$ is strongly measurable by [F2]. For every $N$, $\|f(t)-f_N(t)\|_X\le\sum_{k\ge N}\|f_{k+1}(t)-f_k(t)\|_X$ almost everywhere; the right side tends to zero pointwise and is bounded by $g\in L^p$, so [F5] and dominated convergence imply $\|f-f_N\|_{L^p(X)}\le\sum_{k\ge N}2^{-k}\to0$. Hence $f\in L^p(0,T;X)$ and $f_N\to f$ in that norm.

The original sequence is Cauchy and has the subsequence $f_N\to f$; given $\varepsilon>0$, choose $N$ with $\|f_N-f\|_{L^p(X)}<\varepsilon/2$ and then take the original index sufficiently far out that its distance to $f_N$ is below $\varepsilon/2$. The triangle inequality proves convergence of the entire sequence to $f$, so $L^p(0,T;X)$ is complete.

Let $V$ be a separable reflexive real Banach space, let $H$ be a real Hilbert
space, and let $i:V\to H$ be an injective continuous linear map with dense
range. Let $V^*$ be the continuous real dual of $V$ and write
$\langle\cdot,\cdot\rangle_{V^*,V}$ for its pairing with $V$. The canonical
map $J:H\to V^*$ is
$$J h(v)=(h,iv)_H\qquad(h\in H,\ v\in V).$$
It is continuous because $|Jh(v)|\le \|h\|_H\|i\|\|v\|_V$, and injective
because $i(V)$ is dense in $H$. A triple $(V,H,J)$ with these properties is
a **Banach evolution triple**. If $V$ is Hilbert, this is the real evolution
triple of [[def-parabolic-evolution-triple-and-energy-space]].

For $1<p<\infty$, $L^p(0,T;V)$ denotes the Bochner space of strongly
measurable $V$-valued functions with finite $p$th power norm, and
$p'=p/(p-1)$. For $u\in L^p(0,T;V)$ and $g\in L^{p'}(0,T;V^*)$, say
$g=u'$ in the distributional time sense if
$$\int_0^T (iu(t),iv)_H\,\phi'(t)\,dt =-\int_0^T\langle g(t),v\rangle_{V^*,V}\,\phi(t)\,dt$$
for every $v\in V$ and $\phi\in C_c^\infty(0,T)$. Define
$$W_p(0,T;V)=\{u\in L^p(0,T;V):u'\in L^{p'}(0,T;V^*)\}.$$
This definition assigns no endpoint values; a separate chain-rule theorem is
needed before evaluating a function in this space at an endpoint.

Assume Countable Choice.

Let $X$ be a real Banach space, $0<T<\infty$, and $1\le p<\infty$. For
$f\in L^p(0,T;X)$, translations are continuous in $L^p$ on every compact
subinterval of $(0,T)$. Convolution with a scalar smooth approximate identity
therefore converges to $f$ in $L^p$ on such subintervals. If $\mathcal P_k$
are interval partitions of $[0,T]$ with maximum cell length tending to zero,
the piecewise-constant interval averages of $f$ converge to $f$ in
$L^p(0,T;X)$.

Let $V$ be a separable reflexive real Banach space, let $H$ be a real Hilbert
space, and let $i:V\to H$ be an injective continuous linear map with dense
range. Let $V^*$ be the continuous real dual of $V$ and write
$\langle\cdot,\cdot\rangle_{V^*,V}$ for its pairing with $V$. The canonical
map $J:H\to V^*$ is
$$J h(v)=(h,iv)_H\qquad(h\in H,\ v\in V).$$
It is continuous because $|Jh(v)|\le \|h\|_H\|i\|\|v\|_V$, and injective
because $i(V)$ is dense in $H$. A triple $(V,H,J)$ with these properties is
a **Banach evolution triple**. If $V$ is Hilbert, this is the real evolution
triple of [[def-parabolic-evolution-triple-and-energy-space]].

For $1<p<\infty$, $L^p(0,T;V)$ denotes the Bochner space of strongly
measurable $V$-valued functions with finite $p$th power norm, and
$p'=p/(p-1)$. For $u\in L^p(0,T;V)$ and $g\in L^{p'}(0,T;V^*)$, say
$g=u'$ in the distributional time sense if
$$\int_0^T (iu(t),iv)_H\,\phi'(t)\,dt =-\int_0^T\langle g(t),v\rangle_{V^*,V}\,\phi(t)\,dt$$
for every $v\in V$ and $\phi\in C_c^\infty(0,T)$. Define
$$W_p(0,T;V)=\{u\in L^p(0,T;V):u'\in L^{p'}(0,T;V^*)\}.$$
This definition assigns no endpoint values; a separate chain-rule theorem is
needed before evaluating a function in this space at an endpoint.

A **real Hilbert space** is a real inner-product space $H$ ([[def-real-and-complex-inner-product-space]]) whose induced-length metric is complete in the sense of [[def-complete-metric-space]]: every Cauchy sequence in $H$ for the norm $\|v\|=\sqrt{\langle v,v\rangle}$ ([[cor-inner-product-induces-a-norm]]) converges to a point of $H$. A **complex Hilbert space** is a complex inner-product space with the same completeness property, so that a Hilbert space is exactly a real or complex inner-product space that is a Banach space for its induced norm ([[def-banach-space]]).

**The completion convention is the Cauchy-sequence one.**
[[def-banach-space]] defines completeness by convergence of Cauchy sequences, and this page keeps that convention throughout. It is weaker than $\sigma$-completeness — the assertion that every decreasing sequence of nonempty closed subsets with diameters tending to zero has a nonempty intersection. The two agree in ZFC, but Blackadar, Farah and Karagila note that the closest-point theorem on a $\sigma$-complete inner-product space is provable in ZF, whereas the Cauchy-complete form used below consumes the Axiom of Countable Choice; nothing here silently imports the stronger notion.

Let $(X,\mathcal A,\mu)$ be a measure space, let $p,q\in[1,\infty]$ be
conjugate exponents, and let $f,g$ be measurable real-valued functions.

1. If $1\le p<\infty$ and $q<\infty$ with $f\in\mathcal L^p(\mu)$ and
   $g\in\mathcal L^q(\mu)$, then
   $$\int |fg|\,d\mu\le\|f\|_p\|g\|_q.$$
2. If $p=1$ and $q=\infty$ with $f\in\mathcal L^1(\mu)$ and
   $g\in L^\infty(\mu)$, then
   $$\int |fg|\,d\mu\le\|f\|_1\|g\|_\infty.$$
3. If $p=\infty$ and $q=1$ with $f\in L^\infty(\mu)$ and
   $g\in\mathcal L^1(\mu)$, then
   $$\int |fg|\,d\mu\le\|f\|_\infty\|g\|_1.$$

In every case the right-hand side is finite, so $fg$ is integrable.

Assume the Axiom of Choice for the ACL and absolutely-continuous
fundamental-theorem interfaces. Let $I\subseteq\mathbb R$ be a nonempty open
interval, let $1\le p\le\infty$, let $\mathbb K\in\{\mathbb R,\mathbb C\}$,
and let $u\in W^{1,p}(I;\mathbb K)$, with weak derivative class $Du$. Then
there is exactly one continuous representative $u^*$ of the class of $u$ on
$I$ that is locally absolutely continuous, that is, absolutely continuous on
every compact interval contained in $I$, and satisfies
$$u^*(x)-u^*(y)=\int_y^xDu(t)\,dt\qquad\text{for every }x,y\in I,$$
where for $x<y$ the right-hand side denotes $-\int_x^yDu$, equivalently
$u^*(y)-u^*(x)=\int_x^yDu$ whenever $x\le y$.

If $I=(a,b)$ has finite endpoints, then $Du\in L^1(a,b)$, the representative
$u^*$ extends uniquely to an absolutely continuous function on $[a,b]$, and
the extension satisfies
$$u^*(x)=u^*(a)+\int_a^xDu(t)\,dt\qquad\text{for every }x\in[a,b].$$

The scalar field is arbitrary, $p=1$ and $p=\infty$ are included, and the
one-dimensional interval may be bounded or unbounded. The Axiom of Choice is
used only through the Countable-Choice and Dependent-Choice hypotheses of the
cited characterisation, fundamental-theorem and completeness interfaces.

Let $(X,\mathcal A,\mu)$ be a measure space.

1. If $1\le p<\infty$ and $f,g\in\mathcal L^p(\mu)$, then
   $$\|f+g\|_p\le\|f\|_p+\|g\|_p.$$
2. If $f,g\in L^\infty(\mu)$, then
   $$\|f+g\|_\infty\le\|f\|_\infty+\|g\|_\infty.$$

The **Axiom of Choice** (AC) is the following statement.

> Every family of nonempty sets has a choice function
> ([[def-choice-function]]).

Written out: for every set $\mathcal{F}$ all of whose members are nonempty,
there exists a function $g$ with domain $\mathcal{F}$ satisfying $g(S) \in S$ for
all $S \in \mathcal{F}$.

An equivalent formulation is that a product of nonempty sets is nonempty: if
$X_i \ne \emptyset$ for every $i \in I$, then $\prod_{i \in I} X_i \ne \emptyset$.
Here $\prod_{i \in I} X_i$ is the set of functions $f$ with domain $I$ such that
$f(i) \in X_i$ for every $i \in I$; when a family of nonempty sets is indexed by
itself, such an $f$ is precisely a choice function for it.

In ZF, assume the Axiom of Choice. Then the Axiom of Countable Choice holds.
Moreover, if $R\subseteq X\times X$ is a serial relation on a nonempty set
$X$ and $a\in X$, there is a sequence $(x_n)_{n\in\mathbb N}$ such that
$x_0=a$ and $x_nRx_{n+1}$ for every $n$. Thus AC supplies the
prescribed-initial-point form of Dependent Choice.

The **Axiom of Countable Choice**, written $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$, is the following
statement.

> For every family $(X_n)_{n \in \mathbb{N}}$ of nonempty sets indexed by
> $\mathbb{N}$ there is a function $f$ with domain $\mathbb{N}$ such that
> $f(n) \in X_n$ for every $n \in \mathbb{N}$.

Equivalently, in the vocabulary of [[def-choice-function]]: every at most
countable family of nonempty sets ([[def-countable]]) has a choice function.

Let $X$ be a set and let $R \subseteq X \times X$ be a binary relation on $X$.
Call $R$ **entire on $X$** when

$$\text{for every } x \in X \text{ there is } y \in X \text{ with } x \mathbin{R} y .$$

The **Axiom of Dependent Choice**, written $\mathrm{DC}$, is the following
statement.

> For every nonempty set $X$, every relation $R$ entire on $X$, and every
> $a \in X$, there is a function $x : \mathbb{N} \to X$ ([[def-function]],
> [[def-natural-numbers]]) with
> $$x_0 = a \qquad \text{and} \qquad x_n \mathbin{R} x_{n+1} \ \text{ for every } n \in \mathbb{N}.$$

Here a sequence in $X$ means a function from $\mathbb{N}$ to $X$, not necessarily
a real-valued sequence. As everywhere in this library $\mathbb{N}$ contains $0$, and the sequence is
indexed from $0$; the term $x_0$ is the prescribed starting point $a$ and every
later term is related to its predecessor.

**What DC adds to what came before.** [[def-choice-function]] and
[[def-axiom-of-choice]] select one element from each member of a family that is
fixed in advance, and [[def-countable-choice]] does the same for a family indexed
by $\mathbb{N}$. In both, the family is given before any selection is made. DC is
the principle needed when the $n$-th set to select from is not known until the
first $n$ selections have been made: here the admissible values of $x_{n+1}$ are
exactly the $R$-successors of $x_n$, so the family being chosen from is built
along the choosing. Thus the displayed recursion is directly an instance of
DC; it is not itself an application of the fixed-family formulation of
countable choice. This observation concerns the input to the two axioms and
makes no claim about a nonimplication between them.

**The starting point may be dropped.** The formally weaker statement obtained by
deleting the clause $x_0 = a$ — for every nonempty $X$ and every entire $R$ there
is a sequence with $x_n \mathbin{R} x_{n+1}$ for all $n$ — is an immediate
consequence of the form above, since $X$ is nonempty and any of its elements may
be taken as $a$. Conversely, assume the start-free form, and fix $X$, $R$ and $a$ as above. Let $P$ be the set of all functions $p:k\to X$ with nonzero $k\in\mathbb N$, $p(0)=a$, and $p(i)\mathbin R p(i+1)$ whenever $i+1<k$. It is a set by Separation inside $\mathcal P(\mathbb N\times X)$ ([[def-power-set]], [[def-cartesian-product]], [[def-axiom-schema-of-separation]]); a natural is the set of its predecessors ([[lem-nat-order-is-membership]]). The singleton path $\{(0,a)\}$ lies in $P$.

On $P$ let $p\mathbin S q$ mean that $q$ extends $p$ by exactly one new last entry. This relation is entire: for one particular $p:k\to X$, write $k=j+1$ ([[lem-nat-nonzero-is-successor]]); an $R$-successor $y$ of $p(j)$ exists, and $q=p\cup\{(k,y)\}$ is the required extension. This is existential instantiation for that path, not a simultaneous choice of successors. Start-free DC now supplies a sequence $(p_n)$ with $p_n\mathbin S p_{n+1}$; its first path need not be the singleton path, but every path in $P$ already starts at $a$.

Their graphs are nested. By induction ([[thm-induction-principle]]), $p_n$ has at least $n+1$ entries: the initial path is nonempty, and every step adds one entry. Hence $x=\bigcup_{n\in\mathbb N}p_n$ is a function with domain $\mathbb N$ and values in $X$. Indeed, nestedness makes all common values agree, every natural index eventually lies in a path, and no path has indices outside $\mathbb N$. Each path starts at $a$, so $x(0)=a$; for any $i$, a sufficiently long path contains both $i$ and $i+1$, giving $x(i)\mathbin R x(i+1)$. Replacement and Union form this union of the sequence of graphs. Thus the start-free and prescribed-start forms are equivalent in ZF. Every use below retains the prescribed-start convention.

**$R$ need not be an order and the terms need not be distinct.** What DC delivers
is a sequence, that is a function $\mathbb{N} \to X$, not a chain in the
order-theoretic sense ([[def-chain]]). The relation may be symmetric, and the
sequence may repeat a value or be constant; all that is asserted is
$x_n \mathbin{R} x_{n+1}$ at every index.

derivations.claim: On a compact interval $K\subset(0,T)$, time mollifications $u_\epsilon$ are smooth $V$-valued functions and satisfy $$\frac{d}{dt}\frac12\|u_\epsilon(t)\|_H^2 =\langle u_\epsilon'(t),u_\epsilon(t)\rangle_{V^*,V}.$$ This is the ordinary product rule in $H$ using [F3]. For fixed compact $K$, the mollification result [F2] gives $u_\epsilon\to u$ in $L^p(K;V)$ and $u_\epsilon'\to u'$ in $L^{p'}(K;V^*)$ as $\epsilon\downarrow0$.

For two small radii $\epsilon,\delta$, put $w=u_\epsilon-u_\delta$ on $K$. If $p\ge2$, finite-interval Hölder and [F3] give $\|w\|_{L^2(K;H)}\to0$ as $\epsilon,\delta\downarrow0$. If $p<2$, the norm estimate [F6] gives $\|w\|_{L^\infty(K;H)}\le2\|u\|_{L^\infty(H)}$, and $$\|w\|_{L^2(K;H)}^2 \le\|w\|_{L^\infty(K;H)}^{2-p}\|w\|_{L^p(K;H)}^p$$ give the same convergence. Choose $s\in K$ with $\|w(s)\|_H^2\le |K|^{-1}\|w\|_{L^2(K;H)}^2$. Integrating the identity in step 1.1 from $s$ to any $t\in K$ and applying [F4] yields $$\sup_{t\in K}\|w(t)\|_H^2 \le |K|^{-1}\|w\|_{L^2(K;H)}^2 +2\|w'\|_{L^{p'}(K;V^*)}\|w\|_{L^p(K;V)}\longrightarrow0.$$ Thus the mollifications are Cauchy in the uniform $H$ norm on $K$.

Completeness of $H$ gives a uniform limit in $C(K;H)$, which agrees almost everywhere with $u$ because $u_\epsilon\to u$ in $L^p(K;H)$. The limits agree on overlapping compact intervals, so they define $u\in C((0,T);H)$. Integrate step 1.1 between arbitrary $s,t\in K$. Uniform convergence passes the endpoint norms to those of $u$, while $$\|\langle u_\epsilon',u_\epsilon\rangle-\langle u',u\rangle\|_{L^1(K)} \le\|u_\epsilon'-u'\|_{L^{p'}(V^*)}\|u_\epsilon\|_{L^p(V)} +\|u'\|_{L^{p'}(V^*)}\|u_\epsilon-u\|_{L^p(V)}\to0.$$ Hence for all $0<s\le t<T$, $$\|u(t)\|_H^2-\|u(s)\|_H^2 =2\int_s^t\langle u'(r),u(r)\rangle\,dr.$$

By [F4], the energy pairing is in $L^1(0,T)$. The identity in step 3.1 therefore shows that $\|u(t)\|_H^2$ has finite limits as $t\downarrow0$ and $t\uparrow T$. For each fixed $v\in V$, the distributional derivative of $(u(t),iv)_H$ is $\langle u'(t),v\rangle\in L^1(0,T)$, so [F5] gives an absolutely continuous representative on $[0,T]$ agreeing with the interior pairing.

For $0<\delta<T$, choose a good time $s_\delta\in(0,\delta)$ with $u(s_\delta)\in V$ and $$\|u(s_\delta)\|_V^p \le\frac2\delta\int_0^\delta\|u(r)\|_V^p\,dr.$$ Such a time exists by averaging over $(0,\delta)$. For every interior $t\in(0,\delta)$, use step 3.1 for the two norm squares and [F5] for the scalar pairing against the fixed vector $u(s_\delta)\in V$. Subtracting twice that pairing identity gives $$\|u(t)-u(s_\delta)\|_H^2 =2\int_{s_\delta}^t\langle u'(r),u(r)-u(s_\delta)\rangle\,dr.$$ Hölder and the triangle inequality bound its absolute value by $$2\|u'\|_{L^{p'}(0,\delta;V^*)} \left(\|u\|_{L^p(0,\delta;V)} +\delta^{1/p}\|u(s_\delta)\|_V\right),$$ which tends to zero as $\delta\downarrow0$. The bound is uniform in $t\in(0,\delta)$, so $u(t)$ is Cauchy in $H$ as $t\downarrow0$ and has a strong limit there. The same argument on $(T-\delta,T)$ gives a strong limit at $T$. Thus $u$ extends to $C([0,T];H)$.

Let $s\downarrow0$ and $t\uparrow T$ in step 3.1. Strong endpoint continuity and integrability of $\langle u',u\rangle$ pass the identity to all $0\le s\le t\le T$. If two continuous representatives agree almost everywhere, their difference is continuous and vanishes on a dense subset, so it vanishes everywhere. This proves uniqueness and the claimed chain rule.

Let $X$ and $Y$ be normed spaces over the same field
$\mathbb K\in\{\mathbb R,\mathbb C\}$, read in the real case from
[[def-norm-and-normed-space]] and in the complex case from
[[def-complex-norm-and-complex-normed-space]], and suppose $X\subseteq Y$
with **continuous inclusion** $J:X\to Y$: there is a real $C\ge0$ with
$\|x\|_Y\le C\|x\|_X$ for every $x\in X$.

One says that $X$ is **compactly embedded** in $Y$, written $X\Subset Y$, when
the inclusion operator $J$ is a compact operator in the sense of
[[def-compact-linear-operator]]: the image under $J$ of every bounded
subset of $X$ ([[def-metric-bounded-diameter]]) has compact closure in $Y$
([[def-metric-compactness]]).

**The sequential form.** Assume the Axiom of Countable Choice
([[def-countable-choice]]) and the Axiom of Dependent Choice
([[def-dependent-choice]]). Then $X\Subset Y$ if and only if every bounded

which belongs to the closed set $K$. Thus $K$ is sequentially compact and

compactness theorems below are stated.

Let $V$ be a separable reflexive real Banach space, let $H$ be a real Hilbert
space, and let $i:V\to H$ be an injective continuous linear map with dense
range. Let $V^*$ be the continuous real dual of $V$ and write
$\langle\cdot,\cdot\rangle_{V^*,V}$ for its pairing with $V$. The canonical
map $J:H\to V^*$ is
$$J h(v)=(h,iv)_H\qquad(h\in H,\ v\in V).$$
It is continuous because $|Jh(v)|\le \|h\|_H\|i\|\|v\|_V$, and injective
because $i(V)$ is dense in $H$. A triple $(V,H,J)$ with these properties is
a **Banach evolution triple**. If $V$ is Hilbert, this is the real evolution
triple of [[def-parabolic-evolution-triple-and-energy-space]].

For $1<p<\infty$, $L^p(0,T;V)$ denotes the Bochner space of strongly
measurable $V$-valued functions with finite $p$th power norm, and
$p'=p/(p-1)$. For $u\in L^p(0,T;V)$ and $g\in L^{p'}(0,T;V^*)$, say
$g=u'$ in the distributional time sense if
$$\int_0^T (iu(t),iv)_H\,\phi'(t)\,dt =-\int_0^T\langle g(t),v\rangle_{V^*,V}\,\phi(t)\,dt$$
for every $v\in V$ and $\phi\in C_c^\infty(0,T)$. Define
$$W_p(0,T;V)=\{u\in L^p(0,T;V):u'\in L^{p'}(0,T;V^*)\}.$$
This definition assigns no endpoint values; a separate chain-rule theorem is
needed before evaluating a function in this space at an endpoint.

Let $(X,\mathcal A,\mu)$ be a measure space, let $p,q\in[1,\infty]$ be
conjugate exponents, and let $f,g$ be measurable real-valued functions.

1. If $1\le p<\infty$ and $q<\infty$ with $f\in\mathcal L^p(\mu)$ and
   $g\in\mathcal L^q(\mu)$, then
   $$\int |fg|\,d\mu\le\|f\|_p\|g\|_q.$$
2. If $p=1$ and $q=\infty$ with $f\in\mathcal L^1(\mu)$ and
   $g\in L^\infty(\mu)$, then
   $$\int |fg|\,d\mu\le\|f\|_1\|g\|_\infty.$$
3. If $p=\infty$ and $q=1$ with $f\in L^\infty(\mu)$ and
   $g\in\mathcal L^1(\mu)$, then
   $$\int |fg|\,d\mu\le\|f\|_\infty\|g\|_1.$$

In every case the right-hand side is finite, so $fg$ is integrable.

Let $(X,\mathcal A,\mu)$ be a measure space.

1. If $1\le p<\infty$ and $f,g\in\mathcal L^p(\mu)$, then
   $$\|f+g\|_p\le\|f\|_p+\|g\|_p.$$
2. If $f,g\in L^\infty(\mu)$, then
   $$\|f+g\|_\infty\le\|f\|_\infty+\|g\|_\infty.$$

Assume the Axiom of Choice for the ACL and absolutely-continuous
fundamental-theorem interfaces. Let $I\subseteq\mathbb R$ be a nonempty open
interval, let $1\le p\le\infty$, let $\mathbb K\in\{\mathbb R,\mathbb C\}$,
and let $u\in W^{1,p}(I;\mathbb K)$, with weak derivative class $Du$. Then
there is exactly one continuous representative $u^*$ of the class of $u$ on
$I$ that is locally absolutely continuous, that is, absolutely continuous on
every compact interval contained in $I$, and satisfies
$$u^*(x)-u^*(y)=\int_y^xDu(t)\,dt\qquad\text{for every }x,y\in I,$$
where for $x<y$ the right-hand side denotes $-\int_x^yDu$, equivalently
$u^*(y)-u^*(x)=\int_x^yDu$ whenever $x\le y$.

If $I=(a,b)$ has finite endpoints, then $Du\in L^1(a,b)$, the representative
$u^*$ extends uniquely to an absolutely continuous function on $[a,b]$, and
the extension satisfies
$$u^*(x)=u^*(a)+\int_a^xDu(t)\,dt\qquad\text{for every }x\in[a,b].$$

The scalar field is arbitrary, $p=1$ and $p=\infty$ are included, and the
one-dimensional interval may be bounded or unbounded. The Axiom of Choice is
used only through the Countable-Choice and Dependent-Choice hypotheses of the
cited characterisation, fundamental-theorem and completeness interfaces.

$\|f\|_{L^p(X)}=(\int_0^T\|f(t)\|_X^pdt)^{1/p}$, is complete under Countable
Choice.

The **Axiom of Choice** (AC) is the following statement.

> Every family of nonempty sets has a choice function
> ([[def-choice-function]]).

Written out: for every set $\mathcal{F}$ all of whose members are nonempty,
there exists a function $g$ with domain $\mathcal{F}$ satisfying $g(S) \in S$ for
all $S \in \mathcal{F}$.

An equivalent formulation is that a product of nonempty sets is nonempty: if
$X_i \ne \emptyset$ for every $i \in I$, then $\prod_{i \in I} X_i \ne \emptyset$.
Here $\prod_{i \in I} X_i$ is the set of functions $f$ with domain $I$ such that
$f(i) \in X_i$ for every $i \in I$; when a family of nonempty sets is indexed by
itself, such an $f$ is precisely a choice function for it.

In ZF, assume the Axiom of Choice. Then the Axiom of Countable Choice holds.
Moreover, if $R\subseteq X\times X$ is a serial relation on a nonempty set
$X$ and $a\in X$, there is a sequence $(x_n)_{n\in\mathbb N}$ such that
$x_0=a$ and $x_nRx_{n+1}$ for every $n$. Thus AC supplies the
prescribed-initial-point form of Dependent Choice.

The **Axiom of Countable Choice**, written $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$, is the following
statement.

> For every family $(X_n)_{n \in \mathbb{N}}$ of nonempty sets indexed by
> $\mathbb{N}$ there is a function $f$ with domain $\mathbb{N}$ such that
> $f(n) \in X_n$ for every $n \in \mathbb{N}$.

Equivalently, in the vocabulary of [[def-choice-function]]: every at most
countable family of nonempty sets ([[def-countable]]) has a choice function.

Let $X$ be a set and let $R \subseteq X \times X$ be a binary relation on $X$.
Call $R$ **entire on $X$** when

$$\text{for every } x \in X \text{ there is } y \in X \text{ with } x \mathbin{R} y .$$

The **Axiom of Dependent Choice**, written $\mathrm{DC}$, is the following
statement.

> For every nonempty set $X$, every relation $R$ entire on $X$, and every
> $a \in X$, there is a function $x : \mathbb{N} \to X$ ([[def-function]],
> [[def-natural-numbers]]) with
> $$x_0 = a \qquad \text{and} \qquad x_n \mathbin{R} x_{n+1} \ \text{ for every } n \in \mathbb{N}.$$

Here a sequence in $X$ means a function from $\mathbb{N}$ to $X$, not necessarily
a real-valued sequence. As everywhere in this library $\mathbb{N}$ contains $0$, and the sequence is
indexed from $0$; the term $x_0$ is the prescribed starting point $a$ and every
later term is related to its predecessor.

[[def-axiom-of-choice]] select one element from each member of a family that is
fixed in advance, and [[def-countable-choice]] does the same for a family indexed
by $\mathbb{N}$. In both, the family is given before any selection is made. DC is
the principle needed when the $n$-th set to select from is not known until the
first $n$ selections have been made: here the admissible values of $x_{n+1}$ are
exactly the $R$-successors of $x_n$, so the family being chosen from is built
along the choosing. Thus the displayed recursion is directly an instance of
DC; it is not itself an application of the fixed-family formulation of
countable choice. This observation concerns the input to the two axioms and
makes no claim about a nonimplication between them.

**The starting point may be dropped.** The formally weaker statement obtained by
deleting the clause $x_0 = a$ — for every nonempty $X$ and every entire $R$ there
is a sequence with $x_n \mathbin{R} x_{n+1}$ for all $n$ — is an immediate
consequence of the form above, since $X$ is nonempty and any of its elements may
be taken as $a$. Conversely, assume the start-free form, and fix $X$, $R$ and $a$ as above. Let $P$ be the set of all functions $p:k\to X$ with nonzero $k\in\mathbb N$, $p(0)=a$, and $p(i)\mathbin R p(i+1)$ whenever $i+1<k$. It is a set by Separation inside $\mathcal P(\mathbb N\times X)$ ([[def-power-set]], [[def-cartesian-product]], [[def-axiom-schema-of-separation]]); a natural is the set of its predecessors ([[lem-nat-order-is-membership]]). The singleton path $\{(0,a)\}$ lies in $P$.

On $P$ let $p\mathbin S q$ mean that $q$ extends $p$ by exactly one new last entry. This relation is entire: for one particular $p:k\to X$, write $k=j+1$ ([[lem-nat-nonzero-is-successor]]); an $R$-successor $y$ of $p(j)$ exists, and $q=p\cup\{(k,y)\}$ is the required extension. This is existential instantiation for that path, not a simultaneous choice of successors. Start-free DC now supplies a sequence $(p_n)$ with $p_n\mathbin S p_{n+1}$; its first path need not be the singleton path, but every path in $P$ already starts at $a$.

Their graphs are nested. By induction ([[thm-induction-principle]]), $p_n$ has at least $n+1$ entries: the initial path is nonempty, and every step adds one entry. Hence $x=\bigcup_{n\in\mathbb N}p_n$ is a function with domain $\mathbb N$ and values in $X$. Indeed, nestedness makes all common values agree, every natural index eventually lies in a path, and no path has indices outside $\mathbb N$. Each path starts at $a$, so $x(0)=a$; for any $i$, a sufficiently long path contains both $i$ and $i+1$, giving $x(i)\mathbin R x(i+1)$. Replacement and Union form this union of the sequence of graphs. Thus the start-free and prescribed-start forms are equivalent in ZF. Every use below retains the prescribed-start convention.

**$R$ need not be an order and the terms need not be distinct.** What DC delivers
is a sequence, that is a function $\mathbb{N} \to X$, not a chain in the
order-theoretic sense ([[def-chain]]). The relation may be symmetric, and the
sequence may repeat a value or be constant; all that is asserted is
$x_n \mathbin{R} x_{n+1}$ at every index.

derivations.claim: Fix $\varepsilon>0$. Compactness in [F1] makes the image in $H$ of the $V$ unit ball totally bounded. Choose finitely many points from $i(V)$ within $\varepsilon$ of that image, and let $E\subset i(V)$ be their finite-dimensional span. If $P_E$ is the $H$-orthogonal projection, its best-approximation property gives $$\|(I-P_E)iv\|_H\le\varepsilon\|v\|_V\qquad(v\in V).$$ After orthonormalizing a basis, write $e_\ell=iv_\ell$ with $v_\ell\in V$.

For each $j,\ell$, put $a_{j\ell}(t)=(u_j(t),e_\ell)_H$. Its weak derivative is $\langle u_j'(t),v_\ell\rangle$ by [F2]. The uniform bounds and the continuous $V\to H$ inclusion give uniform $L^p$ bounds on $a_{j\ell}$ and uniform $L^q$ bounds on their derivatives. By [F4] each coefficient has an absolutely continuous representative. For any such representative, some $s\in[0,T]$ has $|a_{j\ell}(s)|\le T^{-1/p}\|a_{j\ell}\|_{L^p}$; otherwise its $L^p$ norm would exceed that bound. Its total variation is at most $T^{1-1/q}\|a'_{j\ell}\|_{L^q}$ (with $T^{1-1/q}=T$ for $q=\infty$). Thus all coefficients are uniformly bounded, and Hölder gives the common modulus $$|a_{j\ell}(t)-a_{j\ell}(s)| \le C|t-s|^{1-1/q}$$ for $q<\infty$, with $C|t-s|$ for $q=\infty$.

The finitely many coefficient functions of $P_Eu_j$ are uniformly bounded and share the modulus from step 1.2. Choose a finite time grid so the modulus between adjacent grid points is below $\varepsilon$, and finite $\varepsilon$-nets for their bounded values at each grid point. Rounding those values gives a finite $\varepsilon$-net in the uniform norm for the coefficient vectors, hence $\{P_Eu_j\}$ is totally bounded in $L^p(0,T;H)$.

By step 1.1, $$\|u_j-P_Eu_j\|_{L^p(0,T;H)} \le\varepsilon\|u_j\|_{L^p(0,T;V)}.$$ For each desired accuracy, choose $\varepsilon$ small and use step 2.1 to approximate the projected family by a finite net. The displayed remainder then shows that the full family is totally bounded in $L^p(0,T;H)$.

From total boundedness, [A1] selects a Cauchy subsequence; [F5] makes it convergent in $L^p(0,T;H)$. This proves relative compactness. If the $L^\infty(H)$ bound is $M$, pairwise differences have $L^\infty(H)$ norm at most $2M$. For $r<p$, finite-interval Hölder gives convergence in $L^r(H)$; for $r\ge p$, $$\|u_j-u_k\|_{L^r(H)}^r \le(2M)^{r-p}\|u_j-u_k\|_{L^p(H)}^p.$$ Completeness in each $L^r(H)$ then gives convergence for every finite $r$.

Their graphs are nested. By induction ([[thm-induction-principle]]), $p_n$ has at least $n+1$ entries: the initial path is nonempty, and every step adds one entry. Hence $x=\bigcup_{n\in\mathbb N}p_n$ is a function with domain $\mathbb N$ and values in $X$. Indeed, nestedness makes all common values agree, every natural index eventually lies in a path, and no path has indices outside $\mathbb N$. Each path starts at $a$, so $x(0)=a$; for any $i$, a sufficiently long path contains both $i$ and $i+1$, giving $x(i)\mathbin R x(i+1)$. Replacement and Union form this union of the sequence of graphs. Thus the start-free and prescribed-start forms are equivalent in ZF. Every use below retains the prescribed-start convention.

**$R$ need not be an order and the terms need not be distinct.** What DC delivers
is a sequence, that is a function $\mathbb{N} \to X$, not a chain in the
order-theoretic sense ([[def-chain]]). The relation may be symmetric, and the
sequence may repeat a value or be constant; all that is asserted is
$x_n \mathbin{R} x_{n+1}$ at every index.

derivations.claim: Let $\widehat U_k$ be the continuous affine interpolation of the nodes. On $I_n^k$ its derivative equals $D_k$. For $0\le s<T$ and $0<t<T-s$, the fundamental theorem for the affine function gives $\widehat U_k(t+s)-\widehat U_k(t)=\int_t^{t+s}D_k(r)\,dr$. Minkowski [F2] and translation invariance of the time integral yield $\|\widehat U_k(\cdot+s)-\widehat U_k\|_{L^q(0,T-s;V^*)} \le s\|D_k\|_{L^q(V^*)}$.

If $t\in I_n^k$, write $t=t_{n-1}^k+\theta\tau_n^k$ with $0<\theta\le1$. Then $\overline U_k(t)-\widehat U_k(t)=(1-\theta)(U_k^n-U_k^{n-1})$. Consequently, for $1<q<\infty$, $$\|\overline U_k-\widehat U_k\|_{L^q(V^*)}^q \le\sum_n\tau_n^k\|U_k^n-U_k^{n-1}\|_{V^*}^q \le\delta_k^q\|D_k\|_{L^q(V^*)}^q.$$ For $q=\infty$, the same pointwise identity gives $\|\overline U_k(t)-\widehat U_k(t)\|_{V^*}\le\delta_k\|D_k\|_{L^\infty(V^*)}$ and hence $\|\overline U_k-\widehat U_k\|_{L^\infty(V^*)}\le\delta_k\|D_k\|_{L^\infty(V^*)}$. Combining the corresponding estimate at $t$ and $t+s$ with step 1.1 proves the stated $(s+2\delta_k)$ translate bound in both cases.

Fix $\varepsilon>0$. By [F1], the image in $H$ of the $V$ unit ball has compact closure. Choose finitely many centers from that image forming an $\varepsilon$-net, let $E\subset i(V)$ be their span, and let $P_E$ be the $H$-orthogonal projection. Its best-approximation property gives $\|(I-P_E)iv\|_H\le\varepsilon\|v\|_V$ for every $v\in V$. Choose an $H$-orthonormal basis $e_j=iv_j$ of $E$. The scalar coefficients $a_{k,j}^n=(U_k^n,e_j)_H$ have weighted $L^p$ bounds from the $L^p(V)$ bound, and their total variation satisfies $$\sum_n|a_{k,j}^n-a_{k,j}^{n-1}| \le\|v_j\|_V\sum_n\tau_n^k\|D_k\|_{V^*} \le T^{1-1/q}\|v_j\|_V\|D_k\|_{L^q(V^*)}.$$ At least one node value is no larger than its weighted $L^p$ average, so the total-variation bound gives a uniform bound for every nodal coefficient.

The affine scalar interpolants of these finitely many coefficients are uniformly bounded. Their derivatives have $L^q$ bounds, so Hölder gives a common modulus $C|t-s|^{1-1/q}$ (or $C|t-s|$ for $q=\infty$). Finite-grid rounding therefore makes the projected affine family totally bounded in $C([0,T];E)$. The maximum nodal jump is at most $\delta_k^{1-1/q}\|D_k\|_{L^q(V^*)}\|v_j\|_V$, so the projected piecewise-constant family differs from it uniformly by a quantity tending to zero. Thus $\{P_E\overline U_k\}$ is relatively compact in $L^p(H)$.

The projection remainder satisfies $\|\overline U_k-P_E\overline U_k\|_{L^p(H)} \le\varepsilon\|\overline U_k\|_{L^p(V)}$. Since $\varepsilon$ is arbitrary, steps 3.1 and 4.1 show the full family is totally bounded in $L^p(H)$; [A1] extracts a Cauchy subsequence, which converges by [F3]. This proves relative compactness.

If the nodal values are uniformly bounded by $M$ in $H$, then $\|\overline U_k-\overline U_\ell\|_{L^\infty(H)}\le2M$. For $r<p$, finite-measure Hölder upgrades the strong $L^p(H)$ convergence to $L^r(H)$. For $r\ge p$, $\|\overline U_k-\overline U_\ell\|_{L^r(H)}^r \le(2M)^{r-p}\|\overline U_k-\overline U_\ell\|_{L^p(H)}^p$, so the same subsequence is Cauchy in every finite $L^r(H)$ and converges there by [F3].

derivations.claim: Suppose, for contradiction, that $F$ has no zero in $\overline B_R(0)$. Then $F(x)\ne0$ there, and $G(x):=-R\,F(x)/|F(x)|$ is a continuous map $\overline B_R(0)\to\overline B_R(0)$ whose values all lie on the sphere. After rescaling the ball to the unit ball, [F1] gives a fixed point $x=G(x)$.

Since $G(x)$ lies on the sphere, $|x|=R$. The fixed-point equation gives $F(x)\cdot x=F(x)\cdot(-R F(x)/|F(x)|)=-R|F(x)|<0$, contradicting the assumed positive boundary pairing. Thus $F$ has a zero in the closed ball.
