citations.quote:
Assume the Axiom of Choice ([[def-axiom-of-choice]]).

Let $d\ge1$, let $\Omega\subset\mathbb R^d$ be a bounded open set, and
let $1<p<\infty$ satisfy $p>\max(1,2d/(d+2))$. Put
$V=W_0^{1,p}(\Omega;\mathbb R)$ with norm
$\|v\|_V=\|\nabla v\|_{L^p(\Omega)}$, $H=L^2(\Omega;\mathbb R)$, and
$p'=p/(p-1)$. The Poincaré inequality makes this norm equivalent to the full
$W^{1,p}$ norm. [[lem-pe12-w0p-separable-reflexive]] gives separability and
reflexivity, while [[lem-pe12-w1p-compact-l2-embedding]] gives the dense
continuous compact inclusion $V\Subset H$; these are the hypotheses of the
evolution triple in [[def-pe12-gelfand-triple]]. The compact-inclusion result
uses the stated threshold also when $d=1$, where it reduces to $p>1$.

A measurable flux $a:\Omega\times\mathbb R^d\to\mathbb R^d$ is an admissible
**coercive monotone diffusion flux of p-growth** if it is Carathéodory (for
each $\xi$, $x\mapsto a(x,\xi)$ is measurable, and for almost every $x$,
$\xi\mapsto a(x,\xi)$ is continuous), and there are constants $C<\infty$,
$\alpha>0$, nonnegative functions $g\in L^{p'}(\Omega)$ and
$h\in L^1(\Omega)$, and one
null set outside which, for all $\xi,\eta\in\mathbb R^d$,
$$|a(x,\xi)|\le C\bigl(g(x)+|\xi|^{p-1}\bigr),\qquad a(x,\xi)\cdot\xi\ge\alpha|\xi|^p-h(x),$$
$$\bigl(a(x,\xi)-a(x,\eta)\bigr)\cdot(\xi-\eta)\ge0.$$
The induced operator $A:V\to V^*$ is
$$\langle A(v),w\rangle_{V^*,V} =\int_\Omega a(x,\nabla v(x))\cdot\nabla w(x)\,dx.$$
The growth bound and Hölder's inequality make this pairing finite and give
$\|A(v)\|_{V^*}\le C_1(\|g\|_{p'}+\|v\|_V^{p-1})$ for a constant $C_1$.
For the finite-dimensional existence result below we additionally require
that this induced map $A:V\to V^*$ is norm-continuous; this is verified
directly for the p-Laplacian in the companion example.

For $f\in L^{p'}(0,T;V^*)$, a weak evolution solution is a function
$u\in W_p(0,T;V)\cap L^\infty(0,T;H)$ with a continuous $H$ representative
such that $u'+A(u)=f$ in $L^{p'}(0,T;V^*)$ and $u(0)=u_0\in H$.

Let $(V,H,J)$ be the Banach evolution triple of
[[def-pe12-gelfand-triple]]. An **admissible stable conforming FEM sequence**
consists of finite-dimensional subspaces $V_k\subset V$ and their
$H$-orthogonal projections $\Pi_k:H\to V_k$ such that:

1. $\Pi_k(V)\subset V$, $\Pi_kv=v$ for $v\in V_k$, and
   $(w_k,z-\Pi_kz)_H=0$ for every $w_k\in V_k$, $z\in H$;
2. $\sup_k\|\Pi_k\|_{V\to V}\le C_\Pi<\infty$ and
   $\Pi_kv\to v$ in $V$ for each $v\in V$;
3. the associated time partitions of $[0,T]$ have maximum step
   $\delta_k\to0$.

The convergence in clause 2 and density of $V$ in $H$ imply
$\Pi_kz\to z$ in $H$ for every $z\in H$: use
$\|\Pi_k(z-v)\|_H\le\|z-v\|_H$, $\Pi_kv\to v$ in $H$, and approximate $z$
by $v\in V$. Thus the range spaces approximate every $H$ vector.

For a fixed $k$, backward Euler with averages $f_k^n$ uses unknowns
$U_k^n\in V_k$ and equations
$$\left(\frac{U_k^n-U_k^{n-1}}{\tau_n},v_k\right)_H +\langle A(U_k^n),v_k\rangle =\langle f_k^n,v_k\rangle\qquad(v_k\in V_k).$$
Its piecewise-constant reconstruction is $\overline U_k(t)=U_k^n$ on
$(t_{n-1},t_n]$; its affine reconstruction joins $U_k^{n-1}$ to $U_k^n$.

Let $N\ge1$, $R>0$, and let $F:\mathbb R^N\to\mathbb R^N$ be continuous.
If $F(x)\cdot x>0$ for every $|x|=R$, then $F$ has a zero in the closed
ball $\overline B_R(0)$.

For every real Hilbert space $H$ and $x,y\in H$,
$$2(x-y,x)_H=\|x\|_H^2-\|y\|_H^2+\|x-y\|_H^2.$$

Let $(X,\mathcal A,\mu)$ be a measure space, let $p,q\in[1,\infty]$ be
conjugate exponents, and let $f,g$ be measurable real-valued functions.

1. If $1\le p<\infty$ and $q<\infty$ with $f\in\mathcal L^p(\mu)$ and
   $g\in\mathcal L^q(\mu)$, then
   $$\int |fg|\,d\mu\le\|f\|_p\|g\|_q.$$
2. If $p=1$ and $q=\infty$ with $f\in\mathcal L^1(\mu)$ and
   $g\in L^\infty(\mu)$, then
   $$\int |fg|\,d\mu\le\|f\|_1\|g\|_\infty.$$
3. If $p=\infty$ and $q=1$ with $f\in L^\infty(\mu)$ and
   $g\in\mathcal L^1(\mu)$, then
   $$\int |fg|\,d\mu\le\|f\|_\infty\|g\|_1.$$

In every case the right-hand side is finite, so $fg$ is integrable.

Let $p,q>1$ satisfy $1/p+1/q=1$. For $u,v\ge0$,
$$uv\le\frac{u^p}{p}+\frac{v^q}{q}.$$

Assume Countable Choice and fix a degree $k\ge1$. Take a sequence of meshes
with $h\to0$ in either branch and use the
zero-boundary Lagrange spaces $V_h$ from
[[lem-pe12-quasiuniform-mass-inverse-decay]]: globally quasi-uniform,
shape-regular matching affine simplices on a bounded Lipschitz polyhedral
open set in $d\ge2$ (with the local graph-chart convention of
[[lem-pe12-boundary-preserving-quasi-interpolation]]), or interval
partitions of a nonempty bounded interval (or a finite nonempty union of
intervals with disjoint closures) in $d=1$. For $f\in L^1(\Omega)$ define
$P_hf\in V_h$ by the finite mass system
$$
\int_\Omega (P_hf)w_h=\int_\Omega fw_h\qquad(w_h\in V_h).
$$
This is well-defined, agrees on $L^2(\Omega)$ with the $L^2$-orthogonal
projection, and is the identity on $V_h$. There are constants independent
of $h$ such that
$$\|P_hf\|_{L^r(\Omega)}\le C_r\|f\|_{L^r(\Omega)}\qquad(1\le r\le\infty).$$
For every $1<p<\infty$ and $v\in W_0^{1,p}(\Omega)$,
$$\|\nabla P_hv\|_{L^p(\Omega)}\le C_p\|\nabla v\|_{L^p(\Omega)},\qquad P_hv\longrightarrow v\quad\text{in }W^{1,p}(\Omega).$$
For the PE12 application, additionally assume the Axiom of Choice and
$p>\max(1,2d/(d+2))$. The compact embedding
[[lem-pe12-w1p-compact-l2-embedding]] makes $V=W_0^{1,p}(\Omega)$ a dense
subspace of $H=L^2(\Omega)$, and
[[lem-pe12-w0p-separable-reflexive]] supplies the separable reflexive Banach
structure. Thus these spaces form the evolution triple of
[[def-pe12-monotone-diffusion-flux]] and
[[def-pe12-gelfand-triple]], and the $P_h$ above is its $H$-orthogonal
projector. Together with any time partitions whose maximum step tends to
zero it satisfies the projector clauses in
[[def-pe12-stable-conforming-fem-family]]. For every $d\ge2$, the uniform
Kuhn/Freudenthal meshes of $\Omega=(0,1)^d$, and for $d=1$ the uniform
interval meshes of $\Omega=(0,1)$, are explicit nonempty instances throughout
that full strict $p$ range. Time refinement is independent of spatial
refinement.

The **Axiom of Choice** (AC) is the following statement.

> Every family of nonempty sets has a choice function
> ([[def-choice-function]]).

Written out: for every set $\mathcal{F}$ all of whose members are nonempty,
there exists a function $g$ with domain $\mathcal{F}$ satisfying $g(S) \in S$ for
all $S \in \mathcal{F}$.

An equivalent formulation is that a product of nonempty sets is nonempty: if
$X_i \ne \emptyset$ for every $i \in I$, then $\prod_{i \in I} X_i \ne \emptyset$.
Here $\prod_{i \in I} X_i$ is the set of functions $f$ with domain $I$ such that
$f(i) \in X_i$ for every $i \in I$; when a family of nonempty sets is indexed by
itself, such an $f$ is precisely a choice function for it.

derivations.claim: Fix $k$. If $V_k=\{0\}$, then $U_k^0=\Pi_ku_0=0$, and setting $U_k^n=0$ for every $n$ satisfies every equation (the only test vector is zero). Assume $V_k\ne\{0\}$. For a time cell $I_k^n$, the Bochner average $f_k^n\in V^*$ exists. Define $F_n:V_k\to V_k^*$ by $$\langle F_n(z),w_k\rangle =\tau_k^{-1}(z-U_k^{n-1},w_k)_H +\langle A(z)-f_k^n,w_k\rangle.$$ This is continuous by [F1]. Choose an $H$-orthonormal basis of $V_k$ and identify $V_k^*$ with $\mathbb R^{\dim V_k}$ by its values on that basis. Finite dimensionality gives constants $c_k,C_k>0$ with $c_k\|z\|_H\le\|z\|_V\le C_k\|z\|_H$ on $V_k$. Coercivity [F1] therefore gives, with $r=\|z\|_H$, $$\langle F_n(z),z\rangle \ge \tau_k^{-1}r^2+\alpha c_k^p r^p -\bigl(\tau_k^{-1}\|U_k^{n-1}\|_H+ C_k\|f_k^n\|_{V^*}\bigr)r-\|h\|_{L^1}.$$ Since $p>1$, the right side is positive for all sufficiently large $r$.

Apply [F3] on such a sphere in the chosen coordinates to obtain $F_n(U_k^n)=0$. Starting with $U_k^0=\Pi_ku_0$, repeat this finite step for $n=1,\ldots,N_k$; this constructs the discrete solution on the partition.

Test the equation with $v_k=U_k^n$. By [F4], $$\frac12\bigl(\|U_k^n\|_H^2-\|U_k^{n-1}\|_H^2+ \|U_k^n-U_k^{n-1}\|_H^2\bigr) +\tau_k^n\alpha\|U_k^n\|_V^p \le\tau_k^n\|f_k^n\|_{V^*}\|U_k^n\|_V+ \tau_k^n\|h\|_{L^1}.$$ Use [F5] to absorb half the coercive term and sum over $n$. Hölder on each cell gives $\sum_n\tau_k^n\|f_k^n\|_{V^*}^{p'}\le\|f\|_{L^{p'}(V^*)}^{p'}$. Consequently $$\frac12\|U_k^m\|_H^2+ \frac12\sum_{n\le m}\|U_k^n-U_k^{n-1}\|_H^2+ \frac\alpha2\sum_{n\le m}\tau_k^n\|U_k^n\|_V^p \le\frac12\|U_k^0\|_H^2+ T\|h\|_{L^1}+C_{\alpha,p}\|f\|_{L^{p'}(V^*)}^{p'},$$ for every $m$. Orthogonality gives $\|U_k^0\|_H\le\|u_0\|_H$; taking the maximum over $m$ bounds the first three quantities uniformly in $k$.

For $v\in V$, orthogonality and $D_k|_{I_k^n}\in V_k$ give $$\langle D_k,v\rangle =(D_k,iv)_H=(D_k,\Pi_kv)_H =\langle f_k^n-A(U_k^n),\Pi_kv\rangle.$$ Thus [F2] yields $\|D_k(t)\|_{V^*}\le C_\Pi(\|f_k^n\|_{V^*}+\|A(U_k^n)\|_{V^*})$. The flux growth bound [F1] and the inequality $(a+b)^{p'}\le2^{p'-1}(a^{p'}+b^{p'})$ give $$\|D_k\|_{L^{p'}(V^*)}^{p'}\le C_{p,C_1}C_\Pi^{p'}\left(\|f\|_{L^{p'}(V^*)}^{p'}+T\|g\|_{L^{p'}(\Omega)}^{p'}+\sum_n\tau_k^n\|U_k^n\|_V^p\right).$$ Here $(p-1)p'=p$, and $g$ is constant in time. Step 3.1 bounds the last sum, proving the derivative estimate with precisely the stated family and data dependencies.

For the fixed-degree interval and cube sequences in the Statement, [F6] verifies the abstract FEM projector hypotheses, including the independent time partitions. The preceding construction and energy estimates therefore apply to these concrete nonempty meshes.

citations.quote:
Assume the Axiom of Choice, used to invoke the published real and complex
$L^p$ completeness results through their Countable-Choice interface. Let
$\Omega\subseteq\mathbb R^n$ be open, $n\ge1$, let $k\in\mathbb N_0$,
$1\le p\le\infty$, and $\mathbb K\in\{\mathbb R,\mathbb C\}$. Then
$W^{k,p}(\Omega;\mathbb K)$, equipped with the displayed norm of
[[def-sobolev-space-wkp-and-its-norm]], is a complete normed space over
$\mathbb K$.

Both endpoints $p=1$ and $p=\infty$ are included, as is $k=0$, where the
assertion reduces to the completeness of $L^p$. If $\Omega=\varnothing$, then
$W^{k,p}(\Omega;\mathbb K)$ is the zero space and the assertion is trivial.
The Axiom of Choice is used only to derive Countable Choice for the two
published completeness interfaces; no other selection is made. Representative
selection inside the finitely many coordinate classes is finite and
choice-free.

Assume Countable Choice. Let $\Omega\subseteq\mathbb R^n$ be open with
$n\ge1$, let $k\in\mathbb N_0$, let $1\le p\le\infty$, and let
$\mathbb K\in\{\mathbb R,\mathbb C\}$.

Every $\varphi\in C_c^\infty(\Omega;\mathbb K)$ belongs to
$W^{k,p}(\Omega;\mathbb K)$. Indeed $\varphi$ is bounded with compact support,
hence lies in $L^p(\Omega;\mathbb K)$ for every exponent in range, and each of
its classical partial derivatives is again smooth and compactly supported,
hence lies in $L^p(\Omega;\mathbb K)$ and is the corresponding weak derivative
by [[lem-classical-derivatives-are-weak-derivatives]].

Define the **zero-boundary Sobolev space**
$$W_0^{k,p}(\Omega;\mathbb K):=\overline{C_c^\infty(\Omega;\mathbb K)},$$
the closure taken in the normed space
$(W^{k,p}(\Omega;\mathbb K),\|\cdot\|_{W^{k,p}(\Omega)})$ of
[[def-sobolev-space-wkp-and-its-norm]]. The norm is a genuine norm on classes
by [[lem-sobolev-norm-is-well-defined-and-definite]], so this is the usual
metric closure of a subset of a normed space: $u\in W_0^{k,p}(\Omega;\mathbb K)$
if and only if for every $\delta>0$ there is
$\varphi\in C_c^\infty(\Omega;\mathbb K)$ with
$\|u-\varphi\|_{W^{k,p}(\Omega)}<\delta$. Write
$H_0^k(\Omega):=W_0^{k,2}(\Omega;\mathbb K)$ when the scalar field is fixed by
context.

Three warnings are part of the definition. First, this is a closure of
almost-everywhere classes, and all its equalities are equalities of Sobolev
classes. Second, no pointwise boundary values and no trace characterization
are asserted: a description of $W_0^{k,p}$ by vanishing boundary data belongs
to the later trace theory and is not used here. Third, the closure is defined
for every $1\le p\le\infty$, but for $p=\infty$ it is not claimed that every
compactly supported $W^{k,\infty}(\Omega)$ function lies in $W_0^{k,\infty}(\Omega)$;
the definition merely names the closure of the test functions.

Let $V$ be a Banach space and let $W\subseteq V$ be a closed linear subspace,
equipped with the restricted norm. Then $W$ is a Banach space.

Assume Countable Choice ([[def-countable-choice]]). Let $\Omega\subseteq\mathbb R^n$ be open and bounded in one direction: there are a unit vector $e$ and $a<b$ with $a<x\cdot e<b$ for every $x\in\Omega$. Let $1\le p<\infty$. Then $\|u\|_{L^p(\Omega)}\le C(p)\,(b-a)\,\|Du\|_{L^p(\Omega)}$ for every $u\in W^{1,p}_0(\Omega;\mathbb K)$.

**Assume the Axiom of Countable Choice $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$.**  For every
measure space $(S,\mathcal A,\mu)$ and every $1<p<\infty$, both
$L^p(\mu;\mathbb R)$ and $L^p(\mu;\mathbb C)$ are reflexive.

Assume the ultrafilter lemma, DC, and HB.  A real or complex Banach space $X$
is reflexive if and only if every norm-bounded sequence in $X$ has a
subsequence that converges weakly to a point of $X$.

Let $\mathbb K=\mathbb R$ or $\mathbb C$. A [[def-banach-space|Banach space]] $X$ is **reflexive** if its canonical map $J_X:X\to X^{**}$ from [[def-canonical-map-into-the-bidual]] is surjective. Assuming the Axiom of Choice ([[def-axiom-of-choice]]), [[thm-canonical-bidual-map-is-an-isometry]] shows that this map is already an isometric embedding. Surjectivity means that every bounded linear functional on $X^*$ is evaluation at a vector of $X$. Merely specifying some isomorphism between $X$ and $X^{**}$ is not this definition.

**Assume HB.**  If $X$ is a real or complex reflexive Banach space and
$Y\subseteq X$ is a closed linear subspace with the restricted norm, then $Y$
is reflexive.

Let $X$ be a real Banach space, $0<T<\infty$, and $1\le p<\infty$. Then
$L^p(0,T;X)$, with norm
$\|f\|_{L^p(X)}=(\int_0^T\|f(t)\|_X^pdt)^{1/p}$, is complete under Countable
Choice.

Let $V$ be a separable reflexive real Banach space, let $H$ be a real Hilbert
space, and let $i:V\to H$ be an injective continuous linear map with dense
range. Let $V^*$ be the continuous real dual of $V$ and write
$\langle\cdot,\cdot\rangle_{V^*,V}$ for its pairing with $V$. The canonical
map $J:H\to V^*$ is
$$J h(v)=(h,iv)_H\qquad(h\in H,\ v\in V).$$
It is continuous because $|Jh(v)|\le \|h\|_H\|i\|\|v\|_V$, and injective
because $i(V)$ is dense in $H$. A triple $(V,H,J)$ with these properties is
a **Banach evolution triple**. If $V$ is Hilbert, this is the real evolution
triple of [[def-parabolic-evolution-triple-and-energy-space]].

For $1<p<\infty$, $L^p(0,T;V)$ denotes the Bochner space of strongly
measurable $V$-valued functions with finite $p$th power norm, and
$p'=p/(p-1)$. For $u\in L^p(0,T;V)$ and $g\in L^{p'}(0,T;V^*)$, say
$g=u'$ in the distributional time sense if
$$\int_0^T (iu(t),iv)_H\,\phi'(t)\,dt =-\int_0^T\langle g(t),v\rangle_{V^*,V}\,\phi(t)\,dt$$
for every $v\in V$ and $\phi\in C_c^\infty(0,T)$. Define
$$W_p(0,T;V)=\{u\in L^p(0,T;V):u'\in L^{p'}(0,T;V^*)\}.$$
This definition assigns no endpoint values; a separate chain-rule theorem is
needed before evaluating a function in this space at an endpoint.

Let $n \ge 1$ and **assume the Axiom of Countable Choice**
([[def-countable-choice]]). Then:

1. $\lambda_n$ is sigma-finite ([[def-finite-sigma-finite-and-semifinite-measures]]):
   the cubes $(-k,k]^n$ are Lebesgue measurable with
   $\lambda_n\big((-k,k]^n\big) = (2k)^n < +\infty$, they increase with $k$, and
   their union over $k \in \mathbb{N}$ is $\mathbb{R}^n$.
2. Every bounded subset $E \subseteq \mathbb{R}^n$
   ([[def-metric-bounded-diameter]]) has $\lambda_n^*(E) < +\infty$; a bounded
   Lebesgue measurable set therefore has finite measure, and every compact
   subset of $\mathbb{R}^n$ is Lebesgue measurable of finite measure.

Let $V$ be a separable reflexive real Banach space, let $H$ be a real Hilbert
space, and let $i:V\to H$ be an injective continuous linear map with dense
range. Let $V^*$ be the continuous real dual of $V$ and write
$\langle\cdot,\cdot\rangle_{V^*,V}$ for its pairing with $V$. The canonical
map $J:H\to V^*$ is
$$J h(v)=(h,iv)_H\qquad(h\in H,\ v\in V).$$
It is continuous because $|Jh(v)|\le \|h\|_H\|i\|\|v\|_V$, and injective
because $i(V)$ is dense in $H$. A triple $(V,H,J)$ with these properties is
a **Banach evolution triple**. If $V$ is Hilbert, this is the real evolution
triple of [[def-parabolic-evolution-triple-and-energy-space]].

For $1<p<\infty$, $L^p(0,T;V)$ denotes the Bochner space of strongly
measurable $V$-valued functions with finite $p$th power norm, and
$p'=p/(p-1)$. For $u\in L^p(0,T;V)$ and $g\in L^{p'}(0,T;V^*)$, say
$g=u'$ in the distributional time sense if
$$\int_0^T (iu(t),iv)_H\,\phi'(t)\,dt =-\int_0^T\langle g(t),v\rangle_{V^*,V}\,\phi(t)\,dt$$
for every $v\in V$ and $\phi\in C_c^\infty(0,T)$. Define
$$W_p(0,T;V)=\{u\in L^p(0,T;V):u'\in L^{p'}(0,T;V^*)\}.$$
This definition assigns no endpoint values; a separate chain-rule theorem is
needed before evaluating a function in this space at an endpoint.

Let $(\Omega,\mathcal A,\mu)$ be a measure space and $X$ a real or complex
Banach space. A function $f:\Omega\to X$ is **strongly measurable** (or
**Bochner measurable**) if there are measurable $X$-valued simple functions
$s_n$ and a measurable null set $N$ such that

$$\lim_{n\to\infty}\|s_n(\omega)-f(\omega)\|=0$$

for every $\omega\in\Omega\setminus N$.

This is a norm-convergence condition. It is not, by definition, merely Borel
measurability of $f$ or measurability of every scalar function $x^*\circ f$.
Changing $f$ on a null set preserves strong measurability: enlarge $N$ by that
null set and retain the same approximants.

Let $(\Omega,\mathcal A,\mu)$ be a measure space and $X$ a real or complex
Banach space. A strongly measurable function $f:\Omega\to X$ is
**Bochner integrable** if there is a sequence of integrable $X$-valued simple
functions $(s_n)$ such that

$$\lim_{n\to\infty}\int_\Omega\|f-s_n\|\,d\mu=0.$$

For such a sequence define

$$\int_\Omega f\,d\mu:=\lim_{n\to\infty}\int_\Omega s_n\,d\mu.$$

The displayed norm limit exists: the simple integral inequality gives

$$\left\|\int s_n-\int s_m\right\|\leq\int\|s_n-s_m\|\leq\int\|s_n-f\|+\int\|f-s_m\|,$$

so the simple integrals form a Cauchy sequence, and $X$ is complete. The next
theorem proves that the value is independent of the approximating sequence and
characterizes existence by integrability of $\|f\|$.

For $E\in\mathcal A$, write
$\int_Ef\,d\mu:=\int_\Omega\mathbf1_Ef\,d\mu$ whenever this function is
Bochner integrable.

Let $(X,\mathcal A,\mu)$ and $(Y,\mathcal B,\nu)$ be sigma-finite measure
spaces. For $E \in \mathcal A \otimes \mathcal B$, define

$$(\mu \times \nu)(E) := \int_X \nu(E_x)\,d\mu = \int_Y \mu(E^y)\,d\nu.$$

The two displayed integrals are well-defined by
[[prop-sigma-finite-section-measure-functions-are-measurable]] and equal by
[[thm-iterated-section-measures-agree-on-product-measurable-sets]]. This is the
**product measure** of $\mu$ and $\nu$.

Let $(X,\mathcal A,\mu)$ and $(Y,\mathcal B,\nu)$ be sigma-finite measure
spaces, and let $f : X \times Y \to [0,\infty]$ be product-measurable. Then
$x \mapsto \int_Y f_x\,d\nu$ and $y \mapsto \int_X f^y\,d\mu$ are measurable,
and

$$\int_{X \times Y} f\,d(\mu \times \nu) = \int_X \left(\int_Y f_x\,d\nu\right)d\mu = \int_Y \left(\int_X f^y\,d\mu\right)d\nu.$$

Let $(X,\mathcal A,\mu)$ be an arbitrary measure space. All functions below have domain $X$. Let $f$ and $(f_n)$ be measurable complex-valued functions such that
$f_n\to f$ almost everywhere and $|f_n|\le g$ almost everywhere for a single
nonnegative measurable function $g$ with $\int g\,d\mu<+\infty$. Then
$f\in L^1(\mu)$,
$$\int|f_n-f|\,d\mu\longrightarrow0,$$
and hence
$$\int f_n\,d\mu\longrightarrow\int f\,d\mu.$$

The **Axiom of Choice** (AC) is the following statement.

> Every family of nonempty sets has a choice function
> ([[def-choice-function]]).

Written out: for every set $\mathcal{F}$ all of whose members are nonempty,
there exists a function $g$ with domain $\mathcal{F}$ satisfying $g(S) \in S$ for
all $S \in \mathcal{F}$.

An equivalent formulation is that a product of nonempty sets is nonempty: if
$X_i \ne \emptyset$ for every $i \in I$, then $\prod_{i \in I} X_i \ne \emptyset$.
Here $\prod_{i \in I} X_i$ is the set of functions $f$ with domain $I$ such that
$f(i) \in X_i$ for every $i \in I$; when a family of nonempty sets is indexed by
itself, such an $f$ is precisely a choice function for it.

In ZF, assume the Axiom of Choice. Then the Axiom of Countable Choice holds.
Moreover, if $R\subseteq X\times X$ is a serial relation on a nonempty set
$X$ and $a\in X$, there is a sequence $(x_n)_{n\in\mathbb N}$ such that
$x_0=a$ and $x_nRx_{n+1}$ for every $n$. Thus AC supplies the
prescribed-initial-point form of Dependent Choice.

**Assume the Axiom of Choice** ([[def-axiom-of-choice]]). Let $X$ be a set and let
$\mathcal{F}_0$ be a filter on $X$ ([[def-filter]]). Then there is an ultrafilter
$\mathcal{U}$ on $X$ ([[def-ultrafilter]]) with $\mathcal{F}_0 \subseteq \mathcal{U}$.

The hypothesis is spent exactly once, through Zorn's lemma at step 4.1; the rest
of the argument is a theorem of ZF.

In particular, every set that carries a filter carries an ultrafilter. The proof
uses Zorn's lemma ([[thm-zorn]]) and therefore the Axiom of Choice. That some
choice principle is unavoidable here, if ZF is consistent, is an external
independence result, not proved in this library; see the remarks below.

Assume the Axiom of Choice. Let $X$ be a real vector space, let
$M \subseteq X$ be a linear subspace, let
$p:X \to \mathbb{R}$ be sublinear, and let $f:M \to \mathbb{R}$ be linear with
$f(m) \le p(m)$ for every $m \in M$. Then there exists a linear functional
$F:X \to \mathbb{R}$ such that $F|_M=f$ and $F(x) \le p(x)$ for every $x \in X$.

The **ultrafilter extension principle** says that every filter on a set is contained in an ultrafilter on that set ([[def-ultrafilter]]).

It is also called the **ultrafilter lemma** and is equivalent over ZF to the Boolean prime ideal theorem, abbreviated BPI. Items below write **assume UL/BPI** precisely when they use this extension principle; they do not thereby assume the full axiom of choice.

Let $X$ be a set and let $R \subseteq X \times X$ be a binary relation on $X$.
Call $R$ **entire on $X$** when

$$\text{for every } x \in X \text{ there is } y \in X \text{ with } x \mathbin{R} y .$$

The **Axiom of Dependent Choice**, written $\mathrm{DC}$, is the following
statement.

> For every nonempty set $X$, every relation $R$ entire on $X$, and every
> $a \in X$, there is a function $x : \mathbb{N} \to X$ ([[def-function]],
> [[def-natural-numbers]]) with
> $$x_0 = a \qquad \text{and} \qquad x_n \mathbin{R} x_{n+1} \ \text{ for every } n \in \mathbb{N}.$$

Here a sequence in $X$ means a function from $\mathbb{N}$ to $X$, not necessarily
a real-valued sequence. As everywhere in this library $\mathbb{N}$ contains $0$, and the sequence is
indexed from $0$; the term $x_0$ is the prescribed starting point $a$ and every
later term is related to its predecessor.

**What DC adds to what came before.** [[def-choice-function]] and
[[def-axiom-of-choice]] select one element from each member of a family that is
fixed in advance, and [[def-countable-choice]] does the same for a family indexed
by $\mathbb{N}$. In both, the family is given before any selection is made. DC is
the principle needed when the $n$-th set to select from is not known until the
first $n$ selections have been made: here the admissible values of $x_{n+1}$ are
exactly the $R$-successors of $x_n$, so the family being chosen from is built
along the choosing. Thus the displayed recursion is directly an instance of
DC; it is not itself an application of the fixed-family formulation of
countable choice. This observation concerns the input to the two axioms and
makes no claim about a nonimplication between them.

**The starting point may be dropped.** The formally weaker statement obtained by
deleting the clause $x_0 = a$ — for every nonempty $X$ and every entire $R$ there
is a sequence with $x_n \mathbin{R} x_{n+1}$ for all $n$ — is an immediate
consequence of the form above, since $X$ is nonempty and any of its elements may
be taken as $a$. Conversely, assume the start-free form, and fix $X$, $R$ and $a$ as above. Let $P$ be the set of all functions $p:k\to X$ with nonzero $k\in\mathbb N$, $p(0)=a$, and $p(i)\mathbin R p(i+1)$ whenever $i+1<k$. It is a set by Separation inside $\mathcal P(\mathbb N\times X)$ ([[def-power-set]], [[def-cartesian-product]], [[def-axiom-schema-of-separation]]); a natural is the set of its predecessors ([[lem-nat-order-is-membership]]). The singleton path $\{(0,a)\}$ lies in $P$.

On $P$ let $p\mathbin S q$ mean that $q$ extends $p$ by exactly one new last entry. This relation is entire: for one particular $p:k\to X$, write $k=j+1$ ([[lem-nat-nonzero-is-successor]]); an $R$-successor $y$ of $p(j)$ exists, and $q=p\cup\{(k,y)\}$ is the required extension. This is existential instantiation for that path, not a simultaneous choice of successors. Start-free DC now supplies a sequence $(p_n)$ with $p_n\mathbin S p_{n+1}$; its first path need not be the singleton path, but every path in $P$ already starts at $a$.

Their graphs are nested. By induction ([[thm-induction-principle]]), $p_n$ has at least $n+1$ entries: the initial path is nonempty, and every step adds one entry. Hence $x=\bigcup_{n\in\mathbb N}p_n$ is a function with domain $\mathbb N$ and values in $X$. Indeed, nestedness makes all common values agree, every natural index eventually lies in a path, and no path has indices outside $\mathbb N$. Each path starts at $a$, so $x(0)=a$; for any $i$, a sufficiently long path contains both $i$ and $i+1$, giving $x(i)\mathbin R x(i+1)$. Replacement and Union form this union of the sequence of graphs. Thus the start-free and prescribed-start forms are equivalent in ZF. Every use below retains the prescribed-start convention.

**$R$ need not be an order and the terms need not be distinct.** What DC delivers
is a sequence, that is a function $\mathbb{N} \to X$, not a chain in the
order-theoretic sense ([[def-chain]]). The relation may be symmetric, and the
sequence may repeat a value or be constant; all that is asserted is
$x_n \mathbin{R} x_{n+1}$ at every index.

Work over ZF. The **real dominated-extension principle**, denoted **HB**, is the following assertion:

For every real vector space $X$, every sublinear functional $p:X\to\mathbb R$ in the sense of [[def-sublinear-functional]], every real linear subspace $M\le X$ in the sense of [[def-linear-subspace]], and every real linear functional $g:M\to\mathbb R$ in the sense of [[def-algebraic-dual-and-linear-functional]],
$$\bigl(\forall m\in M,\ g(m)\le p(m)\bigr)\ \Longrightarrow\ \exists F:X\to\mathbb R\ \bigl(F\text{ is real linear},\ F|_M=g,\ \forall x\in X,\ F(x)\le p(x)\bigr).$$

This names an additional principle; it does not assert a proof of HB in ZF. Subsequent results explicitly state when they assume HB. Neither topology nor completeness is part of this assertion. The subspace may be $\{0\}$ or all of $X$. Sublinearity at scalar zero gives $p(0)=0$, and a linear functional has value zero at zero.

In ZF, the Axiom of Dependent Choice implies the Axiom of Countable Choice:
every at most countable family of nonempty sets has a choice function
([[def-countable-choice]], [[def-choice-function]],
[[def-dependent-choice]]).

The **Axiom of Countable Choice**, written $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$, is the following
statement.

> For every family $(X_n)_{n \in \mathbb{N}}$ of nonempty sets indexed by
> $\mathbb{N}$ there is a function $f$ with domain $\mathbb{N}$ such that
> $f(n) \in X_n$ for every $n \in \mathbb{N}$.

Equivalently, in the vocabulary of [[def-choice-function]]: every at most
countable family of nonempty sets ([[def-countable]]) has a choice function.

derivations.claim: If $\Omega=\varnothing$, the closure definition in [F1] gives $V=\{0\}$, so every $u_j$ and its $H$ image is zero. The assumed strong $L^p(0,T;H)$ limit is therefore $u=0$ even when $H$ is nonzero; taking $U=0$ proves all conclusions.

Assume $\Omega\ne\varnothing$, put $Q=(0,T)\times\Omega$, and give $Y_0=(L^p(Q;\mathbb R))^d$ its finite product norm. Each scalar coordinate space is reflexive by [F2]. A bounded sequence in $Y_0$ has bounded coordinates; apply [F3] successively to the $d$ coordinates to obtain one subsequence weakly converging in every coordinate. A bounded functional on $Y_0$ is the sum of its restrictions to the coordinate embeddings, so this is weak convergence in $Y_0$. The reverse implication in [F3] makes $Y_0$ reflexive. The Euclidean-vector norm of $Y=L^p(Q;\mathbb R^d)$ and the $Y_0$ product norm are equivalent because the Euclidean norm and the finite-dimensional $\ell^p$ norm on $\mathbb R^d$ are equivalent. Equivalent norms have the same continuous dual and weak convergence, so $Y$ is reflexive as well.

The gradient map $\Gamma:V\to L^p(\Omega;\mathbb R^d)$, $\Gamma v=\nabla v$, is an isometry for the chosen norm and has closed range: if $\nabla v_n$ converges in $L^p$, then $(v_n)$ is Cauchy in $V$; [F1] gives a limit in $V$ whose gradient is that limit.

For a finite-valued simple $U(t)=\sum_{\ell=1}^q\mathbf1_{E_\ell}(t)v_\ell$ with $v_\ell\in V$ and disjoint measurable $E_\ell$, apply [F6] to $\Gamma U(t)=\sum_\ell\mathbf1_{E_\ell}(t)\nabla v_\ell$. It supplies the space-time representative and equality of the Bochner and product $L^p$ norms. Simple-function density from [F6] and completeness of $Y$ from [F2] extend this map to an isometry $\Gamma_p:L^p(0,T;V)\to Y$. Its range $S$ is closed: if $\Gamma_pU_n$ converges in $Y$, the isometry makes $U_n$ Cauchy in $L^p(0,T;V)$; completeness [F5] gives $U_n\to U$, and then $\Gamma_pU_n\to\Gamma_pU$. Thus [F4] makes $S$ a reflexive Banach space.

The sequence $\Gamma_pu_j$ is bounded in $S$. Reflexivity of $S$ and [F3] give a weakly convergent subsequence with limit $G\in S$. Since $G=\Gamma_pU$ for some $U\in L^p(0,T;V)$ and $\Gamma_p$ is an isometry, the same subsequence $u_j$ converges weakly to $U$ in $L^p(0,T;V)$; applying any bounded functional after $\Gamma_p^{-1}$ verifies this assertion.

The bounded inclusion in [F5] sends this weak convergence to weak convergence of the $H$-valued images to the image of $U$. By hypothesis those same images converge strongly, hence weakly, to $u$; Hahn–Banach separates distinct points, so $u$ is the image of $U$. Weak convergence in $S$ also implies weak convergence of gradients in $Y$, by restriction of $Y^*$ functionals to $S$.
The subsequence therefore has the asserted weak $L^p(V)$ limit, that limit has $H$ image $u$, and its space-time gradient is the weak limit $G=\nabla U$. This proves all conclusions.

Assume the Axiom of Choice ([[def-axiom-of-choice]]).

Let $d\ge1$, let $\Omega\subset\mathbb R^d$ be a bounded open set, and
let $1<p<\infty$ satisfy $p>\max(1,2d/(d+2))$. Put
$V=W_0^{1,p}(\Omega;\mathbb R)$ with norm
$\|v\|_V=\|\nabla v\|_{L^p(\Omega)}$, $H=L^2(\Omega;\mathbb R)$, and
$p'=p/(p-1)$. The Poincaré inequality makes this norm equivalent to the full
$W^{1,p}$ norm. [[lem-pe12-w0p-separable-reflexive]] gives separability and
reflexivity, while [[lem-pe12-w1p-compact-l2-embedding]] gives the dense
continuous compact inclusion $V\Subset H$; these are the hypotheses of the
evolution triple in [[def-pe12-gelfand-triple]]. The compact-inclusion result
uses the stated threshold also when $d=1$, where it reduces to $p>1$.

A measurable flux $a:\Omega\times\mathbb R^d\to\mathbb R^d$ is an admissible
**coercive monotone diffusion flux of p-growth** if it is Carathéodory (for
each $\xi$, $x\mapsto a(x,\xi)$ is measurable, and for almost every $x$,
$\xi\mapsto a(x,\xi)$ is continuous), and there are constants $C<\infty$,
$\alpha>0$, nonnegative functions $g\in L^{p'}(\Omega)$ and
$h\in L^1(\Omega)$, and one
null set outside which, for all $\xi,\eta\in\mathbb R^d$,
$$|a(x,\xi)|\le C\bigl(g(x)+|\xi|^{p-1}\bigr),\qquad a(x,\xi)\cdot\xi\ge\alpha|\xi|^p-h(x),$$
$$\bigl(a(x,\xi)-a(x,\eta)\bigr)\cdot(\xi-\eta)\ge0.$$
The induced operator $A:V\to V^*$ is
$$\langle A(v),w\rangle_{V^*,V} =\int_\Omega a(x,\nabla v(x))\cdot\nabla w(x)\,dx.$$
The growth bound and Hölder's inequality make this pairing finite and give
$\|A(v)\|_{V^*}\le C_1(\|g\|_{p'}+\|v\|_V^{p-1})$ for a constant $C_1$.
For the finite-dimensional existence result below we additionally require
that this induced map $A:V\to V^*$ is norm-continuous; this is verified
directly for the p-Laplacian in the companion example.

For $f\in L^{p'}(0,T;V^*)$, a weak evolution solution is a function
$u\in W_p(0,T;V)\cap L^\infty(0,T;H)$ with a continuous $H$ representative
such that $u'+A(u)=f$ in $L^{p'}(0,T;V^*)$ and $u(0)=u_0\in H$.

Let $(X,\mathcal A,\mu)$ be a measure space, let $p,q\in[1,\infty]$ be
conjugate exponents, and let $f,g$ be measurable real-valued functions.

1. If $1\le p<\infty$ and $q<\infty$ with $f\in\mathcal L^p(\mu)$ and
   $g\in\mathcal L^q(\mu)$, then
   $$\int |fg|\,d\mu\le\|f\|_p\|g\|_q.$$
2. If $p=1$ and $q=\infty$ with $f\in\mathcal L^1(\mu)$ and
   $g\in L^\infty(\mu)$, then
   $$\int |fg|\,d\mu\le\|f\|_1\|g\|_\infty.$$
3. If $p=\infty$ and $q=1$ with $f\in L^\infty(\mu)$ and
   $g\in\mathcal L^1(\mu)$, then
   $$\int |fg|\,d\mu\le\|f\|_\infty\|g\|_1.$$

In every case the right-hand side is finite, so $fg$ is integrable.

Let $(X,\mathcal A,\mu)$ be an arbitrary measure space. All functions below have domain $X$. Let $f$ and $(f_n)$ be measurable complex-valued functions such that
$f_n\to f$ almost everywhere and $|f_n|\le g$ almost everywhere for a single
nonnegative measurable function $g$ with $\int g\,d\mu<+\infty$. Then
$f\in L^1(\mu)$,
$$\int|f_n-f|\,d\mu\longrightarrow0,$$
and hence

derivations.claim: Fix arbitrary $\eta\in L^p(Q;\mathbb R^d)$. By [F1]–[F3], monotonicity gives the finite nonnegative integrals $$0\le\int_Q(q_n-a(x,\eta))\cdot(\xi_n-\eta).$$ Expanding them and using the two weak convergences for the three terms linear in a weakly convergent factor, the limsup hypothesis yields $$0\le\int_Q(q-a(x,\eta))\cdot(\xi-\eta).$$ Indeed the expanded nonnegative sequence has limsup at most the displayed right-hand side, so that right-hand side cannot be negative.

Let $\zeta\in L^p(Q;\mathbb R^d)$ and $0<\varepsilon\le1$. Substitute $\eta=\xi+\varepsilon\zeta$ and $\eta=\xi-\varepsilon\zeta$ into step 1.1. After dividing by $\varepsilon$, the two inequalities give $$\int_Q(q-a(x,\xi+\varepsilon\zeta))\cdot\zeta\le0,\qquad \int_Q(q-a(x,\xi-\varepsilon\zeta))\cdot\zeta\ge0.$$ For either sign, the absolute value of the flux factor times $|\zeta|$ is bounded by $$C\bigl(g(x)+|\xi|^{p-1}+|\zeta|^{p-1}\bigr)|\zeta|,$$ which is integrable by [F3]; here $g(x)$ is viewed as constant in time and $Q$ has finite time length. Carathéodory continuity gives pointwise $a(x,\xi\pm\varepsilon\zeta)\to a(x,\xi)$ as $\varepsilon\downarrow0$. Dominated convergence [F4] in both inequalities proves $\int_Q(q-a(x,\xi))\cdot\zeta=0$ for every $\zeta\in L^p(Q;\mathbb R^d)$.

Put $w=q-a(x,\xi)\in L^{p'}(Q;\mathbb R^d)$ and choose $\zeta=|w|^{p'-2}w$, defined as zero where $w=0$. Since $(p'-1)p=p'$, this $\zeta$ belongs to $L^p$, and step 2.1 gives $0=\int_Qw\cdot\zeta=\int_Q|w|^{p'}$. Thus $w=0$ almost everywhere, which is the claimed flux identification.

citations.quote: Assume the Axiom of Choice. Let $d\ge1$, let $\Omega\subseteq\mathbb R^d$ be a bounded open set, and let $1<p<\infty$ satisfy $p>\max(1,2d/(d+2))$. Then $W_0^{1,p}(\Omega)$ is continuously and compactly embedded in $L^2(\Omega)$. In particular, the inclusion is dense. No boundary regularity is required.

Assume the Axiom of Choice ([[def-axiom-of-choice]]).

Let $d\ge1$, let $\Omega\subset\mathbb R^d$ be a bounded open set, and
let $1<p<\infty$ satisfy $p>\max(1,2d/(d+2))$. Put
$V=W_0^{1,p}(\Omega;\mathbb R)$ with norm
$\|v\|_V=\|\nabla v\|_{L^p(\Omega)}$, $H=L^2(\Omega;\mathbb R)$, and
$p'=p/(p-1)$. The Poincaré inequality makes this norm equivalent to the full
$W^{1,p}$ norm. [[lem-pe12-w0p-separable-reflexive]] gives separability and
reflexivity, while [[lem-pe12-w1p-compact-l2-embedding]] gives the dense
continuous compact inclusion $V\Subset H$; these are the hypotheses of the
evolution triple in [[def-pe12-gelfand-triple]]. The compact-inclusion result
uses the stated threshold also when $d=1$, where it reduces to $p>1$.

A measurable flux $a:\Omega\times\mathbb R^d\to\mathbb R^d$ is an admissible
**coercive monotone diffusion flux of p-growth** if it is Carathéodory (for
each $\xi$, $x\mapsto a(x,\xi)$ is measurable, and for almost every $x$,
$\xi\mapsto a(x,\xi)$ is continuous), and there are constants $C<\infty$,
$\alpha>0$, nonnegative functions $g\in L^{p'}(\Omega)$ and
$h\in L^1(\Omega)$, and one
null set outside which, for all $\xi,\eta\in\mathbb R^d$,
$$|a(x,\xi)|\le C\bigl(g(x)+|\xi|^{p-1}\bigr),\qquad a(x,\xi)\cdot\xi\ge\alpha|\xi|^p-h(x),$$
$$\bigl(a(x,\xi)-a(x,\eta)\bigr)\cdot(\xi-\eta)\ge0.$$
The induced operator $A:V\to V^*$ is
$$\langle A(v),w\rangle_{V^*,V} =\int_\Omega a(x,\nabla v(x))\cdot\nabla w(x)\,dx.$$
The growth bound and Hölder's inequality make this pairing finite and give
$\|A(v)\|_{V^*}\le C_1(\|g\|_{p'}+\|v\|_V^{p-1})$ for a constant $C_1$.
For the finite-dimensional existence result below we additionally require
that this induced map $A:V\to V^*$ is norm-continuous; this is verified
directly for the p-Laplacian in the companion example.

For $f\in L^{p'}(0,T;V^*)$, a weak evolution solution is a function
$u\in W_p(0,T;V)\cap L^\infty(0,T;H)$ with a continuous $H$ representative
such that $u'+A(u)=f$ in $L^{p'}(0,T;V^*)$ and $u(0)=u_0\in H$.

Let $V$ be a separable reflexive real Banach space, let $H$ be a real Hilbert
space, and let $i:V\to H$ be an injective continuous linear map with dense
range. Let $V^*$ be the continuous real dual of $V$ and write
$\langle\cdot,\cdot\rangle_{V^*,V}$ for its pairing with $V$. The canonical
map $J:H\to V^*$ is
$$J h(v)=(h,iv)_H\qquad(h\in H,\ v\in V).$$
It is continuous because $|Jh(v)|\le \|h\|_H\|i\|\|v\|_V$, and injective
because $i(V)$ is dense in $H$. A triple $(V,H,J)$ with these properties is
a **Banach evolution triple**. If $V$ is Hilbert, this is the real evolution
triple of [[def-parabolic-evolution-triple-and-energy-space]].

For $1<p<\infty$, $L^p(0,T;V)$ denotes the Bochner space of strongly
measurable $V$-valued functions with finite $p$th power norm, and
$p'=p/(p-1)$. For $u\in L^p(0,T;V)$ and $g\in L^{p'}(0,T;V^*)$, say
$g=u'$ in the distributional time sense if
$$\int_0^T (iu(t),iv)_H\,\phi'(t)\,dt =-\int_0^T\langle g(t),v\rangle_{V^*,V}\,\phi(t)\,dt$$
for every $v\in V$ and $\phi\in C_c^\infty(0,T)$. Define
$$W_p(0,T;V)=\{u\in L^p(0,T;V):u'\in L^{p'}(0,T;V^*)\}.$$
This definition assigns no endpoint values; a separate chain-rule theorem is
needed before evaluating a function in this space at an endpoint.

Let $(V,H,J)$ be the Banach evolution triple of
[[def-pe12-gelfand-triple]]. An **admissible stable conforming FEM sequence**
consists of finite-dimensional subspaces $V_k\subset V$ and their
$H$-orthogonal projections $\Pi_k:H\to V_k$ such that:

1. $\Pi_k(V)\subset V$, $\Pi_kv=v$ for $v\in V_k$, and
   $(w_k,z-\Pi_kz)_H=0$ for every $w_k\in V_k$, $z\in H$;
2. $\sup_k\|\Pi_k\|_{V\to V}\le C_\Pi<\infty$ and
   $\Pi_kv\to v$ in $V$ for each $v\in V$;
3. the associated time partitions of $[0,T]$ have maximum step
   $\delta_k\to0$.

The convergence in clause 2 and density of $V$ in $H$ imply
$\Pi_kz\to z$ in $H$ for every $z\in H$: use
$\|\Pi_k(z-v)\|_H\le\|z-v\|_H$, $\Pi_kv\to v$ in $H$, and approximate $z$
by $v\in V$. Thus the range spaces approximate every $H$ vector.

For a fixed $k$, backward Euler with averages $f_k^n$ uses unknowns
$U_k^n\in V_k$ and equations
$$\left(\frac{U_k^n-U_k^{n-1}}{\tau_n},v_k\right)_H +\langle A(U_k^n),v_k\rangle =\langle f_k^n,v_k\rangle\qquad(v_k\in V_k).$$
Its piecewise-constant reconstruction is $\overline U_k(t)=U_k^n$ on
$(t_{n-1},t_n]$; its affine reconstruction joins $U_k^{n-1}$ to $U_k^n$.

Assume the Axiom of Choice.

Assume the hypotheses in [[def-pe12-monotone-diffusion-flux]] and an
admissible stable conforming FEM sequence
$(V_k,\Pi_k,\mathcal P_k)$ from
[[def-pe12-stable-conforming-fem-family]]. Let
$f\in L^{p'}(0,T;V^*)$, $u_0\in H$, and on each partition
$\mathcal P_k=(I_k^n)_{n=1}^{N_k}$ put
$f_k^n=|I_k^n|^{-1}\int_{I_k^n}f(t)\,dt$ and
$U_k^0=\Pi_ku_0$. Then for each $k$ there exist
$U_k^n\in V_k$, $1\le n\le N_k$, satisfying
$$\left(\frac{U_k^n-U_k^{n-1}}{\tau_k^n},v_k\right)_H +\langle A(U_k^n),v_k\rangle =\langle f_k^n,v_k\rangle\qquad(v_k\in V_k).$$
Every such solution obeys a bound, independent of $k$ and the time steps,
on
$$\max_n\|U_k^n\|_H^2+ \sum_n\|U_k^n-U_k^{n-1}\|_H^2+ \sum_n\tau_k^n\|U_k^n\|_V^p+ \|D_k\|_{L^{p'}(0,T;V^*)}^{p'},$$
where $D_k=(U_k^n-U_k^{n-1})/\tau_k^n$ on $I_k^n$. The bound depends only
on the flux constants, $p$, $T$, the family stability constant
$C_\Pi$, $\|u_0\|_H$, $\|f\|_{L^{p'}(V^*)}$,
$\|g\|_{L^{p'}(\Omega)}$, and $\|h\|_{L^1(\Omega)}$.

In particular, the same existence and energy conclusion holds on the
fixed-degree uniform interval meshes of $(0,1)$ in $d=1$ and uniform
Kuhn/Freudenthal simplex meshes of $(0,1)^d$ for $d\ge2$, paired with any
time partitions whose maximum step tends to zero independently of the
spatial mesh.

Assume Countable Choice.

Let $X$ be a real Banach space, $0<T<\infty$, and $1\le p<\infty$. For
$f\in L^p(0,T;X)$, translations are continuous in $L^p$ on every compact
subinterval of $(0,T)$. Convolution with a scalar smooth approximate identity
therefore converges to $f$ in $L^p$ on such subintervals. If $\mathcal P_k$
are interval partitions of $[0,T]$ with maximum cell length tending to zero,
the piecewise-constant interval averages of $f$ converge to $f$ in
$L^p(0,T;X)$.

Assume the Axiom of Choice.

Let $V\Subset H\hookrightarrow V^*$ be a Banach evolution triple. For each
$k$, let $0=t_0^k<\cdots<t_{N_k}^k=T$ be a partition with maximum step
$\delta_k\to0$, let $U_k^n\in V$, and define $\overline U_k(t)=U_k^n$ on
$I_n^k=(t_{n-1}^k,t_n^k]$ and
$D_k(t)=(U_k^n-U_k^{n-1})/\tau_n^k$ there. Suppose, for some
$1<p<\infty$ and $1<q\le\infty$,
$$\sup_k\|\overline U_k\|_{L^p(0,T;V)} +\sup_k\|D_k\|_{L^q(0,T;V^*)}<\infty.$$
Then the time translates satisfy, on their common intervals,
$$\|\overline U_k(\cdot+s)-\overline U_k\|_{L^q(V^*)} \le (s+2\delta_k)\|D_k\|_{L^q(V^*)},$$
and $(\overline U_k)$ is relatively compact in $L^p(0,T;H)$. If also
$\sup_{k,n}\|U_k^n\|_H<\infty$, every convergent subsequence converges in
every $L^r(0,T;H)$ with $1\le r<\infty$.

Assume the Axiom of Choice. Let
$\Omega\subseteq\mathbb R^d$ be bounded and open, $d\ge1$, let
$1<p<\infty$, and let $0<T<\infty$. Put $V=W_0^{1,p}(\Omega;\mathbb R)$ with gradient norm
$\|v\|_V=\|\nabla v\|_{L^p}$, and suppose $V$ has a continuous inclusion in
a real Hilbert space $H$. If $u_j$ is bounded in $L^p(0,T;V)$ and its image
in $L^p(0,T;H)$ converges strongly to $u$, then a subsequence converges
weakly in $L^p(0,T;V)$ to some $U$, the image of $U$ equals $u$, and
$\nabla u_j\rightharpoonup\nabla U$ in
$L^p((0,T)\times\Omega;\mathbb R^d)$.

**Assume the Axiom of Countable Choice $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$.**  For every
measure space $(S,\mathcal A,\mu)$ and every $1<p<\infty$, both
$L^p(\mu;\mathbb R)$ and $L^p(\mu;\mathbb C)$ are reflexive.

Assume the ultrafilter lemma, DC, and HB.  A real or complex Banach space $X$
is reflexive if and only if every norm-bounded sequence in $X$ has a
subsequence that converges weakly to a point of $X$.

Let $\mathbb K=\mathbb R$ or $\mathbb C$. A [[def-banach-space|Banach space]] $X$ is **reflexive** if its canonical map $J_X:X\to X^{**}$ from [[def-canonical-map-into-the-bidual]] is surjective. Assuming the Axiom of Choice ([[def-axiom-of-choice]]), [[thm-canonical-bidual-map-is-an-isometry]] shows that this map is already an isometric embedding. Surjectivity means that every bounded linear functional on $X^*$ is evaluation at a vector of $X$. Merely specifying some isomorphism between $X$ and $X^{**}$ is not this definition.

Assume the Axiom of Choice. Let
$(V,H,J)$ be the Banach evolution triple of
[[def-pe12-gelfand-triple]], let $1<p<\infty$, and suppose
$u\in L^p(0,T;V)\cap L^\infty(0,T;H)$ with distributional derivative
$u'\in L^{p'}(0,T;V^*)$. Then $u$ has a unique representative in
$C([0,T];H)$ and, for every $0\le s\le t\le T$,
$$\|u(t)\|_H^2-\|u(s)\|_H^2 =2\int_s^t\langle u'(r),u(r)\rangle_{V^*,V}\,dr.$$

Assume the Axiom of Choice.

Let $Q=(0,T)\times\Omega$ have finite measure, $1<p<\infty$, and let
$a(x,\xi)$ be a Carathéodory flux with the monotonicity and $p$-growth
hypotheses of [[def-pe12-monotone-diffusion-flux]], independent of time.
Suppose $\xi_n\rightharpoonup\xi$ in $L^p(Q;\mathbb R^d)$,
$q_n=a(x,\xi_n)\rightharpoonup q$ in $L^{p'}(Q;\mathbb R^d)$, and
$$\limsup_{n\to\infty}\int_Q q_n\cdot\xi_n \le\int_Qq\cdot\xi.$$
Then $q(x,t)=a(x,\xi(x,t))$ for almost every $(t,x)\in Q$.

Assume the Axiom of Choice ([[def-axiom-of-choice]]).

Let $d\ge1$, let $\Omega\subset\mathbb R^d$ be a bounded open set, and
let $1<p<\infty$ satisfy $p>\max(1,2d/(d+2))$. Put
$V=W_0^{1,p}(\Omega;\mathbb R)$ with norm
$\|v\|_V=\|\nabla v\|_{L^p(\Omega)}$, $H=L^2(\Omega;\mathbb R)$, and
$p'=p/(p-1)$. The Poincaré inequality makes this norm equivalent to the full
$W^{1,p}$ norm. [[lem-pe12-w0p-separable-reflexive]] gives separability and
reflexivity, while [[lem-pe12-w1p-compact-l2-embedding]] gives the dense
continuous compact inclusion $V\Subset H$; these are the hypotheses of the
evolution triple in [[def-pe12-gelfand-triple]]. The compact-inclusion result
uses the stated threshold also when $d=1$, where it reduces to $p>1$.

A measurable flux $a:\Omega\times\mathbb R^d\to\mathbb R^d$ is an admissible
**coercive monotone diffusion flux of p-growth** if it is Carathéodory (for
each $\xi$, $x\mapsto a(x,\xi)$ is measurable, and for almost every $x$,
$\xi\mapsto a(x,\xi)$ is continuous), and there are constants $C<\infty$,
$\alpha>0$, nonnegative functions $g\in L^{p'}(\Omega)$ and
$h\in L^1(\Omega)$, and one
null set outside which, for all $\xi,\eta\in\mathbb R^d$,
$$|a(x,\xi)|\le C\bigl(g(x)+|\xi|^{p-1}\bigr),\qquad a(x,\xi)\cdot\xi\ge\alpha|\xi|^p-h(x),$$
$$\bigl(a(x,\xi)-a(x,\eta)\bigr)\cdot(\xi-\eta)\ge0.$$
The induced operator $A:V\to V^*$ is
$$\langle A(v),w\rangle_{V^*,V} =\int_\Omega a(x,\nabla v(x))\cdot\nabla w(x)\,dx.$$
The growth bound and Hölder's inequality make this pairing finite and give
$\|A(v)\|_{V^*}\le C_1(\|g\|_{p'}+\|v\|_V^{p-1})$ for a constant $C_1$.
For the finite-dimensional existence result below we additionally require
that this induced map $A:V\to V^*$ is norm-continuous; this is verified
directly for the p-Laplacian in the companion example.

For $f\in L^{p'}(0,T;V^*)$, a weak evolution solution is a function
$u\in W_p(0,T;V)\cap L^\infty(0,T;H)$ with a continuous $H$ representative
such that $u'+A(u)=f$ in $L^{p'}(0,T;V^*)$ and $u(0)=u_0\in H$.

For every real Hilbert space $H$ and $x,y\in H$,
$$2(x-y,x)_H=\|x\|_H^2-\|y\|_H^2+\|x-y\|_H^2.$$

A **real Hilbert space** is a real inner-product space $H$ ([[def-real-and-complex-inner-product-space]]) whose induced-length metric is complete in the sense of [[def-complete-metric-space]]: every Cauchy sequence in $H$ for the norm $\|v\|=\sqrt{\langle v,v\rangle}$ ([[cor-inner-product-induces-a-norm]]) converges to a point of $H$. A **complex Hilbert space** is a complex inner-product space with the same completeness property, so that a Hilbert space is exactly a real or complex inner-product space that is a Banach space for its induced norm ([[def-banach-space]]).

**The completion convention is the Cauchy-sequence one.**
[[def-banach-space]] defines completeness by convergence of Cauchy sequences, and this page keeps that convention throughout. It is weaker than $\sigma$-completeness — the assertion that every decreasing sequence of nonempty closed subsets with diameters tending to zero has a nonempty intersection. The two agree in ZFC, but Blackadar, Farah and Karagila note that the closest-point theorem on a $\sigma$-complete inner-product space is provable in ZF, whereas the Cauchy-complete form used below consumes the Axiom of Countable Choice; nothing here silently imports the stronger notion.

Let $(X,\mathcal A,\mu)$ be a measure space, let $p,q\in[1,\infty]$ be
conjugate exponents, and let $f,g$ be measurable real-valued functions.

1. If $1\le p<\infty$ and $q<\infty$ with $f\in\mathcal L^p(\mu)$ and
   $g\in\mathcal L^q(\mu)$, then
   $$\int |fg|\,d\mu\le\|f\|_p\|g\|_q.$$
2. If $p=1$ and $q=\infty$ with $f\in\mathcal L^1(\mu)$ and
   $g\in L^\infty(\mu)$, then
   $$\int |fg|\,d\mu\le\|f\|_1\|g\|_\infty.$$
3. If $p=\infty$ and $q=1$ with $f\in L^\infty(\mu)$ and
   $g\in\mathcal L^1(\mu)$, then
   $$\int |fg|\,d\mu\le\|f\|_\infty\|g\|_1.$$

In every case the right-hand side is finite, so $fg$ is integrable.

Assume the Axiom of Choice for the ACL and absolutely-continuous
fundamental-theorem interfaces. Let $I\subseteq\mathbb R$ be a nonempty open
interval, let $1\le p\le\infty$, let $\mathbb K\in\{\mathbb R,\mathbb C\}$,
and let $u\in W^{1,p}(I;\mathbb K)$, with weak derivative class $Du$. Then
there is exactly one continuous representative $u^*$ of the class of $u$ on
$I$ that is locally absolutely continuous, that is, absolutely continuous on
every compact interval contained in $I$, and satisfies
$$u^*(x)-u^*(y)=\int_y^xDu(t)\,dt\qquad\text{for every }x,y\in I,$$
where for $x<y$ the right-hand side denotes $-\int_x^yDu$, equivalently
$u^*(y)-u^*(x)=\int_x^yDu$ whenever $x\le y$.

If $I=(a,b)$ has finite endpoints, then $Du\in L^1(a,b)$, the representative
$u^*$ extends uniquely to an absolutely continuous function on $[a,b]$, and
the extension satisfies
$$u^*(x)=u^*(a)+\int_a^xDu(t)\,dt\qquad\text{for every }x\in[a,b].$$

The scalar field is arbitrary, $p=1$ and $p=\infty$ are included, and the
one-dimensional interval may be bounded or unbounded. The Axiom of Choice is
used only through the Countable-Choice and Dependent-Choice hypotheses of the
cited characterisation, fundamental-theorem and completeness interfaces.

Assume Countable Choice and fix a degree $k\ge1$. Take a sequence of meshes
with $h\to0$ in either branch and use the
zero-boundary Lagrange spaces $V_h$ from
[[lem-pe12-quasiuniform-mass-inverse-decay]]: globally quasi-uniform,
shape-regular matching affine simplices on a bounded Lipschitz polyhedral
open set in $d\ge2$ (with the local graph-chart convention of
[[lem-pe12-boundary-preserving-quasi-interpolation]]), or interval
partitions of a nonempty bounded interval (or a finite nonempty union of
intervals with disjoint closures) in $d=1$. For $f\in L^1(\Omega)$ define
$P_hf\in V_h$ by the finite mass system
$$
\int_\Omega (P_hf)w_h=\int_\Omega fw_h\qquad(w_h\in V_h).
$$
This is well-defined, agrees on $L^2(\Omega)$ with the $L^2$-orthogonal
projection, and is the identity on $V_h$. There are constants independent
of $h$ such that
$$\|P_hf\|_{L^r(\Omega)}\le C_r\|f\|_{L^r(\Omega)}\qquad(1\le r\le\infty).$$
For every $1<p<\infty$ and $v\in W_0^{1,p}(\Omega)$,
$$\|\nabla P_hv\|_{L^p(\Omega)}\le C_p\|\nabla v\|_{L^p(\Omega)},\qquad P_hv\longrightarrow v\quad\text{in }W^{1,p}(\Omega).$$
For the PE12 application, additionally assume the Axiom of Choice and
$p>\max(1,2d/(d+2))$. The compact embedding
[[lem-pe12-w1p-compact-l2-embedding]] makes $V=W_0^{1,p}(\Omega)$ a dense
subspace of $H=L^2(\Omega)$, and
[[lem-pe12-w0p-separable-reflexive]] supplies the separable reflexive Banach
structure. Thus these spaces form the evolution triple of
[[def-pe12-monotone-diffusion-flux]] and
[[def-pe12-gelfand-triple]], and the $P_h$ above is its $H$-orthogonal
projector. Together with any time partitions whose maximum step tends to
zero it satisfies the projector clauses in
[[def-pe12-stable-conforming-fem-family]]. For every $d\ge2$, the uniform
Kuhn/Freudenthal meshes of $\Omega=(0,1)^d$, and for $d=1$ the uniform
interval meshes of $\Omega=(0,1)$, are explicit nonempty instances throughout
that full strict $p$ range. Time refinement is independent of spatial
refinement.

The **Axiom of Choice** (AC) is the following statement.

> Every family of nonempty sets has a choice function
> ([[def-choice-function]]).

Written out: for every set $\mathcal{F}$ all of whose members are nonempty,
there exists a function $g$ with domain $\mathcal{F}$ satisfying $g(S) \in S$ for
all $S \in \mathcal{F}$.

An equivalent formulation is that a product of nonempty sets is nonempty: if
$X_i \ne \emptyset$ for every $i \in I$, then $\prod_{i \in I} X_i \ne \emptyset$.
Here $\prod_{i \in I} X_i$ is the set of functions $f$ with domain $I$ such that
$f(i) \in X_i$ for every $i \in I$; when a family of nonempty sets is indexed by
itself, such an $f$ is precisely a choice function for it.

In ZF, assume the Axiom of Choice. Then the Axiom of Countable Choice holds.
Moreover, if $R\subseteq X\times X$ is a serial relation on a nonempty set
$X$ and $a\in X$, there is a sequence $(x_n)_{n\in\mathbb N}$ such that
$x_0=a$ and $x_nRx_{n+1}$ for every $n$. Thus AC supplies the
prescribed-initial-point form of Dependent Choice.

**Assume the Axiom of Choice** ([[def-axiom-of-choice]]). Let $X$ be a set and let
$\mathcal{F}_0$ be a filter on $X$ ([[def-filter]]). Then there is an ultrafilter
$\mathcal{U}$ on $X$ ([[def-ultrafilter]]) with $\mathcal{F}_0 \subseteq \mathcal{U}$.

The hypothesis is spent exactly once, through Zorn's lemma at step 4.1; the rest
of the argument is a theorem of ZF.

In particular, every set that carries a filter carries an ultrafilter. The proof
uses Zorn's lemma ([[thm-zorn]]) and therefore the Axiom of Choice. That some
choice principle is unavoidable here, if ZF is consistent, is an external
independence result, not proved in this library; see the remarks below.

Assume the Axiom of Choice. Let $X$ be a real vector space, let
$M \subseteq X$ be a linear subspace, let
$p:X \to \mathbb{R}$ be sublinear, and let $f:M \to \mathbb{R}$ be linear with
$f(m) \le p(m)$ for every $m \in M$. Then there exists a linear functional
$F:X \to \mathbb{R}$ such that $F|_M=f$ and $F(x) \le p(x)$ for every $x \in X$.

The **Axiom of Countable Choice**, written $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$, is the following
statement.

> For every family $(X_n)_{n \in \mathbb{N}}$ of nonempty sets indexed by
> $\mathbb{N}$ there is a function $f$ with domain $\mathbb{N}$ such that
> $f(n) \in X_n$ for every $n \in \mathbb{N}$.

Equivalently, in the vocabulary of [[def-choice-function]]: every at most
countable family of nonempty sets ([[def-countable]]) has a choice function.

Let $X$ be a set and let $R \subseteq X \times X$ be a binary relation on $X$.
Call $R$ **entire on $X$** when

$$\text{for every } x \in X \text{ there is } y \in X \text{ with } x \mathbin{R} y .$$

The **Axiom of Dependent Choice**, written $\mathrm{DC}$, is the following
statement.

> For every nonempty set $X$, every relation $R$ entire on $X$, and every
> $a \in X$, there is a function $x : \mathbb{N} \to X$ ([[def-function]],
> [[def-natural-numbers]]) with
> $$x_0 = a \qquad \text{and} \qquad x_n \mathbin{R} x_{n+1} \ \text{ for every } n \in \mathbb{N}.$$

Here a sequence in $X$ means a function from $\mathbb{N}$ to $X$, not necessarily
a real-valued sequence. As everywhere in this library $\mathbb{N}$ contains $0$, and the sequence is
indexed from $0$; the term $x_0$ is the prescribed starting point $a$ and every
later term is related to its predecessor.

**What DC adds to what came before.** [[def-choice-function]] and
[[def-axiom-of-choice]] select one element from each member of a family that is
fixed in advance, and [[def-countable-choice]] does the same for a family indexed
by $\mathbb{N}$. In both, the family is given before any selection is made. DC is
the principle needed when the $n$-th set to select from is not known until the
first $n$ selections have been made: here the admissible values of $x_{n+1}$ are
exactly the $R$-successors of $x_n$, so the family being chosen from is built
along the choosing. Thus the displayed recursion is directly an instance of
DC; it is not itself an application of the fixed-family formulation of
countable choice. This observation concerns the input to the two axioms and
makes no claim about a nonimplication between them.

**The starting point may be dropped.** The formally weaker statement obtained by
deleting the clause $x_0 = a$ — for every nonempty $X$ and every entire $R$ there
is a sequence with $x_n \mathbin{R} x_{n+1}$ for all $n$ — is an immediate
consequence of the form above, since $X$ is nonempty and any of its elements may
be taken as $a$. Conversely, assume the start-free form, and fix $X$, $R$ and $a$ as above. Let $P$ be the set of all functions $p:k\to X$ with nonzero $k\in\mathbb N$, $p(0)=a$, and $p(i)\mathbin R p(i+1)$ whenever $i+1<k$. It is a set by Separation inside $\mathcal P(\mathbb N\times X)$ ([[def-power-set]], [[def-cartesian-product]], [[def-axiom-schema-of-separation]]); a natural is the set of its predecessors ([[lem-nat-order-is-membership]]). The singleton path $\{(0,a)\}$ lies in $P$.

On $P$ let $p\mathbin S q$ mean that $q$ extends $p$ by exactly one new last entry. This relation is entire: for one particular $p:k\to X$, write $k=j+1$ ([[lem-nat-nonzero-is-successor]]); an $R$-successor $y$ of $p(j)$ exists, and $q=p\cup\{(k,y)\}$ is the required extension. This is existential instantiation for that path, not a simultaneous choice of successors. Start-free DC now supplies a sequence $(p_n)$ with $p_n\mathbin S p_{n+1}$; its first path need not be the singleton path, but every path in $P$ already starts at $a$.

Their graphs are nested. By induction ([[thm-induction-principle]]), $p_n$ has at least $n+1$ entries: the initial path is nonempty, and every step adds one entry. Hence $x=\bigcup_{n\in\mathbb N}p_n$ is a function with domain $\mathbb N$ and values in $X$. Indeed, nestedness makes all common values agree, every natural index eventually lies in a path, and no path has indices outside $\mathbb N$. Each path starts at $a$, so $x(0)=a$; for any $i$, a sufficiently long path contains both $i$ and $i+1$, giving $x(i)\mathbin R x(i+1)$. Replacement and Union form this union of the sequence of graphs. Thus the start-free and prescribed-start forms are equivalent in ZF. Every use below retains the prescribed-start convention.

**$R$ need not be an order and the terms need not be distinct.** What DC delivers
is a sequence, that is a function $\mathbb{N} \to X$, not a chain in the
order-theoretic sense ([[def-chain]]). The relation may be symmetric, and the
sequence may repeat a value or be constant; all that is asserted is
$x_n \mathbin{R} x_{n+1}$ at every index.

The **ultrafilter extension principle** says that every filter on a set is contained in an ultrafilter on that set ([[def-ultrafilter]]).

It is also called the **ultrafilter lemma** and is equivalent over ZF to the Boolean prime ideal theorem, abbreviated BPI. Items below write **assume UL/BPI** precisely when they use this extension principle; they do not thereby assume the full axiom of choice.

Work over ZF. The **real dominated-extension principle**, denoted **HB**, is the following assertion:

For every real vector space $X$, every sublinear functional $p:X\to\mathbb R$ in the sense of [[def-sublinear-functional]], every real linear subspace $M\le X$ in the sense of [[def-linear-subspace]], and every real linear functional $g:M\to\mathbb R$ in the sense of [[def-algebraic-dual-and-linear-functional]],
$$\bigl(\forall m\in M,\ g(m)\le p(m)\bigr)\ \Longrightarrow\ \exists F:X\to\mathbb R\ \bigl(F\text{ is real linear},\ F|_M=g,\ \forall x\in X,\ F(x)\le p(x)\bigr).$$

This names an additional principle; it does not assert a proof of HB in ZF. Subsequent results explicitly state when they assume HB. Neither topology nor completeness is part of this assertion. The subspace may be $\{0\}$ or all of $X$. Sublinearity at scalar zero gives $p(0)=0$, and a linear functional has value zero at zero.

derivations.claim: The orthogonal projections are contractions on $H$, and for any $v\in V$, $\Pi_kv\to v$ in $V$ and hence in $H$. Given $u_0\in H$, choose $v\in V$ close to $u_0$ using density in [F1]. Then $$\|\Pi_ku_0-u_0\|_H \le2\|u_0-v\|_H+\|\Pi_kv-v\|_H\to2\|u_0-v\|_H.$$ Letting $v$ approach $u_0$ proves $\Pi_ku_0\to u_0$ in $H$. Also [F4] gives $f_k\to f$ strongly in $L^{p'}(V^*)$ for the piecewise-constant averages $f_k(t)=f_k^n$ on $I_k^n$.

By [F3], the reconstructions $\overline U_k$ are uniformly bounded in $L^p(V)$ and $L^\infty(H)$, and their discrete derivatives $D_k$ are uniformly bounded in $L^{p'}(V^*)$. The maximum partition step tends to zero, so [F5] gives a subsequence converging strongly in $L^p(H)$ and, by the $L^\infty(H)$ bound, in every finite $L^r(H)$. Applying [F6] to this subsequence gives a further subsequence and $u\in L^p(V)$ such that $\overline U_k\rightharpoonup u$ in $L^p(V)$, its image in $L^p(H)$ is the strong limit, and $\nabla\overline U_k\rightharpoonup\nabla u$ in $L^p(Q;\mathbb R^d)$.

If $u$ and $\widetilde u$ are two solutions with the same data, their difference $w=u-\widetilde u$ has zero initial value and satisfies $w'+A(u)-A(\widetilde u)=0$. By [F8], for every $t$, $$\frac12\|w(t)\|_H^2+ \int_0^t\langle A(u)-A(\widetilde u),w\rangle=0.$$ Pointwise monotonicity in [F1] makes the integral nonnegative, so $w(t)=0$ for every $t$. This proves uniqueness in the abstract conclusion.

Put $q_k(t,x)=a(x,\nabla\overline U_k(t,x))$. Measurability and the growth hypothesis [F1] give $$\|q_k\|_{L^{p'}(Q)} \le C\bigl(T^{1/p'}\|g\|_{L^{p'}(\Omega)} +\|\nabla\overline U_k\|_{L^p(Q)}^{p-1}\bigr),$$ so $(q_k)$ is bounded in vector-valued $L^{p'}(Q)$. Each of its $d$ coordinates is bounded in scalar $L^{p'}(Q)$ and hence has a weakly convergent subsequence by [F7]. Successive extraction over the finite coordinate set gives one subsequence weakly convergent in every coordinate; restriction of any bounded functional on the finite product to its coordinate embeddings shows weak convergence of the vector fields. Write the limit as $q\in L^{p'}(Q;\mathbb R^d)$.

abla\Pi_kv\,\phi =\int_0^T\langle f_k,\Pi_kvangle\phi.$$ On each cell, $\|\widehat U_k-\overline U_k\|_{V^*}\le	au_k^n\|D_k\|_{V^*}$, hence $$\|\widehat U_k-\overline U_k\|_{L^{p'}(0,T;V^*)} \le\delta_k\|D_k\|_{L^{p'}(0,T;V^*)}	o0.$$ Now [F2] gives $\Pi_kv	o v$ in $V$; steps 1.2 and 2.1 give the strong state convergence and weak flux convergence; [F4] gives strong convergence of $f_k$. Hölder [F11] therefore permits passage in every term, yielding $$-\int_0^T(u,v)_H\phi' +\int_Qq\cdot
abla v\,\phi =\int_0^T\langle f,vangle\phi.$$ Thus the distributional derivative of $u$ is $f-B_q$, where $\langle B_q(t),vangle=\int_\Omega q(t,x)\cdot
abla v(x)\,dx$ and $B_q\in L^{p'}(0,T;V^*)$.

The uniform bound $\|\overline U_k(t)\|_H\le M$ and strong $L^p(H)$ convergence imply $\bigl(\|u(t)\|_H-M\bigr)_+\le\|u(t)-\overline U_k(t)\|_H$ almost everywhere. Taking $L^p$ norms and passing to the limit shows $u\in L^\infty(0,T;H)$. Step 3.1 places $u$ in $L^p(V)$ with derivative $f-B_q\in L^{p'}(V^*)$; [F8] therefore gives its continuous $H$ representative and energy identity.

Fix $v\in V$. The scalar affine interpolants $\alpha_k(t)=(\widehat U_k(t),v)_H$ are uniformly bounded, and $\alpha_k'(t)=\langle D_k(t),v\rangle$ is uniformly bounded in $L^{p'}$. Hölder gives a common modulus $|\alpha_k(t)-\alpha_k(s)|\le C_v|t-s|^{1/p}$. The reconstruction defect in step 3.1 and the strong state convergence imply $\alpha_k\to\alpha:=(u,v)_H$ in $L^1(0,T)$; $\alpha$ is continuous by step 4.1. This convergence is uniform: if $|\alpha_k(t_k)-\alpha(t_k)|\ge\varepsilon$ along a subsequence, the common modulus and continuity of $\alpha$ give a fixed $\delta>0$ on which the difference is at least $\varepsilon/3$ around $t_k$. The intersected interval has length at least $\min(\delta,T)$, contradicting $L^1$ convergence. Therefore $(U_k^{N_k},v)_H=\alpha_k(T)\to(u(T),v)_H$.

Use a smooth $\phi$ with $\phi(0)=1$ and $\phi(T)=0$. abla\overline U_k \le\int_0^T\langle f_k,\overline U_kangle + rac12\|U_k^0\|_H^2- rac12\|U_k^{N_k}\|_H^2.$$ Strong convergence $f_k	o f$ and weak convergence $\overline U_kightharpoonup u$ make the first term on the right converge to $\int_0^T\langle f,uangle$. Assume the Axiom of Choice. Let
$(V,H,J)$ be the Banach evolution triple of
[[def-pe12-gelfand-triple]], let $1<p<\infty$, and suppose
$u\in L^p(0,T;V)\cap L^\infty(0,T;H)$ with distributional derivative
$u'\in L^{p'}(0,T;V^*)$. Then $u$ has a unique representative in
$C([0,T];H)$ and, for every $0\le s\le t\le T$,
$$\|u(t)\|_H^2-\|u(s)\|_H^2 =2\int_s^t\langle u'(r),u(r)\rangle_{V^*,V}\,dr.$$

Let $(X,\mathcal A,\mu)$ be a measure space, let $p,q\in[1,\infty]$ be
conjugate exponents, and let $f,g$ be measurable real-valued functions.

1. If $1\le p<\infty$ and $q<\infty$ with $f\in\mathcal L^p(\mu)$ and
   $g\in\mathcal L^q(\mu)$, then
   $$\int |fg|\,d\mu\le\|f\|_p\|g\|_q.$$
2. If $p=1$ and $q=\infty$ with $f\in\mathcal L^1(\mu)$ and
   $g\in L^\infty(\mu)$, then
   $$\int |fg|\,d\mu\le\|f\|_1\|g\|_\infty.$$
3. If $p=\infty$ and $q=1$ with $f\in L^\infty(\mu)$ and
   $g\in\mathcal L^1(\mu)$, then
   $$\int |fg|\,d\mu\le\|f\|_\infty\|g\|_1.$$

In every case the right-hand side is finite, so $fg$ is integrable.

Assume the Axiom of Choice ([[def-axiom-of-choice]]).

Let $d\ge1$, let $\Omega\subset\mathbb R^d$ be a bounded open set, and
let $1<p<\infty$ satisfy $p>\max(1,2d/(d+2))$. Put
$V=W_0^{1,p}(\Omega;\mathbb R)$ with norm
$\|v\|_V=\|\nabla v\|_{L^p(\Omega)}$, $H=L^2(\Omega;\mathbb R)$, and
$p'=p/(p-1)$. The Poincaré inequality makes this norm equivalent to the full
$W^{1,p}$ norm. [[lem-pe12-w0p-separable-reflexive]] gives separability and
reflexivity, while [[lem-pe12-w1p-compact-l2-embedding]] gives the dense
continuous compact inclusion $V\Subset H$; these are the hypotheses of the
evolution triple in [[def-pe12-gelfand-triple]]. The compact-inclusion result
uses the stated threshold also when $d=1$, where it reduces to $p>1$.

A measurable flux $a:\Omega\times\mathbb R^d\to\mathbb R^d$ is an admissible
**coercive monotone diffusion flux of p-growth** if it is Carathéodory (for
each $\xi$, $x\mapsto a(x,\xi)$ is measurable, and for almost every $x$,
$\xi\mapsto a(x,\xi)$ is continuous), and there are constants $C<\infty$,
$\alpha>0$, nonnegative functions $g\in L^{p'}(\Omega)$ and
$h\in L^1(\Omega)$, and one
null set outside which, for all $\xi,\eta\in\mathbb R^d$,
$$|a(x,\xi)|\le C\bigl(g(x)+|\xi|^{p-1}\bigr),\qquad a(x,\xi)\cdot\xi\ge\alpha|\xi|^p-h(x),$$
$$\bigl(a(x,\xi)-a(x,\eta)\bigr)\cdot(\xi-\eta)\ge0.$$
The induced operator $A:V\to V^*$ is
$$\langle A(v),w\rangle_{V^*,V} =\int_\Omega a(x,\nabla v(x))\cdot\nabla w(x)\,dx.$$
The growth bound and Hölder's inequality make this pairing finite and give
$\|A(v)\|_{V^*}\le C_1(\|g\|_{p'}+\|v\|_V^{p-1})$ for a constant $C_1$.
For the finite-dimensional existence result below we additionally require
that this induced map $A:V\to V^*$ is norm-continuous; this is verified
directly for the p-Laplacian in the companion example.

For $f\in L^{p'}(0,T;V^*)$, a weak evolution solution is a function
$u\in W_p(0,T;V)\cap L^\infty(0,T;H)$ with a continuous $H$ representative
such that $u'+A(u)=f$ in $L^{p'}(0,T;V^*)$ and $u(0)=u_0\in H$.

The **Axiom of Choice** (AC) is the following statement.

> Every family of nonempty sets has a choice function
> ([[def-choice-function]]).

Written out: for every set $\mathcal{F}$ all of whose members are nonempty,
there exists a function $g$ with domain $\mathcal{F}$ satisfying $g(S) \in S$ for
all $S \in \mathcal{F}$.

An equivalent formulation is that a product of nonempty sets is nonempty: if
$X_i \ne \emptyset$ for every $i \in I$, then $\prod_{i \in I} X_i \ne \emptyset$.
Here $\prod_{i \in I} X_i$ is the set of functions $f$ with domain $I$ such that
$f(i) \in X_i$ for every $i \in I$; when a family of nonempty sets is indexed by
itself, such an $f$ is precisely a choice function for it.

derivations.claim: Set $e=u-v$. Subtracting the residual definitions gives $e'+A(u)-A(v)=R$ in $L^{p'}(0,T;V^*)$. By [F1], testing this identity against $e\in L^p(0,T;V)$ is integrable by [F2], and for every $t$, $$\frac12\|e(t)\|_H^2-\frac12\|e(0)\|_H^2 +\int_0^t\langle A(u)-A(v),e\rangle =\int_0^t\langle R,e\rangle.$$

Strong monotonicity bounds the left integral below by $\mu\int_0^t\|e\|_V^p$. Young's inequality in the scaled form $$ab\le\frac\mu2a^p+ \frac1{p'}\left(\frac2{\mu p}\right)^{1/(p-1)}b^{p'}$$ gives $|\langle R,e\rangle|\le\frac\mu2\|e\|_V^p+ C_{\mu,p}\|R\|_{V^*}^{p'}$. Integrating and absorbing the first term yields $$\frac12\|e(t)\|_H^2+\frac\mu2\int_0^t\|e\|_V^p \le\frac12\|e(0)\|_H^2+ C_{\mu,p}\|R\|_{L^{p'}(0,t;V^*)}^{p'}.$$ Multiplying by two proves the estimate. If $e(0)=0$ and $R=0$, the nonnegative left side vanishes for every $t$, hence $e(t)=0$ in $H$ and $e=0$ in $L^p(V)$.

$\Omega=(0,1)$ in $d=1$ and $\Omega=(0,1)^d$ in each $d\ge2$, the explicit
fixed-degree interval and Kuhn/Freudenthal simplex families of
[[thm-pe12-l2-projector-w1p-stability]] verify those clauses for any
independent time partitions with vanishing maximum step. These are concrete
nonempty instances of the theorem on the full approved strict $p$ range.

Let $(V,H,J)$ be the Banach evolution triple of
[[def-pe12-gelfand-triple]]. An **admissible stable conforming FEM sequence**
consists of finite-dimensional subspaces $V_k\subset V$ and their
$H$-orthogonal projections $\Pi_k:H\to V_k$ such that:

1. $\Pi_k(V)\subset V$, $\Pi_kv=v$ for $v\in V_k$, and
   $(w_k,z-\Pi_kz)_H=0$ for every $w_k\in V_k$, $z\in H$;
2. $\sup_k\|\Pi_k\|_{V\to V}\le C_\Pi<\infty$ and
   $\Pi_kv\to v$ in $V$ for each $v\in V$;
3. the associated time partitions of $[0,T]$ have maximum step
   $\delta_k\to0$.

The convergence in clause 2 and density of $V$ in $H$ imply
$\Pi_kz\to z$ in $H$ for every $z\in H$: use
$\|\Pi_k(z-v)\|_H\le\|z-v\|_H$, $\Pi_kv\to v$ in $H$, and approximate $z$
by $v\in V$. Thus the range spaces approximate every $H$ vector.

For a fixed $k$, backward Euler with averages $f_k^n$ uses unknowns
$U_k^n\in V_k$ and equations
$$\left(\frac{U_k^n-U_k^{n-1}}{\tau_n},v_k\right)_H +\langle A(U_k^n),v_k\rangle =\langle f_k^n,v_k\rangle\qquad(v_k\in V_k).$$
Its piecewise-constant reconstruction is $\overline U_k(t)=U_k^n$ on
$(t_{n-1},t_n]$; its affine reconstruction joins $U_k^{n-1}$ to $U_k^n$.

Assume Countable Choice and fix a degree $k\ge1$. Take a sequence of meshes
with $h\to0$ in either branch and use the
zero-boundary Lagrange spaces $V_h$ from
[[lem-pe12-quasiuniform-mass-inverse-decay]]: globally quasi-uniform,
shape-regular matching affine simplices on a bounded Lipschitz polyhedral
open set in $d\ge2$ (with the local graph-chart convention of
[[lem-pe12-boundary-preserving-quasi-interpolation]]), or interval
partitions of a nonempty bounded interval (or a finite nonempty union of
intervals with disjoint closures) in $d=1$. For $f\in L^1(\Omega)$ define
$P_hf\in V_h$ by the finite mass system
$$
\int_\Omega (P_hf)w_h=\int_\Omega fw_h\qquad(w_h\in V_h).
$$
This is well-defined, agrees on $L^2(\Omega)$ with the $L^2$-orthogonal
projection, and is the identity on $V_h$. There are constants independent
of $h$ such that
$$\|P_hf\|_{L^r(\Omega)}\le C_r\|f\|_{L^r(\Omega)}\qquad(1\le r\le\infty).$$
For every $1<p<\infty$ and $v\in W_0^{1,p}(\Omega)$,
$$\|\nabla P_hv\|_{L^p(\Omega)}\le C_p\|\nabla v\|_{L^p(\Omega)},\qquad P_hv\longrightarrow v\quad\text{in }W^{1,p}(\Omega).$$
For the PE12 application, additionally assume the Axiom of Choice and
$p>\max(1,2d/(d+2))$. The compact embedding
[[lem-pe12-w1p-compact-l2-embedding]] makes $V=W_0^{1,p}(\Omega)$ a dense
subspace of $H=L^2(\Omega)$, and
[[lem-pe12-w0p-separable-reflexive]] supplies the separable reflexive Banach
structure. Thus these spaces form the evolution triple of
[[def-pe12-monotone-diffusion-flux]] and
[[def-pe12-gelfand-triple]], and the $P_h$ above is its $H$-orthogonal
projector. Together with any time partitions whose maximum step tends to
zero it satisfies the projector clauses in
[[def-pe12-stable-conforming-fem-family]]. For every $d\ge2$, the uniform
Kuhn/Freudenthal meshes of $\Omega=(0,1)^d$, and for $d=1$ the uniform
interval meshes of $\Omega=(0,1)$, are explicit nonempty instances throughout
that full strict $p$ range. Time refinement is independent of spatial
refinement.

The **Axiom of Choice** (AC) is the following statement.

> Every family of nonempty sets has a choice function
> ([[def-choice-function]]).

Written out: for every set $\mathcal{F}$ all of whose members are nonempty,
there exists a function $g$ with domain $\mathcal{F}$ satisfying $g(S) \in S$ for
all $S \in \mathcal{F}$.

An equivalent formulation is that a product of nonempty sets is nonempty: if
$X_i \ne \emptyset$ for every $i \in I$, then $\prod_{i \in I} X_i \ne \emptyset$.
Here $\prod_{i \in I} X_i$ is the set of functions $f$ with domain $I$ such that
$f(i) \in X_i$ for every $i \in I$; when a family of nonempty sets is indexed by
itself, such an $f$ is precisely a choice function for it.

Assume the Axiom of Choice ([[def-axiom-of-choice]]).

Let $d\ge1$, let $\Omega\subset\mathbb R^d$ be a bounded open set, and
let $1<p<\infty$ satisfy $p>\max(1,2d/(d+2))$. Put
$V=W_0^{1,p}(\Omega;\mathbb R)$ with norm
$\|v\|_V=\|\nabla v\|_{L^p(\Omega)}$, $H=L^2(\Omega;\mathbb R)$, and
$p'=p/(p-1)$. The Poincaré inequality makes this norm equivalent to the full
$W^{1,p}$ norm. [[lem-pe12-w0p-separable-reflexive]] gives separability and
reflexivity, while [[lem-pe12-w1p-compact-l2-embedding]] gives the dense
continuous compact inclusion $V\Subset H$; these are the hypotheses of the
evolution triple in [[def-pe12-gelfand-triple]]. The compact-inclusion result
uses the stated threshold also when $d=1$, where it reduces to $p>1$.

A measurable flux $a:\Omega\times\mathbb R^d\to\mathbb R^d$ is an admissible
**coercive monotone diffusion flux of p-growth** if it is Carathéodory (for
each $\xi$, $x\mapsto a(x,\xi)$ is measurable, and for almost every $x$,
$\xi\mapsto a(x,\xi)$ is continuous), and there are constants $C<\infty$,
$\alpha>0$, nonnegative functions $g\in L^{p'}(\Omega)$ and
$h\in L^1(\Omega)$, and one
null set outside which, for all $\xi,\eta\in\mathbb R^d$,
$$|a(x,\xi)|\le C\bigl(g(x)+|\xi|^{p-1}\bigr),\qquad a(x,\xi)\cdot\xi\ge\alpha|\xi|^p-h(x),$$
$$\bigl(a(x,\xi)-a(x,\eta)\bigr)\cdot(\xi-\eta)\ge0.$$
The induced operator $A:V\to V^*$ is
$$\langle A(v),w\rangle_{V^*,V} =\int_\Omega a(x,\nabla v(x))\cdot\nabla w(x)\,dx.$$
The growth bound and Hölder's inequality make this pairing finite and give
$\|A(v)\|_{V^*}\le C_1(\|g\|_{p'}+\|v\|_V^{p-1})$ for a constant $C_1$.
For the finite-dimensional existence result below we additionally require
that this induced map $A:V\to V^*$ is norm-continuous; this is verified
directly for the p-Laplacian in the companion example.

For $f\in L^{p'}(0,T;V^*)$, a weak evolution solution is a function
$u\in W_p(0,T;V)\cap L^\infty(0,T;H)$ with a continuous $H$ representative
such that $u'+A(u)=f$ in $L^{p'}(0,T;V^*)$ and $u(0)=u_0\in H$.

Assume the Axiom of Choice. Let $d\ge1$, let $\Omega\subseteq\mathbb R^d$ be a bounded open set, and let $1<p<\infty$ satisfy $p>\max(1,2d/(d+2))$. Then $W_0^{1,p}(\Omega)$ is continuously and compactly embedded in $L^2(\Omega)$. In particular, the inclusion is dense. No boundary regularity is required.

derivations.claim: Let $J_p(\xi)=|\xi|^{p-2}\xi$ and $\Phi(\xi)=|\xi|^p/p$. The function $\Phi$ is convex: the triangle inequality gives $|\theta\xi+(1-\theta)\eta|\le\theta|\xi|+(1-\theta)|\eta|$, and $r\mapsto r^p$ is increasing and convex for $r\ge0$. It is differentiable with $\nabla\Phi=J_p$, including at zero because $p>1$. For a differentiable convex function, restriction to the segment from $\eta$ to $\xi$ gives the tangent inequalities $$\Phi(\xi)\ge\Phi(\eta)+J_p(\eta)\cdot(\xi-\eta),\qquad \Phi(\eta)\ge\Phi(\xi)+J_p(\xi)\cdot(\eta-\xi).$$ Adding them yields $(J_p(\xi)-J_p(\eta))\cdot(\xi-\eta)\ge0$. Also $J_p(\xi)\cdot\xi=|\xi|^p$ and $|J_p(\xi)|=|\xi|^{p-1}$, giving monotonicity, coercivity with $\alpha=1,h=0$, and growth with $C=1,g=0$.

For $p\ge2$, the derivative of $J_p$ has operator norm at most $(p-1)|z|^{p-2}$. Integrating it along the segment from $\eta$ to $\xi$ gives $$|J_p(\xi)-J_p(\eta)| \le(p-1)(|\xi|+|\eta|)^{p-2}|\xi-\eta|.$$ For $1<p<2$, put $d_0=|\xi-\eta|$ and $M_0=\max(|\xi|,|\eta|)$. If $d_0\ge M_0/2$, then $|J_p(\xi)-J_p(\eta)|\le2M_0^{p-1}\le2^{p}d_0^{p-1}$. If $0<d_0<M_0/2$, every point on the segment has norm at least $M_0/2$; there the derivative norm is at most $(M_0/2)^{p-2}$. Hence $$|J_p(\xi)-J_p(\eta)| \le (M_0/2)^{p-2}d_0\le C_p d_0^{p-1},$$ because $(d_0/M_0)^{2-p}\le1$. The case $d_0=0$ is immediate. Thus for $1<p<2$ the global estimate $|J_p(\xi)-J_p(\eta)|\le C_p|\xi-\eta|^{p-1}$ holds.

derivations.claim: Write $\alpha=1/(m-1)$, $y=xt^{-\beta}$, and $F(y)=(C-ky^2)_+^\alpha$. Then $u=t^{-\beta}F(y)$ and $u^m=t^{-m\beta}G(y)$, where $G(y)=(C-ky^2)_+^{\alpha+1}$. Inside the positivity set, $$u_t=t^{-\beta-1}(-\beta F-\beta yF'),\qquad (u^m)_{xx}=t^{-(m+2)\beta}G''.$$ Equality of the time powers requires $\beta+1=(m+2)\beta$, giving $\beta=1/(m+1)$.

In the positivity set put $q=C-ky^2>0$. Direct differentiation gives $$F'= -2k\alpha yq^{\alpha-1},\qquad G''=-2k(\alpha+1)q^{\alpha-1}(q-2k\alpha y^2) =-2k(\alpha+1)(F+yF').$$ Choosing $2k(\alpha+1)=\beta$ makes $G''=-\beta(F+yF')$, exactly the remaining profile equation. Since $\alpha+1=m/(m-1)$, this choice is $k=(m-1)/(2m(m+1))$. Thus the PDE holds pointwise wherever $u>0$; both sides vanish in the open set where $u=0$.

The interface is $q=0$. The profile $u$ tends to zero there because $\alpha>0$. The spatial flux $G$ and its first derivative $G'=-2k(\alpha+1)yq_+^\alpha$ also tend to zero at the interface, so distributional differentiation of $G$ creates no boundary delta. Its interior second derivative is locally integrable: its only possible singularity is proportional to $q^{\alpha-1}$ and $\alpha-1>-1$. Likewise, $u_t$ has only a locally integrable $q^{\alpha-1}$ singularity; the moving interface contributes no time delta because the jump of $u$ across it is zero. Hence the pointwise identity of step 2.1 extends distributionally across the interface.

The positivity condition is $C-kx^2t^{-2\beta}>0$, equivalent to $|x|<\sqrt{C/k}\,t^\beta$. Therefore the support is the stated closed interval, with radius proportional to $t^\beta=t^{1/(m+1)}$. This proves finite propagation and the claimed scaling.
