Let $(V,H,V^*)$ be a real evolution triple and let $V_h\subset V$ be a
finite-dimensional conforming subspace. In a mesh instance, the algebraic
piecewise-polynomial conventions are those of
[[def-broken-and-conforming-polynomial-spaces]]; the required inclusion into
$V$ is an explicit hypothesis of this definition. Let
$a:V\times V\to\mathbb R$ be time-independent,
bounded, and coercive as in
[[def-bounded-coercive-and-symmetric-sesquilinear-forms]], with constants
$M$ and $\alpha>0$. For $u\in V$, the equation for the unknown $z_h\in V_h$
$$a(z_h,v_h)=a(u,v_h)\qquad\text{for every }v_h\in V_h$$
is the **Ritz equation**; any solution $z_h$ is called a Ritz projection of
$u$. The item [[lem-parabolic-ritz-projection-well-defined]] proves that for
every $u$ there is exactly one solution, denoted $R_hu$, and that these
solutions define a bounded linear map $R_h:V\to V_h$. The form need not be
symmetric.

Assume Countable Choice. Let $I=(0,1)$ and define
$$\phi(x)=\begin{cases}2x,&0\le x\le\frac12,\\2(1-x),&\frac12\le x\le1,\end{cases} \qquad p(x)=\frac12x(1-x).$$
Then $\phi|_I,p|_I\in H^1_0(I)=W^{1,2}_0(I)$, the closure of
$C_c^\infty(I)$ in $W^{1,2}(I)$ ([[def-wkp-zero-as-a-sobolev-closure]]).

Assume Countable Choice ([[def-countable-choice]]). Let $\Omega\subseteq\mathbb R^n$ be open and bounded in one direction: there are a unit vector $e$ and $a<b$ with $a<x\cdot e<b$ for every $x\in\Omega$. Let $1\le p<\infty$. Then $\|u\|_{L^p(\Omega)}\le C(p)\,(b-a)\,\|Du\|_{L^p(\Omega)}$ for every $u\in W^{1,p}_0(\Omega;\mathbb K)$.

Assume Countable Choice. Let $\Omega\subseteq\mathbb R^d$ be a bounded
polyhedral open set with $d\ge1$. Put
$$H=L^2(\Omega;\mathbb R),\qquad V=W^{1,2}_0(\Omega;\mathbb R),\qquad \|v\|_V=\|v\|_{W^{1,2}(\Omega)}.$$
Then $V$ is a separable real Hilbert space, and the inclusion
$V\hookrightarrow H$ is continuous, injective and dense. Consequently
$(V,H,V^*)$ is a real evolution triple in the sense of
[[def-parabolic-evolution-triple-and-energy-space]]. The gradient norm
$\|\nabla v\|_{L^2}$ is equivalent to this norm on $V$ by Poincare's
inequality.

The **Axiom of Countable Choice**, written $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$, is the following
statement.

> For every family $(X_n)_{n \in \mathbb{N}}$ of nonempty sets indexed by
> $\mathbb{N}$ there is a function $f$ with domain $\mathbb{N}$ such that
> $f(n) \in X_n$ for every $n \in \mathbb{N}$.

Equivalently, in the vocabulary of [[def-choice-function]]: every at most
countable family of nonempty sets ([[def-countable]]) has a choice function.

derivations.claim: By [F2], $V_h\subset V$ and $v\in V$. By [F3], $|a(f,g)|\le\|f\|_{H^1}\|g\|_{H^1}$ and $a(f,f)=\|f'\|_2^2\ge\frac12\|f\|_{H^1}^2$, so $a$ is bounded, symmetric and coercive as required by [F1]. The displayed hat has slopes $2$ and $-2$. Also $v'(x)=1-2x$, and direct integration gives $$a(v,w)=2\int_0^{1/2}(1-2x)\,dx -2\int_{1/2}^1(1-2x)\,dx=1,\qquad a(w,w)=4.$$ Since $R_hv=cw$, [F1] with test $w$ gives $4c=1$, so $R_hv=w/4$ and its slopes are $1/2$ and $-1/2$.

On each half interval, $|(R_hv)'|(R_hv)'w'=1/2$, so its integral is $1/2$. On the left half, $v'\ge0$ and $|v'|v'w'=2(1-2x)^2$, whose integral is $1/3$. On the right half, $v'\le0$ and the same integrand $2(1-2x)^2$ also integrates to $1/3$. Therefore $\int_0^1|v'|v'w'=2/3$.

The two residual pairings are $1/2$ and $2/3$, so they are unequal. This explicit conforming Ritz space refutes any general claim that a linear Ritz projection preserves every nonlinear $p$-Laplacian Galerkin residual.

Let $V$ be a separable reflexive real Banach space, let $H$ be a real Hilbert
space, and let $i:V\to H$ be an injective continuous linear map with dense
range. Let $V^*$ be the continuous real dual of $V$ and write
$\langle\cdot,\cdot\rangle_{V^*,V}$ for its pairing with $V$. The canonical
map $J:H\to V^*$ is
$$J h(v)=(h,iv)_H\qquad(h\in H,\ v\in V).$$
It is continuous because $|Jh(v)|\le \|h\|_H\|i\|\|v\|_V$, and injective
because $i(V)$ is dense in $H$. A triple $(V,H,J)$ with these properties is
a **Banach evolution triple**. If $V$ is Hilbert, this is the real evolution
triple of [[def-parabolic-evolution-triple-and-energy-space]].

For $1<p<\infty$, $L^p(0,T;V)$ denotes the Bochner space of strongly
measurable $V$-valued functions with finite $p$th power norm, and
$p'=p/(p-1)$. For $u\in L^p(0,T;V)$ and $g\in L^{p'}(0,T;V^*)$, say
$g=u'$ in the distributional time sense if
$$\int_0^T (iu(t),iv)_H\,\phi'(t)\,dt =-\int_0^T\langle g(t),v\rangle_{V^*,V}\,\phi(t)\,dt$$
for every $v\in V$ and $\phi\in C_c^\infty(0,T)$. Define
$$W_p(0,T;V)=\{u\in L^p(0,T;V):u'\in L^{p'}(0,T;V^*)\}.$$
This definition assigns no endpoint values; a separate chain-rule theorem is
needed before evaluating a function in this space at an endpoint.

derivations.claim: Since each interval $[0,T]$ contains exactly $n$ periods of $\sin(2\pi nt/T)$, a change of variable gives $$\|u_n\|_{L^p(0,T;V)}^p =\|v\|_V^p\frac{T}{2\pi} \int_0^{2\pi}|\sin s|^p\,ds,$$ independent of $n$. Thus the family is uniformly bounded in each stated $L^p(V)$.

For distinct positive integers $n\ne m$, sine orthogonality over $[0,T]$ gives $$\|u_n-u_m\|_{L^2(0,T;H)}^2 =\|iv\|_H^2\int_0^T (\sin(2\pi nt/T)-\sin(2\pi mt/T))^2\,dt =T\|iv\|_H^2>0,$$ where positivity follows from injectivity in [F1]. Every two distinct members therefore stay a fixed positive distance apart, so no subsequence is Cauchy and none converges strongly in the complete space $L^2(0,T;H)$.

The weak derivative is $u_n'(t)=(2\pi n/T)\cos(2\pi nt/T)\,Jv$. Its $L^q(V^*)$ norm is $$(2\pi n/T)\|Jv\|_{V^*} \left(\frac{T}{2\pi}\int_0^{2\pi}|\cos s|^q\,ds\right)^{1/q}$$ for finite $q$, and $(2\pi n/T)\|Jv\|_{V^*}$ for $q=\infty$. Since $Jv\ne0$ by [F1], these norms grow linearly in $n$. Hence no positive exponent derivative bound is present.

Fix an integer $d\ge2$. The **reference open simplex** is
$$\widehat S_d:=\{\widehat x\in\mathbb R^d:\widehat x_i>0\ (1\le i\le d),\ \sum_{i=1}^d\widehat x_i<1\},$$
with closure $\overline{\widehat S_d}=\operatorname{conv}\{0,e_1,\ldots,e_d\}$.

A **matching affine simplicial mesh** of a bounded polyhedral open set
$\Omega\subset\mathbb R^d$ is a finite set $\mathcal T$ of closed,
nondegenerate $d$-simplices such that their union is $\overline\Omega$,
their interiors are pairwise disjoint, $\Omega$ is the interior of their
union, and the intersection of two distinct cells is either empty or a
whole face of each. Thus no lower-dimensional crack is omitted from
$\Omega$ while its surrounding cells are retained. Every interior facet is
incident to exactly two cells and every boundary facet to one. The faces of
a cell are the convex hulls of its vertex subsets. A facet means a face of
dimension $d-1$.

For each cell $K\in\mathcal T$, an affine bijection
$$F_K:\overline{\widehat S_d}\to K,\qquad F_K(\widehat x)=b_K+A_K\widehat x,$$
with invertible $A_K\in\mathbb R^{d\times d}$ is a **reference map**.
Choose the vertex order so $\det A_K>0$; this is the orientation convention
used for Piola formulas. Write $h_K:=\operatorname{diam}(K)$ and let
$\rho_K$ be the radius of the largest Euclidean ball contained in $K$.
A family $\{\mathcal T_h\}_{h\in H}$ is **shape regular** if there is a
finite $\sigma$ such that $h_K/\rho_K\le\sigma$ for every
$h\in H$ and $K\in\mathcal T_h$. This universal condition is vacuous for
an empty family.
This definition uses radius; references using the diameter of the inscribed
ball differ by a factor of two.

An affine image of the reference square is a parallelogram. A general
quadrilateral requires a nonaffine map and is outside this affine definition;
curved-cell approximation is not included here.

Assume Countable Choice. Let $\mathbb K\in\{\mathbb R,\mathbb C\}$,
$\widehat S_d$ be the reference simplex, let $\widehat P$ be a finite
dimensional $\mathbb K$-space of polynomial functions on it, let
$\widehat F$ be any facet, and let integer $m\ge0$. For $1\le p,q\le\infty$ there is a finite
constant $C$ such that
$$|v|_{W^{m,p}(\widehat S_d)}+\|v\|_{L^p(\widehat F)}\le C\|v\|_{L^q(\widehat S_d)}\qquad(v\in\widehat P).$$
For every pair of integers $0\le m\le\ell$, there is also a finite
constant $C$ such that
$$|v|_{W^{\ell,p}(\widehat S_d)} \le C|v|_{W^{m,q}(\widehat S_d)}\qquad(v\in\widehat P).$$
For finitely many facets, one constant works for all of them. In particular,
every linear degree-of-freedom functional on $\widehat P$ is bounded with
respect to the $L^q(\widehat S_d)$ norm.

Assume Countable Choice. Let $F_K(\widehat x)=b_K+A_K\widehat x$ map the fixed reference simplex
$\widehat S_d$ bijectively to a cell $K$ of a shape-regular family, and let
$h_K$ be its diameter and $\rho_K$ its inradius. There are constants
$c,C>0$, depending only on $d$, the reference simplex, and the shape
regularity bound, such that
$$c h_K\le s_{\min}(A_K)\le \|A_K\|\le C h_K, \qquad c h_K^d\le\det A_K\le C h_K^d.$$
For each facet $F$, its affine surface Jacobian is comparable to
$h_K^{d-1}$, and its altitude from the opposite vertex is comparable to
$h_K$. Thus Sobolev scaling constants can be expressed using $h_K$ alone,
with constants uniform over the family.

Assume Countable Choice. Fix polynomial degree $k\ge0$, $1\le p,q\le\infty$, and integers
$0\le m\le\ell\le k$. Let the shape-regular affine simplex family be as in
[[def-matching-affine-simplicial-meshes]]. For every cell $K$ in that family,
there is a constant independent of cell size such that, for every
$v\in\mathbb P_k(K)$ and every facet $F\subset\partial K$,
$$|v|_{W^{\ell,p}(K)} \le C h_K^{m-\ell+d(1/p-1/q)}|v|_{W^{m,q}(K)},$$
$$\|v\|_{L^p(F)} \le C h_K^{(d-1)/p-d/q}\|v\|_{L^q(K)}.$$
Use $1/\infty=0$. Constants may depend on $d,k,p,q$ and the family shape
regularity bound, but not on $K$ or $h_K$.

Let $V$ be a finite-dimensional real inner product space and let $T:V\to V$ be
self-adjoint. Then $V$ has an orthonormal basis consisting of eigenvectors of
$T$.

The **Axiom of Countable Choice**, written $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$, is the following
statement.

> For every family $(X_n)_{n \in \mathbb{N}}$ of nonempty sets indexed by
> $\mathbb{N}$ there is a function $f$ with domain $\mathbb{N}$ such that
> $f(n) \in X_n$ for every $n \in \mathbb{N}$.

Equivalently, in the vocabulary of [[def-choice-function]]: every at most
countable family of nonempty sets ([[def-countable]]) has a choice function.

derivations.claim: On a $d\ge2$ reference simplex with barycentric coordinates $\lambda_0,\ldots,\lambda_d$, take the nodes $(\alpha_0/k,\ldots,\alpha_d/k)$ for nonnegative integers $\alpha_j$ with $\sum_j\alpha_j=k$. They are unisolvent for $\mathbb P_k$. Indeed, use induction on $d+k$, with the zero-dimensional constant case and the degree-one vertex case as bases. For $k\ge2$, restriction to the face $\lambda_0=0$ vanishes identically by the dimension induction, so the polynomial is $\lambda_0 R$ with $\deg R\le k-1$. At nodes with $\alpha_0\ge1$, the affine change $\lambda_0=(1+(k-1)\mu_0)/k$ and $\lambda_j=(k-1)\mu_j/k$ for $j\ge1$ identifies the remaining nodes with the degree-$(k-1)$ barycentric lattice. The induction makes $R$ vanish at every node of that lattice, hence $R=0$. The number of barycentric nodes is $\binom{k+d}{d}$ by placing $d$ separators among $k$ stars; this equals the number of degree-at-most-$k$ monomials in $d$ variables, so it is $\dim\mathbb P_k$ and the unisolvent values define a basis. In $d=1$, the equally spaced $k+1$ nodes are unisolvent because a nonzero degree-$k$ polynomial has at most $k$ roots. On a shared face the two cells have the same face nodes; unisolvence of the face restriction makes their polynomial traces agree when the shared nodal values agree. The same face-node unisolvence shows that zero nodal coefficients on a boundary facet give its zero polynomial trace; in $d=1$ the boundary facets are the zero-valued endpoints. Unisolvence also means that local nodal interpolation reproduces every polynomial in $\mathbb P_k$, so the local basis sums to one and reproduces affine polynomials. Thus the constructed nodal functions are conforming and have the declared zero boundary values.

If $\delta_h(i,j)\le m$, a path of $m$ common-cell links gives $|z_i-z_j|\le mh$. Charge every node within this graph ball to one incident cell; that cell is contained in $B(z_i,(m+1)h)$. The cells have disjoint interiors and volume at least $c h^d$, so at most $C(m+1)^d$ cells, and therefore at most $C(d,k)(m+1)^d$ nodes, can be charged. In $d=1$ this same estimate follows by counting intervals of length at least $\theta h$ in an interval of length $2(m+1)h$. Hence $$ \#\{j:\delta_h(i,j)\le m\}\le C(m+1)^d. $$

On each reference cell, [F2] bounds the $L^r$ norm above and below by the $\ell^r$ norm of the finitely many nodal coefficients; it also bounds the reference gradient norm above by that coefficient norm. Affine scaling then gives, for $1\le r<\infty$, $$ \Big\|\sum_{i\in I(K)}c_i\phi_i\Big\|_{L^r(K)}^r\asymp h_K^d\sum_{i\in I(K)}|c_i|^r, \qquad \Big\|\nabla\sum_{i\in I(K)}c_i\phi_i\Big\|_{L^r(K)} \le C h_K^{d/r-1}\|c\|_{\ell^r(I(K))}. $$ For $r=\infty$ replace the first factor $h_K^{d/r}$ by $1$. The same statements follow on an interval from $x=a+h_K t$ and the fixed one-dimensional nodal basis. Since $\theta h\le h_K\le h$, all cell scales are uniform in $h$.

For finite $r$, sum the local $L^r$ equivalence in step 2.1 over all cells. Each cell contains a fixed number $N(d,k)$ of nodes, and each global node is incident to uniformly many cells: in $d\ge2$ its incident cells are contained in a ball of radius $h$ and have disjoint interiors and volume at least $c h^d$; in $d=1$ at most two intervals meet at a node. Thus each global coefficient occurs between one and a uniformly bounded number of times, giving the asserted global lower and upper $\ell^r$ scaling. Taking maxima of local polynomial norm equivalences gives the $r=\infty$ scaling.

The interior-node mass matrix is symmetric positive definite because $c^TMc=\|\sum_i c_i\phi_i\|_{L^2(\Omega)}^2$, which is positive for every nonzero coefficient vector by the lower scaling in step 3.1. Taking $r=2$ there shows $a\|c\|_2^2\le c^TA_hc\le b\|c\|_2^2$ for positive constants independent of the mesh.

Put $\beta=2b$ and $B=I-A_h/\beta$. By step 4.1 and [F4], $\|B\|_{2\to2}\le q:=1-a/(2b)<1$. The matrix $A_h$ has zero $ij$ entry unless $i=j$ or $i,j$ occur in a common cell. Consequently $(B^n)_{ij}=0$ for $n<\delta_h(i,j)$, since a nonzero product of $n$ entries would give a graph path of length at most $n$. The norm-convergent Neumann series gives $$ A_h^{-1}=\beta^{-1}\sum_{n=0}^\infty B^n, \qquad |(A_h^{-1})_{ij}|\le\beta^{-1}\sum_{n\ge\delta_h(i,j)}q^n =\frac{q^{\delta_h(i,j)}}{\beta(1-q)}. $$ If $\delta_h(i,j)=\infty$, every summand is zero and the inverse entry is zero.

Grouping the entry bound of step 5.1 by graph distance and applying the ball count of step 1.2 gives each absolute row sum at most $C\sum_{m\ge0}(m+1)^d q^m<\infty$; the series converges by the ratio test because its term ratio tends to $q<1$. Symmetry of $A_h^{-1}$ gives the same column bound. These constants do not depend on the number of cells.

citations.quote:
Assume Countable Choice. Fix a degree $k\ge1$. The mesh contract has two
branches. In dimensions $d\ge2$, let $\Omega\subset\mathbb R^d$ be a bounded
polyhedral open set and let $\mathcal T_h$ be finite matching affine
simplex meshes as in [[def-matching-affine-simplicial-meshes]], with
$h=\max_{K\in\mathcal T_h}\operatorname{diam}K$, $h\to0$,
$\operatorname{diam}K\le h$, $\operatorname{diam}K\ge\theta h$, and
$\operatorname{diam}K/\rho_K\le\sigma$ for constants $\theta>0$ and
$\sigma<\infty$ independent of $h$. In dimension $d=1$, let $\Omega$ be a
bounded interval or a finite union of bounded intervals with pairwise
disjoint closures, and let $\mathcal T_h$ be finite interval partitions of
the component closures meeting only at whole endpoints, with interval lengths
between $\theta h$ and $h$ and $h\to0$.

For each mesh, place the degree-$k$ barycentric Lagrange nodes on every
$d\ge2$ simplex, or the $k+1$ equally spaced Lagrange nodes on every
$d=1$ interval, identify coincident nodes of matching cells, and impose zero
coefficients at every node on $\partial\Omega$. Let $V_h$ be the resulting
scalar continuous piecewise-$\mathbb P_k$ space. If $z_i$ are its interior
nodes, $\phi_i$ the global nodal basis, and
$$
M_{ij}=\int_\Omega\phi_i\phi_j,\qquad A_h=h^{-d}M,
$$
join distinct nodes when they occur in one cell and write $\delta_h(i,j)$ for
the shortest path length in this graph (with $\delta_h(i,j)=\infty$ when
there is no path, and use $q^\infty=0$). Whenever $V_h\ne\{0\}$, there are
$a,b,C>0$ and
$q\in(0,1)$, independent of the mesh, such that
$$\operatorname{spec}(A_h)\subset[a,b],\qquad |(A_h^{-1})_{ij}|\le Cq^{\delta_h(i,j)},\qquad \sup_i\sum_j|(A_h^{-1})_{ij}|+\sup_j\sum_i|(A_h^{-1})_{ij}|\le C.$$
For every cell $K$ and $1\le r<\infty$, if $c_K$ are its local nodal
coefficients and $w_h=\sum_{i\in I(K)}c_i\phi_i$ on $K$, then
$$c_r h_K^{d/r}\|c_K\|_{\ell^r}\le\|w_h\|_{L^r(K)}\le C_r h_K^{d/r}\|c_K\|_{\ell^r},\qquad \|\nabla w_h\|_{L^r(K)}\le C_rh_K^{d/r-1}\|c_K\|_{\ell^r}.$$
At $r=\infty$, omit $h_K^{d/r}$ in the function estimate and replace the
gradient bound by
$\|\nabla w_h\|_{L^\infty(K)}\le Ch_K^{-1}\|c_K\|_{\ell^\infty}$.
Summing gives, for all global nodal coefficients including zero boundary
coefficients,
$$c_r h^{d/r}\|c\|_{\ell^r}\le\Big\|\sum_i c_i\phi_i\Big\|_{L^r(\Omega)}\le C_r h^{d/r}\|c\|_{\ell^r}.$$
with the factor $h^{d/r}$ omitted at $r=\infty$. The empty interior-node
case is interpreted as $V_h=\{0\}$ and has no mass matrix to invert.

Assume Countable Choice. For any open $\Omega\subseteq\mathbb R^n$,
$n\ge1$, any $1\le p\le\infty$ and any
$\mathbb K\in\{\mathbb R,\mathbb C\}$, extension by zero
$$E_0u(x)=u(x)\ \ (x\in\Omega),\qquad E_0u(x)=0\ \ (x\notin\Omega),$$
acted on representatives, sends $W_0^{1,p}(\Omega;\mathbb K)$ linearly into
$W^{1,p}(\mathbb R^n;\mathbb K)$. For every $u\in W_0^{1,p}(\Omega;\mathbb K)$
and every coordinate direction $i$, the class $D_i(E_0u)$ is the zero
extension of the class $D_iu$, and every $L^p$ component norm is preserved:
$$\|E_0u\|_{L^p(\mathbb R^n)}=\|u\|_{L^p(\Omega)},\qquad \|D_i(E_0u)\|_{L^p(\mathbb R^n)}=\|D_iu\|_{L^p(\Omega)},$$
so that $\|E_0u\|_{W^{1,p}(\mathbb R^n)}=\|u\|_{W^{1,p}(\Omega)}$.

Assume Countable Choice. Let $\Omega$ be a bounded polyhedral open set with a finite matching
affine simplicial mesh, let $1\le p<\infty$, and let $v$ be a real-valued
conforming piecewise polynomial whose polynomial trace vanishes on every boundary
facet. Then
$$v\in W^{1,p}_0(\Omega),\qquad \|v\|_{L^p(\Omega)}\le C_\Omega\|\nabla v\|_{L^p(\Omega)}.$$
Here $W^{1,p}_0$ is the norm closure of $C_c^\infty(\Omega)$; no C1
trace characterization is used.

Assume the Axiom of Countable Choice ([[def-countable-choice]]).

Let $f : \mathbb{R}^n \to \mathbb{C}$ be locally integrable, let
$\varphi \in C_c^\infty(\mathbb{R}^n)$ have mass $1$, and let
$\varphi_\varepsilon$ be the associated mollifier. Then for every
$\varepsilon > 0$, the convolution

$$ (f*\varphi_\varepsilon)(x) := \int_{\mathbb{R}^n} f(y)\varphi_\varepsilon(x-y)\,dy $$

is smooth, and for every multi-index $\alpha$,

$$ \partial^\alpha(f*\varphi_\varepsilon) = f*(\partial^\alpha \varphi_\varepsilon). $$

Assume Countable Choice. Let $\Omega\subseteq\mathbb R^n$ be open with
$n\ge1$, let $u\in W^{k,p}(\Omega;\mathbb K)$ with $k\in\mathbb N_0$,
$1\le p\le\infty$ and $\mathbb K\in\{\mathbb R,\mathbb C\}$, and let
$\rho\in C_c^\infty(\mathbb R^n)$ be nonnegative with
$\int_{\mathbb R^n}\rho=1$ and $\operatorname{supp}\rho\subseteq\overline B_1(0)$.
For $\varepsilon>0$ put $\rho_\varepsilon(x)=\varepsilon^{-n}\rho(x/\varepsilon)$
and
$$\Omega_\varepsilon=\{x\in\Omega:\operatorname{dist}(x,\mathbb R^n\setminus\Omega)>\varepsilon\},\qquad\Omega_\varepsilon=\mathbb R^n\ \text{when }\Omega=\mathbb R^n .$$
Then $\rho_\varepsilon*u$ is defined and smooth on $\Omega_\varepsilon$, and
for every multi-index $\alpha$ with $|\alpha|\le k$,
$$D^\alpha(\rho_\varepsilon*u)=\rho_\varepsilon*(D^\alpha u)\qquad\text{on }\Omega_\varepsilon,$$
as pointwise smooth functions for the constructed representatives and as
almost-everywhere classes. Here $D^\alpha u$ is extended by zero off $\Omega$
in the convolution.

Let $\varphi \in C_c^\infty(\mathbb{R}^n)$ satisfy

$$ \int_{\mathbb{R}^n} \varphi(x)\,dx = 1. $$

For $\varepsilon > 0$, define

$$ \varphi_\varepsilon(x) := \varepsilon^{-n}\varphi(x/\varepsilon) \qquad(x \in \mathbb{R}^n). $$

The family $(\varphi_\varepsilon)_{\varepsilon>0}$ is the **mollifier family
generated by $\varphi$**.

Assume the Axiom of Countable Choice.

Let $\varphi \in C_c^\infty(\mathbb{R}^n)$ satisfy
$\int \varphi = 1$, and let
$\varphi_\varepsilon(x) = \varepsilon^{-n}\varphi(x/\varepsilon)$. Then
$(\varphi_\varepsilon)_{\varepsilon>0}$ is an $L^1$ approximate identity.

Assume the Axiom of Countable Choice.

Let $(K_\varepsilon)_{\varepsilon>0}$ be an $L^1$ approximate identity on
$\mathbb{R}^n$. If $1 \le p < \infty$ and $f \in L^p(\mathbb{R}^n)$, then

$$\|f*K_\varepsilon - f\|_p \longrightarrow 0 \qquad(\varepsilon \to 0^+).$$

Let $(X,\mathcal A,\mu)$ be a measure space, let $p,q\in[1,\infty]$ be
conjugate exponents, and let $f,g$ be measurable real-valued functions.

1. If $1\le p<\infty$ and $q<\infty$ with $f\in\mathcal L^p(\mu)$ and
   $g\in\mathcal L^q(\mu)$, then
   $$\int |fg|\,d\mu\le\|f\|_p\|g\|_q.$$
2. If $p=1$ and $q=\infty$ with $f\in\mathcal L^1(\mu)$ and
   $g\in L^\infty(\mu)$, then
   $$\int |fg|\,d\mu\le\|f\|_1\|g\|_\infty.$$
3. If $p=\infty$ and $q=1$ with $f\in L^\infty(\mu)$ and
   $g\in\mathcal L^1(\mu)$, then
   $$\int |fg|\,d\mu\le\|f\|_\infty\|g\|_1.$$

In every case the right-hand side is finite, so $fg$ is integrable.

Let $m \in \mathbb{N}$ with $m \ge 1$ and let $a, b \in \mathbb{R}$ with $a < b$.

1. **Fundamental theorem, second part, in $\mathbb{R}^{m}$.** Let
   $f : [a,b] \to \mathbb{R}^{m}$ be differentiable at every point of $[a,b]$ as
   a function on $[a,b]$ ([[def-vector-valued-derivative-and-integral]]), and
   suppose $f' : [a,b] \to \mathbb{R}^{m}$ is integrable. Then
   $$\int_a^b f' \;=\; f(b) - f(a).$$
2. **A bounded derivative gives a Lipschitz function.** Let
   $f : [a,b] \to \mathbb{R}^{m}$ be continuous on $[a,b]$ and differentiable at
   every point of $(a,b)$, and let $M \ge 0$ satisfy
   $\lVert f'(t)\rVert_2 \le M$ for every $t \in (a,b)$. Then
   $$\lVert f(t) - f(s)\rVert_2 \;\le\; M\,|t-s| \qquad \text{for all } s,t \in [a,b],$$
   that is, $f$ is Lipschitz with constant $M$ as a map
   $([a,b], d_{\mathbb{R}}) \to (\mathbb{R}^{m}, d_2)$
   ([[def-lipschitz-holder-contraction]], [[lem-real-line-is-a-metric-space]],
   [[lem-metrics-on-rn]]).

Assume Countable Choice. Let $n\ge1$, $k\in\mathbb N_0$, $1\le p<\infty$ and
$\mathbb K\in\{\mathbb R,\mathbb C\}$. Then the compactly supported smooth
functions $C_c^\infty(\mathbb R^n;\mathbb K)$ are dense in
$W^{k,p}(\mathbb R^n;\mathbb K)$: for every
$u\in W^{k,p}(\mathbb R^n;\mathbb K)$ and every $\delta>0$ there is
$\varphi\in C_c^\infty(\mathbb R^n;\mathbb K)$ with
$$\|\varphi-u\|_{W^{k,p}(\mathbb R^n)}<\delta.$$
No such norm-density assertion is made for $p=\infty$.

Let $f,g \in L^1(\mathbb{R}^n)$ be represented by Borel functions still
denoted $f,g$. For any complex-valued function $u$ on $\mathbb R^n$, use the
support convention

$$\operatorname{supp}(u):=\overline{\{x\in\mathbb R^n:u(x)\ne0\}},$$

which extends the real-valued definition of
[[def-support-and-compactly-supported-riemann-integral-in-rn]]. Define
$$ h(x) := \begin{cases} \int_{\mathbb{R}^n} f(x-y)g(y)\,dy,& \text{if the integral exists},\\ 0,& \text{otherwise}. \end{cases} $$
Then

$$ \operatorname{supp}(h) \subseteq \overline{\operatorname{supp}(f) + \operatorname{supp}(g)}. $$

Assume Countable Choice. Let $\Omega\subseteq\mathbb R^n$ be open with
$n\ge1$, let $k\in\mathbb N_0$, let $1\le p\le\infty$, and let
$\mathbb K\in\{\mathbb R,\mathbb C\}$.

Every $\varphi\in C_c^\infty(\Omega;\mathbb K)$ belongs to
$W^{k,p}(\Omega;\mathbb K)$. Indeed $\varphi$ is bounded with compact support,
hence lies in $L^p(\Omega;\mathbb K)$ for every exponent in range, and each of
its classical partial derivatives is again smooth and compactly supported,
hence lies in $L^p(\Omega;\mathbb K)$ and is the corresponding weak derivative
by [[lem-classical-derivatives-are-weak-derivatives]].

Define the **zero-boundary Sobolev space**
$$W_0^{k,p}(\Omega;\mathbb K):=\overline{C_c^\infty(\Omega;\mathbb K)},$$
the closure taken in the normed space
$(W^{k,p}(\Omega;\mathbb K),\|\cdot\|_{W^{k,p}(\Omega)})$ of
[[def-sobolev-space-wkp-and-its-norm]]. The norm is a genuine norm on classes
by [[lem-sobolev-norm-is-well-defined-and-definite]], so this is the usual
metric closure of a subset of a normed space: $u\in W_0^{k,p}(\Omega;\mathbb K)$
if and only if for every $\delta>0$ there is
$\varphi\in C_c^\infty(\Omega;\mathbb K)$ with
$\|u-\varphi\|_{W^{k,p}(\Omega)}<\delta$. Write
$H_0^k(\Omega):=W_0^{k,2}(\Omega;\mathbb K)$ when the scalar field is fixed by
context.

Three warnings are part of the definition. First, this is a closure of
almost-everywhere classes, and all its equalities are equalities of Sobolev
classes. Second, no pointwise boundary values and no trace characterization
are asserted: a description of $W_0^{k,p}$ by vanishing boundary data belongs
to the later trace theory and is not used here. Third, the closure is defined
for every $1\le p\le\infty$, but for $p=\infty$ it is not claimed that every
compactly supported $W^{k,\infty}(\Omega)$ function lies in $W_0^{k,\infty}(\Omega)$;
the definition merely names the closure of the test functions.

Assume Countable Choice. Let $\Omega\subseteq\mathbb R^n$ be open with
$n\ge1$, $k\in\mathbb N_0$, $1\le p\le\infty$, and
$\mathbb K\in\{\mathbb R,\mathbb C\}$. Write
$$\mathcal A_k=\{\alpha\in\mathbb N_0^n:|\alpha|\le k\}.$$
This is a finite nonempty set: every coordinate of such an $\alpha$ lies in
$\{0,\ldots,k\}$, and it contains the zero multi-index.

The real and complex $L^p$ classes use the conventions in
[[def-l-p-space-as-a-quotient-by-null-functions]] and
[[def-complex-lp-and-euclidean-test-function-conventions]]. Their quotient
norm values are supplied by
[[thm-the-l-p-norm-descends-to-the-quotient-and-makes-l-p-a-normed-space]]
for real scalars and
[[thm-complex-holder-minkowski-and-the-quotient-norm]] for complex scalars.

Define $W^{k,p}(\Omega;\mathbb K)$ to be the set of classes
$u\in L^p(\Omega;\mathbb K)$ such that, for every $\alpha\in\mathcal A_k$,
there is an $L^p(\Omega;\mathbb K)$ class with a locally integrable
representative $v_\alpha$ satisfying
$$\int_\Omega u\,D^\alpha\varphi\,dx =(-1)^{|\alpha|}\int_\Omega v_\alpha\varphi\,dx \qquad\text{for every }\varphi\in C_c^\infty(\Omega).$$
Here the weak derivative is the one in
[[def-weak-derivative-of-a-locally-integrable-function]]. Under
[[def-countable-choice]], local integrability of $L^p$ representatives and
invariance under null-set changes follow from
[[lem-weak-derivative-is-independent-of-lp-representatives]], while
[[lem-weak-derivatives-are-unique-almost-everywhere]] gives uniqueness of each
locally integrable derivative class. Thus this condition is a condition on the
$L^p$ class $u$, and each resulting derivative determines one $L^p$ class,
denoted $D^\alpha u$. The test pairing is bilinear, without conjugation.

For the zero multi-index, set $D^0u=u$. Since $\mathcal A_0=\{0\}$,
$$W^{0,p}(\Omega;\mathbb K)=L^p(\Omega;\mathbb K).$$
The Sobolev norm expression is
$$\|u\|_{W^{k,p}(\Omega)}= \begin{cases} \left(\displaystyle\sum_{\alpha\in\mathcal A_k} \|D^\alpha u\|_{L^p(\Omega)}^p\right)^{1/p},&1\le p<\infty,\\[1ex] \displaystyle\max_{\alpha\in\mathcal A_k} \|D^\alpha u\|_{L^\infty(\Omega)},&p=\infty. \end{cases}$$
The formula is finite because each derivative class belongs to $L^p$ and
$\mathcal A_k$ is finite; at $k=0$ it reduces to the $L^p$ norm expression.
The finite maximum is defined because $\mathcal A_k$ is nonempty. The norm
axioms for this expression are a separate assertion from this definition.

For open $U\subseteq\Omega$ with $\overline U$ compact and contained in
$\Omega$, the notation $W^{k,p}_{\mathrm{loc}}(\Omega;\mathbb K)$ means that
the restriction of the class belongs to $W^{k,p}(U;\mathbb K)$ for every such
$U$.

If $\Omega=\varnothing$, the $L^p$ space and every $W^{k,p}$ space contain
only the zero class, and the displayed norm expression is zero.
Let $0<r<R$ and $n\ge 1$. Then there exists a smooth function $\rho:\mathbb R^n\to [0,1]$ such that $\rho=1$ on $\overline B_r(0)$ and $\operatorname{supp}(\rho)\subseteq B_R(0)$.

Let $n \ge 1$, **assume the Axiom of Countable Choice**
([[def-countable-choice]]), and let $a_i \le b_i$ be reals for $i<n$. Write

$$R^{\circ} := \{\, x \in \mathbb{R}^n : a_i < x_i < b_i \text{ for every } i<n \,\}, \qquad \overline{R} := [a,b] = \{\, x \in \mathbb{R}^n : a_i \le x_i \le b_i \text{ for every } i<n \,\}$$

([[def-multidimensional-rectangle-and-volume]]). Then $R^{\circ}$ is open and
$\overline{R}$ is closed, so both are Borel and Lebesgue measurable, and **every**
set $R$ with $R^{\circ} \subseteq R \subseteq \overline{R}$ is Lebesgue
measurable with

$$\lambda_n(R) \;=\; \prod_{i<n}(b_i-a_i).$$

In particular this covers the four one-dimensional face conventions in each
coordinate — the open box, the closed box $[a,b]$, the half-open box
$B(a,b) = \prod_{i<n}(a_i,b_i]$ of [[def-half-open-box]], and every mixture of
them, in any combination of coordinates — and it gives measure $0$ to all of them
whenever $a_i = b_i$ for some $i<n$. For a half-open box with infinite
parameters the value is already
$\lambda_n(B) = \operatorname{vol}(B)$ ([[thm-lebesgue-measure-is-a-complete-measure]]).

The **Axiom of Countable Choice**, written $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$, is the following
statement.

> For every family $(X_n)_{n \in \mathbb{N}}$ of nonempty sets indexed by
> $\mathbb{N}$ there is a function $f$ with domain $\mathbb{N}$ such that
> $f(n) \in X_n$ for every $n \in \mathbb{N}$.

Equivalently, in the vocabulary of [[def-choice-function]]: every at most
countable family of nonempty sets ([[def-countable]]) has a choice function.

derivations.claim: The coefficients define a linear map into the algebraic conforming piecewise-polynomial space: shared-face nodes coincide, so the face polynomials have identical nodal data and hence identical traces; all boundary coefficients are zero, so each boundary-facet polynomial vanishes. For $d\ge2$, [F3] therefore gives $V_h\subset W_0^{1,p}(\Omega)$. For $d=1$, write a mesh function as $w$, let $M$ bound its finitely many piecewise derivatives, and extend it by zero. It is continuous at every mesh node and at every component endpoint. Integrating the derivative on each of the finitely many subintervals between two points using the fundamental theorem in [F6] shows $|w(x)-w(y)|\le M|x-y|$ on $\mathbb R$; integration by parts on those subintervals shows that the zero extension has the piecewise derivative as its weak derivative. Thus it is compactly supported in $W^{1,p}(\mathbb R)$.

Let $u=E_0v$. For a cell $K$, choose a cube $C_K$ of side $Rh$ centered at an interior point of $K$, where the fixed $R$ is large enough that $K$, every radius-$h$ ball centered at one of its nodes, and every radius-$2h$ ball centered at a point of $K$ lie in $C_K$. The cubes have bounded overlap: if $x\in C_K$, then $K\subset B(x,C_Rh)$; the cells have disjoint interiors and volume at least $c h^d$, so only uniformly many can meet that ball. For smooth $u$ on a cube $C$, the segment fundamental theorem, Hölder, Jensen's inequality, and a change of variables on the two ranges $t\le1/2$ and $t\ge1/2$ give $$ \|u-u_C\|_{L^p(C)}\le C_d\operatorname{diam}(C)\|
abla u\|_{L^p(C)}, \qquad u_C=|C|^{-1}\int_Cu. $$ Indeed, Jensen's inequality and $u(x)-u(y)=\int_0^1
abla u(tx+(1-t)y)\cdot(x-y)\,dt$ give $$ \|u-u_C\|_{L^p(C)}^p\le rac{\operatorname{diam}(C)^p}{|C|} \int_C\int_C\int_0^1|
abla u(tx+(1-t)y)|^p\,dt\,dy\,dx. $$ For $t\ge1/2$ change the $x$ variable, and for $t\le1/2$ change the $y$ variable; both inverse Jacobians are at most $2^d$ and the images stay in $C$. This proves the displayed Poincaré estimate. Since $u=E_0v$ is compactly supported in $W^{1,p}(\mathbb R^d)$, [F6] approximates it by smooth functions in that norm, so the same cube estimate holds for $u$.

In the one-dimensional branch, for $x$ in a component interval choose the nearer endpoint; integrating the derivative from that endpoint by [F6] gives $|w(x)|\le M\operatorname{dist}(x,\mathbb R\setminus\Omega)$. Because there are finitely many distinct endpoints, choose $\varepsilon$ smaller than one quarter of their minimum separation. Translate and rescale the bump from [F9] at each endpoint to obtain $\chi_{a,\varepsilon}$ equal to one within $\varepsilon$ of $a$ and zero outside distance $2\varepsilon$. The endpoint supports are disjoint; the product $\eta_\varepsilon=\prod_{a\in\partial\Omega}(1-\chi_{a,\varepsilon})$ is smooth, vanishes within distance $\varepsilon$ of each endpoint, equals one at distance at least $2\varepsilon$, and satisfies $|\eta_\varepsilon'|\le C/\varepsilon$. Thus $w-\eta_\varepsilon w$ and its weak derivative are supported in a boundary layer of measure $O_\Omega(\varepsilon)$ and bounded there by $C_\Omega M$. On each partition interval $\eta_\varepsilon w$ is smooth times polynomial, is continuous at nodes, and vanishes near component endpoints; integration by parts on the finitely many intervals cancels all interior endpoint terms. Its zero extension therefore belongs to $W^{1,p}(\mathbb R)$ with derivative $\eta_\varepsilon'w+ \eta_\varepsilon w'$ on the pieces. Hence $\eta_\varepsilon w\to w$ in $W^{1,p}(\mathbb R)$. Each cutoff product has compact support a positive distance from $\mathbb R\setminus\Omega$; convolving it with a sufficiently small mollifier gives a function in $C_c^\infty(\Omega)$ by [F4] and [F7], and the convolution converges in $W^{1,p}$ by [F4]. This proves $w\in W_0^{1,p}(\Omega)$ by [F8] and completes the range assertion in $d=1$.

If $K$ has no boundary node, put $c_K=u_{C_K}$. If it has a boundary node, put $c_K=0$. In $d\ge2$, compactness of the boundary gives a finite subcover of its Lipschitz graph charts; taking the largest chart Lipschitz constant and the smallest chart radius yields uniform $\eta,r_0>0$ such that each boundary point $z$ and $0<r\le r_0$ have an exterior cone sector in $B(z,r)$ of measure at least $\eta r^d$: in a chart $x_d>g(x')$ with Lipschitz constant $L$, the cone $x_d<g(z')-L|x'-z'|$ is exterior, and a fixed smaller cone has that volume. For sufficiently small $h$, a boundary node $z$ of $K$ therefore gives $|C_K\setminus\Omega|\ge\eta'|C_K|$. In $d=1$, at a boundary endpoint the exterior interval inside $C_K$ has a fixed positive fraction of its length; for finitely many separated components take $h$ smaller than their minimum gap divided by $2R$. In the boundary case $u=0$ on $C_K\setminus\Omega$, so $$ |u_{C_K}|\,|C_K\setminus\Omega|^{1/p} \le\|u-u_{C_K}\|_{L^p(C_K\setminus\Omega)}. $$ The cube estimate of step 1.2 then gives, in either case, $$ \|u-c_K\|_{L^p(C_K)}\le Ch\|\nabla u\|_{L^p(C_K)}. $$

Fix $\psi\in C_c^\infty(\Omega)$ and let $\delta=\operatorname{dist}(\operatorname{supp}\psi,\partial\Omega)>0$. For $h<\delta/2$, $S_h\psi$ is zero on every cell with a boundary node: every point of such a cell is within distance $h$ of the boundary, while the convolution samples only a radius-$h$ ball. Thus $Q_h\psi=0=S_h\psi$ on those cells. Every other cell has only interior nodes, so $Q_h\psi$ is the ordinary nodal interpolant of $S_h\psi$ there. Since $k\ge1$, this interpolant reproduces affine polynomials. Taylor's formula about a cell vertex and the local coefficient estimates in [F1] give $$ \|Q_h\psi-S_h\psi\|_{L^p(K)}\le Ch^2|K|^{1/p}\|D^2\psi\|_\infty, \qquad \|\nabla(Q_h\psi-S_h\psi)\|_{L^p(K)} \le Ch|K|^{1/p}\|D^2\psi\|_\infty. $$ The nonnegative unit-mass kernel gives $S_h\psi\to\psi$ in $W^{1,p}(\Omega)$ and $\|D^2S_h\psi\|_\infty\le\|D^2\psi\|_\infty$. Summing cell bounds proves $Q_h\psi\to\psi$ in $W^{1,p}$.

For each interior node $z$ of $K$, Hölder [F5] gives $$ |S_hv(z)-c_K|\le\|ho_h\|_{L^{p'}(\mathbb R^d)} \|u-c_K\|_{L^p(B(z,h))} \le Ch^{-d/p}\|u-c_K\|_{L^p(C_K)}. $$ At a boundary node both the coefficient and $c_K$ are zero in the boundary case. If $K$ has no boundary node, every local node is interior and the local nodal basis reproduces the constant $c_K$. Applying the local coefficient estimate of [F1] to the coefficients of $Q_hv-c_K$, and using step 2.2, gives $$ \|Q_hv-c_K\|_{L^p(K)}\le Ch\|
abla u\|_{L^p(C_K)},\qquad \|
abla Q_hv\|_{L^p(K)}\le C\|
abla u\|_{L^p(C_K)}. $$ The boundary-node case uses $c_K=0$; the no-boundary-node case uses $\sum_{z\in K}\phi_z=1$.

Since $v=u$ on $K$, step 2.2 and the first estimate of step 3.1 imply $$ \|v-Q_hv\|_{L^p(K)}\le Ch\|\nabla u\|_{L^p(C_K)}. $$ Raise this and the gradient estimate of step 3.1 to the $p$th power, sum over cells, and use the bounded overlap from step 1.2 and the norm preservation in [F2]. This proves both global estimates in the Statement. Also $\|Q_hw\|_{W^{1,p}}\le C\|w\|_{W^{1,p}}$ for every $w\in W_0^{1,p}$ and all sufficiently small $h$, by the gradient bound and $\|Q_hw\|_p\le\|w\|_p+Ch\|\nabla w\|_p$.

For arbitrary $v\in W_0^{1,p}(\Omega)$ and $\varepsilon>0$, [F8] provides $\psi\in C_c^\infty(\Omega)$ with $\|v-\psi\|_{W^{1,p}}<\varepsilon$. The uniform bound in step 4.1 and the smooth convergence in step 2.3 imply $$ \limsup_{h\to0}\|Q_hv-v\|_{W^{1,p}} \le(C+1)\|v-\psi\|_{W^{1,p}}<(C+1)\varepsilon. $$ Letting $\varepsilon\downarrow0$ proves strong convergence for every $v\in W_0^{1,p}(\Omega)$.

boundaries.evidence: Statement: the mesh domains are nonempty; the zero-space case for a coarse mesh is handled by the local estimates in steps 3.1–4.1.
Step 1.1: the map is linear in the zero extension and nodal coefficients, so Q_h(0)=0 and both estimates vanish.
Steps 3.1 and 4.1 include p=1; Hölder uses the L-infinity kernel norm at this conjugate endpoint.
Step 3.1: cells with boundary nodes use c_K=0; this covers boundary-only and zero-dimensional V_h meshes.
Steps 1.1–1.2 set all boundary-node coefficients to zero and prove interval endpoint closure membership.
Step 1.1 and Facts & Assumptions [A1]: Countable Choice is assumed through zero extension, mollification, Sobolev closure, and density suppliers.

citations.quote:
Assume Countable Choice. Fix a degree $k\ge1$. The mesh contract has two
branches. In dimensions $d\ge2$, let $\Omega\subset\mathbb R^d$ be a bounded
polyhedral open set and let $\mathcal T_h$ be finite matching affine
simplex meshes as in [[def-matching-affine-simplicial-meshes]], with
$h=\max_{K\in\mathcal T_h}\operatorname{diam}K$, $h\to0$,
$\operatorname{diam}K\le h$, $\operatorname{diam}K\ge\theta h$, and
$\operatorname{diam}K/\rho_K\le\sigma$ for constants $\theta>0$ and
$\sigma<\infty$ independent of $h$. In dimension $d=1$, let $\Omega$ be a
bounded interval or a finite union of bounded intervals with pairwise
disjoint closures, and let $\mathcal T_h$ be finite interval partitions of
the component closures meeting only at whole endpoints, with interval lengths
between $\theta h$ and $h$ and $h\to0$.

For each mesh, place the degree-$k$ barycentric Lagrange nodes on every
$d\ge2$ simplex, or the $k+1$ equally spaced Lagrange nodes on every
$d=1$ interval, identify coincident nodes of matching cells, and impose zero
coefficients at every node on $\partial\Omega$. Let $V_h$ be the resulting
scalar continuous piecewise-$\mathbb P_k$ space. If $z_i$ are its interior
nodes, $\phi_i$ the global nodal basis, and
$$
M_{ij}=\int_\Omega\phi_i\phi_j,\qquad A_h=h^{-d}M,
$$
join distinct nodes when they occur in one cell and write $\delta_h(i,j)$ for
the shortest path length in this graph (with $\delta_h(i,j)=\infty$ when
there is no path, and use $q^\infty=0$). Whenever $V_h\ne\{0\}$, there are
$a,b,C>0$ and
$q\in(0,1)$, independent of the mesh, such that
$$\operatorname{spec}(A_h)\subset[a,b],\qquad |(A_h^{-1})_{ij}|\le Cq^{\delta_h(i,j)},\qquad \sup_i\sum_j|(A_h^{-1})_{ij}|+\sup_j\sum_i|(A_h^{-1})_{ij}|\le C.$$
For every cell $K$ and $1\le r<\infty$, if $c_K$ are its local nodal
coefficients and $w_h=\sum_{i\in I(K)}c_i\phi_i$ on $K$, then
$$c_r h_K^{d/r}\|c_K\|_{\ell^r}\le\|w_h\|_{L^r(K)}\le C_r h_K^{d/r}\|c_K\|_{\ell^r},\qquad \|\nabla w_h\|_{L^r(K)}\le C_rh_K^{d/r-1}\|c_K\|_{\ell^r}.$$
At $r=\infty$, omit $h_K^{d/r}$ in the function estimate and replace the
gradient bound by
$\|\nabla w_h\|_{L^\infty(K)}\le Ch_K^{-1}\|c_K\|_{\ell^\infty}$.
Summing gives, for all global nodal coefficients including zero boundary
coefficients,
$$c_r h^{d/r}\|c\|_{\ell^r}\le\Big\|\sum_i c_i\phi_i\Big\|_{L^r(\Omega)}\le C_r h^{d/r}\|c\|_{\ell^r}.$$
with the factor $h^{d/r}$ omitted at $r=\infty$. The empty interior-node
case is interpreted as $V_h=\{0\}$ and has no mass matrix to invert.

Assume Countable Choice. Use either mesh branch and the nodal space defined
in [[lem-pe12-quasiuniform-mass-inverse-decay]]. For $d\ge2$, assume
$\Omega$ is a bounded polyhedral open set whose boundary is locally a graph
of a Lipschitz function with $\Omega$ on one side; for $d=1$, use a bounded
nonempty interval or a finite nonempty union of bounded intervals with
pairwise disjoint closures. Let $1\le p<\infty$. There is a linear map
$$
Q_h:W_0^{1,p}(\Omega)\longrightarrow V_h
$$
with the following construction. Fix a nonnegative $\rho\in C_c^\infty(B(0,1))$
with $\int\rho=1$, let $E_0$ be extension by zero, and set
$S_hv=\rho_h*E_0v$ with $\rho_h(x)=h^{-d}\rho(x/h)$. The degree-$k$
coefficient of $Q_hv$ at every interior node $z$ is $S_hv(z)$; every
boundary-node coefficient is zero. For all sufficiently fine meshes,
$$\|v-Q_hv\|_{L^p(\Omega)}\le Ch\|\nabla v\|_{L^p(\Omega)},\qquad \|\nabla Q_hv\|_{L^p(\Omega)}\le C\|\nabla v\|_{L^p(\Omega)}.$$
Consequently $Q_hv\to v$ in $W^{1,p}(\Omega)$ for each
$v\in W_0^{1,p}(\Omega)$. Constants are uniform over the fixed mesh family
and may depend on $d,k,p,\Omega,\theta,\sigma$ and $\rho$. The operator
$Q_h$ is not asserted to be a projector.

Assume Countable Choice. Fix polynomial degree $k\ge0$, $1\le p,q\le\infty$, and integers
$0\le m\le\ell\le k$. Let the shape-regular affine simplex family be as in
[[def-matching-affine-simplicial-meshes]]. For every cell $K$ in that family,
there is a constant independent of cell size such that, for every
$v\in\mathbb P_k(K)$ and every facet $F\subset\partial K$,
$$|v|_{W^{\ell,p}(K)} \le C h_K^{m-\ell+d(1/p-1/q)}|v|_{W^{m,q}(K)},$$
$$\|v\|_{L^p(F)} \le C h_K^{(d-1)/p-d/q}\|v\|_{L^q(K)}.$$
Use $1/\infty=0$. Constants may depend on $d,k,p,q$ and the family shape
regularity bound, but not on $K$ or $h_K$.

Assume Countable Choice. Let $\Omega$ be a bounded polyhedral open set with a finite matching
affine simplicial mesh, let $1\le p<\infty$, and let $v$ be a real-valued
conforming piecewise polynomial whose polynomial trace vanishes on every boundary
facet. Then
$$v\in W^{1,p}_0(\Omega),\qquad \|v\|_{L^p(\Omega)}\le C_\Omega\|\nabla v\|_{L^p(\Omega)}.$$
Here $W^{1,p}_0$ is the norm closure of $C_c^\infty(\Omega)$; no C1
trace characterization is used.

Assume Countable Choice. Let $\Omega\subseteq\mathbb R^n$ be open with $n\ge1$ and $\mathbb K\in\{\mathbb R,\mathbb C\}$. Then $C_c^\infty(\Omega;\mathbb K)$ is dense in $L^2(\Omega;\mathbb K)$: for every $f\in L^2(\Omega;\mathbb K)$ and every $\delta>0$ there is $\varphi\in C_c^\infty(\Omega;\mathbb K)$ with $\|\varphi-f\|_{L^2(\Omega)}<\delta$. Consequently $H^1_0(\Omega)$ is dense in $L^2(\Omega)$, and if a class $h\in L^2(\Omega)$ satisfies $(h,v)_{L^2}=0$ for all $v\in H^1_0(\Omega)$, then $h=0$.

Let $(V,H,J)$ be the Banach evolution triple of
[[def-pe12-gelfand-triple]]. An **admissible stable conforming FEM sequence**
consists of finite-dimensional subspaces $V_k\subset V$ and their
$H$-orthogonal projections $\Pi_k:H\to V_k$ such that:

1. $\Pi_k(V)\subset V$, $\Pi_kv=v$ for $v\in V_k$, and
   $(w_k,z-\Pi_kz)_H=0$ for every $w_k\in V_k$, $z\in H$;
2. $\sup_k\|\Pi_k\|_{V\to V}\le C_\Pi<\infty$ and
   $\Pi_kv\to v$ in $V$ for each $v\in V$;
3. the associated time partitions of $[0,T]$ have maximum step
   $\delta_k\to0$.

The convergence in clause 2 and density of $V$ in $H$ imply
$\Pi_kz\to z$ in $H$ for every $z\in H$: use
$\|\Pi_k(z-v)\|_H\le\|z-v\|_H$, $\Pi_kv\to v$ in $H$, and approximate $z$
by $v\in V$. Thus the range spaces approximate every $H$ vector.

For a fixed $k$, backward Euler with averages $f_k^n$ uses unknowns
$U_k^n\in V_k$ and equations
$$\left(\frac{U_k^n-U_k^{n-1}}{\tau_n},v_k\right)_H +\langle A(U_k^n),v_k\rangle =\langle f_k^n,v_k\rangle\qquad(v_k\in V_k).$$
Its piecewise-constant reconstruction is $\overline U_k(t)=U_k^n$ on
$(t_{n-1},t_n]$; its affine reconstruction joins $U_k^{n-1}$ to $U_k^n$.

Assume Countable Choice ([[def-countable-choice]]). Let $\Omega\subseteq\mathbb R^n$ be open and bounded in one direction: there are a unit vector $e$ and $a<b$ with $a<x\cdot e<b$ for every $x\in\Omega$. Let $1\le p<\infty$. Then $\|u\|_{L^p(\Omega)}\le C(p)\,(b-a)\,\|Du\|_{L^p(\Omega)}$ for every $u\in W^{1,p}_0(\Omega;\mathbb K)$.

Let $(X,\mathcal A,\mu)$ be a measure space, let $p,q\in[1,\infty]$ be
conjugate exponents, and let $f,g$ be measurable real-valued functions.

1. If $1\le p<\infty$ and $q<\infty$ with $f\in\mathcal L^p(\mu)$ and
   $g\in\mathcal L^q(\mu)$, then
   $$\int |fg|\,d\mu\le\|f\|_p\|g\|_q.$$
2. If $p=1$ and $q=\infty$ with $f\in\mathcal L^1(\mu)$ and
   $g\in L^\infty(\mu)$, then
   $$\int |fg|\,d\mu\le\|f\|_1\|g\|_\infty.$$
3. If $p=\infty$ and $q=1$ with $f\in L^\infty(\mu)$ and
   $g\in\mathcal L^1(\mu)$, then
   $$\int |fg|\,d\mu\le\|f\|_\infty\|g\|_1.$$

In every case the right-hand side is finite, so $fg$ is integrable.

Assume the Axiom of Choice. Let $d\ge1$, let $\Omega\subseteq\mathbb R^d$ be a bounded open set, and let $1<p<\infty$ satisfy $p>\max(1,2d/(d+2))$. Then $W_0^{1,p}(\Omega)$ is continuously and compactly embedded in $L^2(\Omega)$. In particular, the inclusion is dense. No boundary regularity is required.

Assume the Axiom of Choice. Let
$\Omega\subseteq\mathbb R^d$ be bounded and open, $d\ge1$, and let
$1<p<\infty$. Then $W_0^{1,p}(\Omega;\mathbb R)$, with the norm inherited
from $W^{1,p}(\Omega;\mathbb R)$, is a separable reflexive real Banach space.

Assume the Axiom of Choice ([[def-axiom-of-choice]]).

Let $d\ge1$, let $\Omega\subset\mathbb R^d$ be a bounded open set, and
let $1<p<\infty$ satisfy $p>\max(1,2d/(d+2))$. Put
$V=W_0^{1,p}(\Omega;\mathbb R)$ with norm
$\|v\|_V=\|\nabla v\|_{L^p(\Omega)}$, $H=L^2(\Omega;\mathbb R)$, and
$p'=p/(p-1)$. The Poincaré inequality makes this norm equivalent to the full
$W^{1,p}$ norm. [[lem-pe12-w0p-separable-reflexive]] gives separability and
reflexivity, while [[lem-pe12-w1p-compact-l2-embedding]] gives the dense
continuous compact inclusion $V\Subset H$; these are the hypotheses of the
evolution triple in [[def-pe12-gelfand-triple]]. The compact-inclusion result
uses the stated threshold also when $d=1$, where it reduces to $p>1$.

A measurable flux $a:\Omega\times\mathbb R^d\to\mathbb R^d$ is an admissible
**coercive monotone diffusion flux of p-growth** if it is Carathéodory (for
each $\xi$, $x\mapsto a(x,\xi)$ is measurable, and for almost every $x$,
$\xi\mapsto a(x,\xi)$ is continuous), and there are constants $C<\infty$,
$\alpha>0$, nonnegative functions $g\in L^{p'}(\Omega)$ and
$h\in L^1(\Omega)$, and one
null set outside which, for all $\xi,\eta\in\mathbb R^d$,
$$|a(x,\xi)|\le C\bigl(g(x)+|\xi|^{p-1}\bigr),\qquad a(x,\xi)\cdot\xi\ge\alpha|\xi|^p-h(x),$$
$$\bigl(a(x,\xi)-a(x,\eta)\bigr)\cdot(\xi-\eta)\ge0.$$
The induced operator $A:V\to V^*$ is
$$\langle A(v),w\rangle_{V^*,V} =\int_\Omega a(x,\nabla v(x))\cdot\nabla w(x)\,dx.$$
The growth bound and Hölder's inequality make this pairing finite and give
$\|A(v)\|_{V^*}\le C_1(\|g\|_{p'}+\|v\|_V^{p-1})$ for a constant $C_1$.
For the finite-dimensional existence result below we additionally require
that this induced map $A:V\to V^*$ is norm-continuous; this is verified
directly for the p-Laplacian in the companion example.

For $f\in L^{p'}(0,T;V^*)$, a weak evolution solution is a function
$u\in W_p(0,T;V)\cap L^\infty(0,T;H)$ with a continuous $H$ representative
such that $u'+A(u)=f$ in $L^{p'}(0,T;V^*)$ and $u(0)=u_0\in H$.

Let $V$ be a separable reflexive real Banach space, let $H$ be a real Hilbert
space, and let $i:V\to H$ be an injective continuous linear map with dense
range. Let $V^*$ be the continuous real dual of $V$ and write
$\langle\cdot,\cdot\rangle_{V^*,V}$ for its pairing with $V$. The canonical
map $J:H\to V^*$ is
$$J h(v)=(h,iv)_H\qquad(h\in H,\ v\in V).$$
It is continuous because $|Jh(v)|\le \|h\|_H\|i\|\|v\|_V$, and injective
because $i(V)$ is dense in $H$. A triple $(V,H,J)$ with these properties is
a **Banach evolution triple**. If $V$ is Hilbert, this is the real evolution
triple of [[def-parabolic-evolution-triple-and-energy-space]].

For $1<p<\infty$, $L^p(0,T;V)$ denotes the Bochner space of strongly
measurable $V$-valued functions with finite $p$th power norm, and
$p'=p/(p-1)$. For $u\in L^p(0,T;V)$ and $g\in L^{p'}(0,T;V^*)$, say
$g=u'$ in the distributional time sense if
$$\int_0^T (iu(t),iv)_H\,\phi'(t)\,dt =-\int_0^T\langle g(t),v\rangle_{V^*,V}\,\phi(t)\,dt$$
for every $v\in V$ and $\phi\in C_c^\infty(0,T)$. Define
$$W_p(0,T;V)=\{u\in L^p(0,T;V):u'\in L^{p'}(0,T;V^*)\}.$$
This definition assigns no endpoint values; a separate chain-rule theorem is
needed before evaluating a function in this space at an endpoint.

The **Axiom of Countable Choice**, written $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$, is the following
statement.

> For every family $(X_n)_{n \in \mathbb{N}}$ of nonempty sets indexed by
> $\mathbb{N}$ there is a function $f$ with domain $\mathbb{N}$ such that
> $f(n) \in X_n$ for every $n \in \mathbb{N}$.

Equivalently, in the vocabulary of [[def-choice-function]]: every at most
countable family of nonempty sets ([[def-countable]]) has a choice function.

The **Axiom of Choice** (AC) is the following statement.

> Every family of nonempty sets has a choice function
> ([[def-choice-function]]).

Written out: for every set $\mathcal{F}$ all of whose members are nonempty,
there exists a function $g$ with domain $\mathcal{F}$ satisfying $g(S) \in S$ for
all $S \in \mathcal{F}$.

An equivalent formulation is that a product of nonempty sets is nonempty: if
$X_i \ne \emptyset$ for every $i \in I$, then $\prod_{i \in I} X_i \ne \emptyset$.
Here $\prod_{i \in I} X_i$ is the set of functions $f$ with domain $I$ such that
$f(i) \in X_i$ for every $i \in I$; when a family of nonempty sets is indexed by
itself, such an $f$ is precisely a choice function for it.

derivations.claim: The nodal system in [F1] has an invertible interior mass matrix whenever $V_h\ne\{0\}$; if $V_h=\{0\}$, set $P_hf=0$. For finite $r$, every basis function is bounded by a mesh-independent constant and is supported on the cells incident to its node. Hölder and the coefficient scaling in [F1] therefore give, for $b_i=h^{-d}\int_\Omega f\phi_i$, $$ |b_i|^r\le C h^{-d}\int_{\operatorname{supp}\phi_i}|f|^r, \qquad \|b\|_{\ell^r}\le Ch^{-d/r}\|f\|_{L^r(\Omega)}. $$ The second inequality follows because on each cell only the fixed number $N(d,k)$ of local basis supports occur, so their overlap is bounded. For $r=\infty$, $\|b\|_{\ell^\infty}\le C\|f\|_\infty$.

For $d=1$, the explicit meshes of $\Omega=(0,1)$ are $K_j=[j/N,(j+1)/N]$, $0\le j<N$. They meet at whole endpoints, $h_N=1/N$, each inradius is $1/(2N)$, their shape ratio is $2$, and $\theta=1$; hence $h_N\to0$. For $d\ge2$, in every grid cube $a+[0,1/N]^d$, take the $d!$ simplices with cumulative vertices $$ a,\quad a+N^{-1}e_{\pi_1},\quad a+N^{-1}(e_{\pi_1}+e_{\pi_2}),\quad\ldots,\quad a+N^{-1}\sum_{j=1}^de_j $$ for permutations $\pi$ of $\{1,\ldots,d\}$. In coordinates $t=N(x-a)$ each is $1\ge t_{\pi_1}\ge\cdots\ge t_{\pi_d}\ge0$. Sorting coordinates covers the cube and strict orderings have disjoint interiors. For a permutation $\pi$, the barycentric gaps are $g_0=1-t_{\pi_1}$, $g_j=t_{\pi_j}-t_{\pi_{j+1}}$ for $1\le j<d$, and $g_d=t_{\pi_d}$; the simplex is $g_j\ge0$, $\sum_jg_j=1$. For two permutations, every pair of coordinates ordered oppositely must be equal in their intersection. In either order chain, that equality forces every intervening coordinate equal, hence sets the corresponding consecutive barycentric gaps to zero. The resulting equality blocks have the same relative order in both permutations: otherwise a pair of blocks would be oppositely ordered and would have been merged by an inversion equality. Thus the intersection is exactly the face obtained by setting those gaps to zero, so the within-cube triangulation is matching. On a cube face, coordinates fixed to $1$ occur first and those fixed to $0$ occur last in every compatible ordering; the induced ordering of the remaining coordinates is identical from either adjacent cube. Thus the global simplices meet only in whole faces and form a matching mesh.

If $V_h=\{0\}$, then $P_hf=0$ and the $L^r$ bounds are immediate. Otherwise, if $c$ is the coefficient vector of $P_hf$, then $A_hc=b$. Let $D=A_h^{-1}$, and let $R,C_0$ bound its absolute row and column sums from [F1]. For $1\le r<\infty$, weighted Jensen gives $$ \sum_i\Big|\sum_jD_{ij}b_j\Big|^r \le R^{r-1}\sum_{i,j}|D_{ij}|\,|b_j|^r \le R^{r-1}C_0\sum_j|b_j|^r. $$ For $r=\infty$, the row-sum bound gives $\|Db\|_{\ell^\infty}\le R\|b\|_{\ell^\infty}$. Combining these coefficient estimates with [F1] proves the asserted $L^r$ bound for $P_h$. If $f\in L^2$, the mass equations are exactly orthogonality to $V_h$, so $P_h$ is the orthogonal projection and fixes every $w_h\in V_h$.

Each cube simplex contains opposite cube corners and lies in its cube, so its diameter is $h_N=\sqrt d/N$. In row order $\pi_1,\ldots,\pi_d$, the cumulative-vertex edge matrix has columns $e_{\pi_1},e_{\pi_1}+e_{\pi_2},\ldots,\sum_{j=1}^de_{\pi_j}$ before scaling by $1/N$. Subtracting each preceding column from the next gives the permuted identity matrix, so its determinant has absolute value $N^{-d}$; the simplex volume is $1/(d!N^d)$. Its facets in ordered coordinates are $t_{\pi_1}=1$, $t_{\pi_d}=0$, and $t_{\pi_j}=t_{\pi_{j+1}}$. Put $r=1/(2+(d-1)\sqrt2)$ and set $t_{\pi_j}=r+(d-j)\sqrt2r$. The endpoint gaps are $r$ and successive coordinate gaps are $\sqrt2r$, so this point is at perpendicular distance $r$ from every facet and is the center of an inscribed ball of radius $r$. For any inscribed ball of radius $s$, its center must have endpoint gaps at least $s$ and successive coordinate gaps at least $\sqrt2s$; adding these gaps gives $1\ge2s+(d-1)\sqrt2s$. Thus the inradius is exactly $r/N$ and the shape ratio is $\sqrt d(2+(d-1)\sqrt2)$, independent of $N$, all cell diameters equal $h_N$ (global quasi-uniformity with $\theta=1$), and only the $d!$ ordered shapes occur. The cube is a bounded Lipschitz polyhedral open set. At a boundary point choose a vector $v$ with $n_j\cdot v>0$ for each active inward face normal $n_j$, and write nearby points as $z+y+sv$ with $y\perp v$. The active inequalities become $s>-n_j\cdot y/(n_j\cdot v)$; inactive face inequalities remain strict in a sufficiently small neighborhood. Thus locally the cube is the epigraph of the maximum of finitely many affine functions, which is Lipschitz. These are nonempty mesh families satisfying the $d\ge2$ hypotheses.

Fix $1<p<\infty$ and $v\in W_0^{1,p}(\Omega)$. For sufficiently fine meshes, since $P_hQ_hv=Q_hv$, the inverse inequality in [F3] and the $L^p$ bound from step 2.1 give $$ \|
abla P_hv\|_p \le \|
abla Q_hv\|_p+C h^{-1}\|P_h(v-Q_hv)\|_p \le \|
abla Q_hv\|_p+C h^{-1}\|v-Q_hv\|_p \le C_p\|
abla v\|_p, $$ by [F2]. The inverse estimate holds on the interval branch as recorded in [F3]; on simplex meshes summing its cell estimates uses $h_K\ge	heta h$. A sequence with $h	o0$ has only finitely many coarser initial meshes. On each such mesh, $P_h$ is finite rank and its coefficient functionals $v\mapsto\int_\Omega v\phi_i$ are bounded on $L^p$; hence its $W^{1,p}$ output norm is bounded by a mesh-dependent multiple of $\|v\|_{L^p}$ by [F8]. Poincaré [F7] bounds this by a multiple of $\|
abla v\|_p$. Enlarging $C_p$ over the finitely many initial meshes gives the stated uniform estimate.

Step 2.1 and the approximation estimate of [F2] show $\|P_hv-v\|_p\le C h\|\nabla v\|_p$. For gradients, write $P_hv-v=P_h(v-Q_hv)+(Q_hv-v)$. Apply the uniform gradient bound proved in the preceding step to $v-Q_hv\in W_0^{1,p}$ and the strong approximation in [F2]; both gradient terms tend to zero. Hence $P_hv\to v$ in the full $W^{1,p}$ norm.

Let $\psi\in C_c^\infty(\Omega)$. Since $Q_h\psi\in V_h$ and $P_hQ_h\psi=Q_h\psi$, the $L^2$ bound in step 2.1 gives $$ \|P_h\psi-\psi\|_2 \le\|P_h(\psi-Q_h\psi)\|_2+\|Q_h\psi-\psi\|_2 \le(C_2+1)\|Q_h\psi-\psi\|_{W^{1,2}}\longrightarrow0 $$ by [F2]. For arbitrary $f\in L^2(\Omega)$, choose $\psi\in C_c^\infty(\Omega)$ with $\|f-\psi\|_2<\varepsilon$ using [F5]. The $L^2$ orthogonal projection is a contraction, so $$ \limsup_{h\to0}\|P_hf-f\|_2\le2\varepsilon. $$ Letting $\varepsilon\downarrow0$ proves strong $L^2$ convergence for every $f\in L^2(\Omega)$.

On each explicit mesh family, $V_h\subset V$: [F4] proves this for matching simplices and the interval membership argument is part of [F2]. The preceding estimates give the $H$-orthogonal projectors, uniform $V$-stability, and strong $V$ approximation; pair the spatial index $N$ with any time partitions whose maximum steps tend to zero. The resulting family satisfies all clauses of [F6], with no coupling between spatial and time refinement.

In the PE12 branch, [A2], [F7], [F9], [F10], and [F11] give the evolution triple with dense continuous compact inclusion. The explicit stable families from step 6.1 therefore instantiate the stated PE12 application for every strict $p$ in the Statement.
